tools.name: asset
tools.description:
RETIRED IN FULL 2026-08-09. This tool writes nothing. Assets are created, read and moved
through the unreal_gc_ verbs now, and every operation answers by name with the call that
replaced it.

Where the work went:
  create              unreal_gc_apply create:true with a whole document. The header states
      the kind and `parent:` states what it derives from, so identity and inheritance are
      lines in the text rather than arguments here. Kinds: blueprint, widget_blueprint,
      animation_blueprint, blueprint_interface, blueprint_function_library,
      blueprint_macro_library, material, material_instance, material_function, data_asset,
      data_table, curve_float, curve_vector, curve_linear_color, user_enum, user_struct.
      Ask unreal_gc_describe kind:"<token>" for what one requires.
  delete/duplicate/rename/move   unreal_gc_asset mode:"<that word>"
  list_assets         unreal_gc_search kind:"asset"
  get_asset_info      unreal_gc_read, or unreal_gc_describe for the grammar
  set_asset_property  unreal_gc_apply with the block that owns the field
  reimport            unreal_gc_import (plan, then import)
  save_asset          nothing replaces it. Every unreal_gc_ verb that writes now saves what
      it wrote, each taking save:false to leave the asset dirty on purpose.

Two facts this card carried that outlive the operation. actor_blueprint and
object_blueprint were create's own conveniences, which defaulted a parent; they are not .gc
kinds, so a document states kind:blueprint and its own parent:. And an EDITOR UTILITY WIDGET
is kind:widget_blueprint with a parent deriving from /Script/Blutility.EditorUtilityWidget —
greenfield notices that parent and switches factory and asset class, so it produces a real
UEditorUtilityWidgetBlueprint, the one the Content Browser's Run action and
EditorUtilitySubsystem::SpawnAndRegisterTab are typed on. That is a different asset CLASS
from a plain widget, reached here through a parenting choice.

parameters.description: ALL TEN OPERATIONS ARE RETIRED. Each answers by name with its successor: create -> unreal_gc_apply create:true with a whole document whose header states the kind; delete/duplicate/rename/move -> unreal_gc_asset mode:"<that word>"; list_assets -> unreal_gc_search kind:"asset"; get_asset_info -> unreal_gc_read or unreal_gc_describe; set_asset_property -> unreal_gc_apply with the block that owns the field; reimport -> unreal_gc_import; and save_asset has NO successor, because every unreal_gc_ verb that writes now saves what it wrote.

- class_filter (NOT 'asset_type'): Asset class, e.g., 'StaticMesh', 'Blueprint'

tools.name: blueprint_modify
tools.description:
RETIRED 2026-08-09. Blueprint authoring is unreal_gc_apply, and every operation this tool used to dispatch answers by name with the call that replaced it.

Where the work went:
  declarations       unreal_gc_apply block:"properties" - the whole variable list, in one call and one compile. Adds, removals, renames and edits together; a rename keeps the variable's GUID, and a removal reports every node it orphans.
  functions, macros  unreal_gc_apply block:"functions" / block:"macros", signature and body in one statement, with the entry specifiers on the declaration line.
  nodes and wiring   unreal_gc_apply block:"graph" with graph_name. The block is the WHOLE graph, so nodes, wires, pin literals and comments land in a single write.
  descriptions       unreal_gc_apply block:"settings" for the asset's own description and display name; per-declaration metadata rides the functions/macros entry line.
  layout             unreal_gc_render mode:"layout", the one gc_render mode that writes.
  new Blueprints     unreal_gc_apply create:true with a whole document. An Interface, a Function Library and a Macro Library are the same call under their own kind: - blueprint_interface parents to /Script/CoreUObject.Interface, blueprint_function_library to /Script/Engine.BlueprintFunctionLibrary exactly, and blueprint_macro_library to an ordinary Actor class.

Read with unreal_gc_read first and send the block back carrying the sig: it came with. The write saves the asset itself.

tools.description:
Look up Blueprint-callable identities and their indexed metadata: functions, macros, casts, operators, enums (and their entries), structs (and their members). Use exact=true when you already have a canonical identity; use gc_search kind:"node" for a natural-language description of what a node should do.
Returns EXACT pin names and types, not display labels - the output is directly usable in IR.
Operators resolve both ways: '+' and 'Add_VectorVector' both hit.
Blueprint-authored enum entries and struct members are shown by their editor labels, with the mangled internal name (NewEnumerator3, MemberName_2_GUID) reported alongside. It does not make fuzzy spelling guesses or silently choose a result.

tools.name: bp_search_nodes
tools.description:
Search for ADDABLE Blueprint nodes by what they are called or what they do. Unlike bp_find's identity lookup, this tokenizes natural phrases and searches Unreal's palette title, keywords, category, exact pin signature, and tooltip/description.
Pass query for one search or queries for a batch of up to 8. Results contain writable op/canonical identities and describe_ir, a one-node fragment ready for gc_describe block:"graph" ir:. This is lexical Unreal-metadata search, not an embedding guess. Each result carries matched_terms - why THAT one ranked - and each search carries unmatched_terms, every query word that matched nothing in the whole index. The second is computed BEFORE the result cap, so a word that only matched page two is not reported as a miss. Every reply also reports total_matches, returned, offset, truncated and next_offset, and no result is silently selected for you.
Workflow: bp_search_nodes -> gc_describe block:"graph" -> gc_apply block:"graph" dry_run:true -> gc_apply. Only the first step is this family; the node-level describe and apply are retired and gc_* is the route.

tools.name: export_world_snapshot
tools.description:
Project the live world to a `.gcp` text file and return where it went. This is the read
direction for runtime state - what an actor's properties ARE right now - as opposed to
gc_read, which reads the asset that decides what they start as.

It writes a file and returns its path; the text is not inlined, because a snapshot can be
any size and the file is what you diff. Read it, or diff two of them.

`.gcp` is NOT a `.gc`. It names no asset, carries no sig:, and there is no way back in -
gc_apply refuses the extension. It lands under Saved/GraphCode/snapshots, which is already
gitignored, because a snapshot holds whatever the game holds.

select is MANDATORY and there is no default. 'everything in the world' produces a file
whose diff cannot be read, so '*' exists, is opt-in, and warns. The forms:
  class:BP_Door          the class AND its subclasses; each actor's own class is written
                         on its line, so a subclass match is visible rather than silent
  name:PlayerCharacter   actor name or editor label
  tag:Interactable       actor tag
  near:PlayerCharacter,500   within 500 uu of that actor; a missing anchor is an error,
                         not a silent empty match
  *                      everything, warned
Selectors union. found: and select: are both echoed into the header so a typo reads as
'looked for BP_Door, found none' rather than as 'nothing happened'.

Two snapshots of an UNCHANGED world differ in exactly one line - `at:`, the frame and time
- and that is deliberate: everything volatile is isolated there so a real change is the
only other thing a diff can show. body_digest in this result covers the body alone, so
'did anything change' is a string comparison and not an eyeball.

Whole-file diff is valid WITHIN one session. Across sessions it is not: spawn numbering and
PIE prefixes move independently of anything the game did. Across two files with different
pie: values, compare a named property of a named actor, never the files.

IT CAPTURES THE EDITOR WORLD BY DEFAULT, EVEN WHILE PIE IS RUNNING, and says so in
warnings rather than quietly answering a different question than you asked. world:'play'
is the running game - the state gc_play mode:"apply" can put back, and the only one that
moves.

parameters.name: select
parameters.description: One or more selectors: class:<Class>, name:<NameOrLabel>, tag:<Tag>, near:<Actor>,<Radius>, or '*'. Required - there is no default. A single string is accepted for one selector.

parameters.name: precision
parameters.description: Quantisation for every exported float, powers of ten from 1 down to 0.000001. The default reads 'did the door open'; 0.0001 is the physics-jitter setting and 1 is the 'only changes a player would notice' setting. A non-power-of-ten is refused with the nearest legal value named, never snapped silently, and the value used is written into the header - two files are only comparable when it matches.

parameters.name: properties
parameters.description: 'visible' (the default) writes what a graph or a designer can see, plus the transform. 'all' writes everything reflected - for a human chasing one mystery, not for a test: it buries the changed line in engine bookkeeping. Transient, deprecated and editor-only state is dropped either way, and omits: in the header names what was dropped.

parameters.name: show
parameters.description: Property names to surface WHEN THEY DIFFER, past the rules that would have hidden them - the setting between 'visible' and 'all'. show:['Velocity'] answers 'what is moving' without the 2,915 lines properties:'all' returns. Lifts transient, deprecated, editor-only and non-visible for that name; the at-default rule still applies, so a resting actor writes no line and that absence MEANS at rest. Echoed as `shows:`.

parameters.name: always
parameters.description: Property names to write unconditionally, differing or not - the same names as `show`, asking the other question. `show` is the reading for a DIFF ('what moved'); `always` is the reading for a REPORT ('the velocity of every actor, including the zeros'), where the line cannot go missing so the file can be read as a table. Beats every rule including at-default, and beats `show` when a name is in both. Echoed as `always:`. For both parameters the match is on the WHOLE property name, never a substring - 'Velocity' does not pick up 'LinearVelocity' or 'AngularVelocity' - and is case-INSENSITIVE, because these are FNames and FName comparison folds case, so 'velocity' works. It applies to actors and components alike, and a name nothing in the world had warns rather than passing silently.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: File leaf, without the extension. Reused names overwrite, which is what makes name:'before' and name:'after' work. Defaults to a UTC timestamp so an unnamed capture never destroys the one you were about to diff against.

parameters.name: world
parameters.description: 'editor' (the default) or 'play'. The editor world is the level as authored - it does not move while the game runs, and it is what every capture read before this parameter existed. 'play' is the PIE world: what the game has actually done since Play was pressed, and the state a `gc_play` apply restores into. It refuses when nothing is playing rather than falling back, because the two worlds are copies of each other and the wrong one looks entirely plausible. Both write world: as the EDITOR map path, with the PIE instance as a separate pie: attribute, so an editor capture and a play capture of one map are comparable instead of differing on every line.

tools.name: gc_apply
tools.description:
WRITES a `.gc` back into the asset it was projected from. This is the direction that
closes the loop.

EDIT THE FILE ON DISK AND APPLY IT. DO NOT ECHO A DOCUMENT BACK. The `.gc` beside the
asset IS the document: change the lines you mean in that file with an ordinary text edit,
then call this with asset_path ALONE - no block:, no ir:. Every block is compared against
a fresh projection and ONLY THE ONES WHOSE TEXT CHANGED are written; an untouched block is
not applied and not recompiled, so the file route costs what your edit costs rather than
what the document weighs. Re-sending a document you have just read is the same write with
the whole file paid for twice - once to read it and once to say it back - and on a graph
block it is worse than costly: applying a block REBUILDS every graph in it, and a rebuild
can settle state the `.gc` does not show.

block: + ir: IS FOR TEXT YOU ARE COMPOSING, not for a file that already exists - a block
written from nothing, or one changed where there is no sidecar to edit (source:"live").
EDITING ONE GRAPH OF MANY IS graph_name: ON THE FILE ROUTE, not a hand-echoed block: the
file may carry every graph the asset has, because a projection of it does, and the ones
you did not name are read and left untouched.

IT ALSO MAKES ASSETS THAT DO NOT EXIST YET. There is no separate create tool and you do
not have to know in advance which one you need: write a .gc at the sidecar path and call
this with create:true and no block/ir. Without create:true an empty path is not an error -
the create is planned, PROVEN on a throwaway scratch asset, and reported as would_create
with the kind and the parent it resolved, so a mistyped path tells you rather than
silently building the wrong thing. See the create parameter.

AND IT WRITES A LEVEL'S REGIONS. A payload whose header is `gcw 1` is a level's authored
region file, not a block of an asset, and routes to the .gcw beside that level's .gc:
asset_path names the LEVEL and the document names itself, so there is no kind: to pass
and no block:.

AND A `gcmove 1` PAYLOAD IS A MOTION PROGRAM - GraphCode Move's authored animation, routed by
its header exactly as a `gcshape 1` payload is (below), and it BUILDS animation sequences.
The header needs `skeleton:` - a bone name means nothing without a rig - beside `into:` and
`fps:`; `build { }` holds one line per asset (`A_Walk = $Walk [loop]`, also `[root_motion]`,
`[fps=N]` and `[settle=seconds]`), then `Name = clip(frames=N) { ... }` entries, frames=N being N frames and N+1
stored samples. `swing(<bone>, axis=X|-Y|(x,y,z), by=...)` turns a bone in its own space, and
`CR_JointLimits = constraints()` emits a stock Control Rig from declared ik_rig joint limits.
Wire it after runtime IK; it warns on undefined joints, protects manual edits, and exposes
GC_JointLimitExcess curves. Limiting joints can leave unreachable contact/aim goals unmet.
`clip(gravity=true, collision=$Floor)` bakes native physics; `constraints(gravity=true,
collision=world)` emits native live physics. The character's Physics Asset supplies defaults;
physics_profile=Name is an optional Physical Animation override. `contact(body,on=$Floor,
weight=...)` acquires support using that body's position drive. `physics(body|$Bones,
weight=...)` releases animation drives: 0 preserves following, 1 yields to physics. It takes
a scalar profile or literal percentage and preserves joints/collision. Generated rigs read
GC_PhysicsWeight_<bone> curves. No AnimBP is generated. See Guides/MOVE-PHYSICS.md.
`constraints(collision=world, contacts=($Heel,$Toe,...))` also emits final world-contact
queries and limb correction using named controls: rig contacts, with limits reapplied.
Optional channel=Visibility, up=+Z, slope=45 degrees, tolerance=0.1 cm, iterations=16.
align=surface opts into signed standing-contact placement and terrain-frame rotation;
align=none (default) retains upward-only clearance. Surface alignment preserves incoming
foot roll, requires one locally planar support, and reports GC_GroundValid_<chain>,
GC_GroundError_<chain> in cm and GC_GroundAngle_<chain> in degrees after joint limits.
All selected chains are active whenever the rig runs: host-gate it for stance. No gait
inference, retained platform anchor or additional body adjustment. constraints(from=...) is not
supported. See Guides/SURFACE-ALIGNMENT.md for calibration, composition and final checks.
GC_GroundPenetration reports residual cm and GC_GroundMissing reports absent support;
both warn when unresolved. Contact samples do not cover all skin or anticipate a step.
lines on one bone STACK. by= is degrees: a number holds a pose, and a declared
`Name = profile(0.0 = -22, 0.5 = 18, loop=true)` read as by=$Name varies it over the clip, a
loop wrapping through its seam; `[phase=0.3]` on the line delays it, which is what makes four
legs a gait. `clip(source=/Game/.../A_Walk)` starts from native AnimSequence bone motion and
float curves on the same skeleton; omit frames= to retain its duration at the document fps.
Events, markers and custom attributes are not copied. `from=` and `source=` are exclusive.
`Limp = clip(from=$Walk) { ... }` starts from another clip's motion and keeps its
length unless it states frames=; its own lines stack on top, a second axis on a bone included.
`Tail = bones(a, b, c)` is a group one line moves: `swing($Tail, axis=Z, by=(50, tail_01=30))
[phase=(0, tail_03=0.2)]` gives every bone 50 and tail_01 30, and the phase works the same way.
`shift(<bone>, axis=, by=<cm>)` moves a bone along its own axis. Like a .gcshape it
rebuilds only an asset it made and refuses one EDITED since, it leaves its program at
asset_path as a .gcmove, and each built clip's .gc names it on a `move:` line beside
`omits: bone_animation`. dry_run:true plans every build line and writes nothing.
Needs GraphCode Move; without it the call refuses naming the product.

AND A `gcshape 1` PAYLOAD IS A SHAPE PROGRAM, which is the sixth product and its own file.
A .gcshape is DECLARATIVE where a .gc is reflective: nothing exists until it runs, so it
names no asset and takes no kind: and no block:. Its own `build { }` block says which
assets it makes, one line each, and `into:` says where they go. asset_path is the DOCUMENT'S
OWN ADDRESS: nothing resolves or loads it, and each asset records it as the .gcshape that
made it, so a `kind:static_mesh` .gc can say where its geometry came from.
Needs GraphCode Shape; without it the call refuses by naming the product, never silently.
dry_run:true evaluates the whole program - every shape, every triangle - and writes nothing,
and it PRICES A REBUILD: whatever a real run would refuse, the dry run refuses first.
IT REBUILDS OVER AN ASSET IT MADE AND NOTHING ELSE. Each built asset carries the .gcshape,
a digest of the program and the shape it came out as, so edit the file and send it again -
an untouched asset is rebuilt in place, keeping whatever material each slot wears. Refused
by name in three cases and each says which: the asset has been EDITED since it was built
(rebuilding would destroy that silently - delete it, or carry the edit back into the file);
NOTHING CLAIMS IT, so it was imported or made by hand and is never ours to write over; or
the question cannot be answered at all, which says so rather than claiming a difference.
EVERY ONE OF THE GRAMMAR'S SIX GROUPS IS BUILT, so a word that is not here is a spelling
mistake rather than a milestone. The direct mesh start `polyhedron`; the outlines `circle`
`rect` `arc` `points` `curve` - the
last two taking `loop=true` to close them, which is what `polygon` used to be, and `polygon`
itself is now refused by name; `round` and `widen` on an outline; the depth instructions
`extrude` `revolve` `sweep` `fill` `loft` - and `sweep` of an OPEN section is the vertical
RIBBON, a surface standing along the path, so a wall that follows a road is
`points((0,0), (0,300)) sweep(along=$Road)`: the section's own +y is UP and its +x is across
the path, and a cap there is refused because an open line encloses no area to close;
a profile anywhere a number goes; `add` `subtract`
`intersect`, placed by `at=` with `against()` `center()` `on()` `under()`, `align=`, `rotate=`
and `scale=`; group 4's `taper` `bend` `roughen` `weather` `round` `shell` `cut` `trim` `fracture`
`place` `resize`; and group 6's
For bend, optional fixed=base keeps material below at-extent along along= unchanged,
curves through the declared interval, and rotates the distal remainder rigidly.
Omission or fixed=none keeps the existing bidirectional bend.
`material($Slot)` and `uv(keep|auto|box|cylinder|plane|none, at=, facing=, up=, scale=, offset=)`,
which writes CHANNEL 0 only. The named frame arguments belong to box/cylinder/plane: at= is the
local origin, facing= frame +Z, up= frame +X, scale= physical cm per tile (plane (u,v), box
(x,y,z), cylinder (around,along)), and offset=(u,v) tile phase. Defaults keep the old
bounds-centred identity frame; keep/auto/none refuse projection arguments. All aimed by the `[ ]` modifiers - `top` `bottom` `side` `cut` and their `!` forms, `rim`
`sharp` and `border=$Patch` for edges, `above=` and `below=` in centimetres, two in one bracket
meaning AND, and `fade=` on `taper` and `roughen` (a fade finer than the line's feature buys its
density only in the band it ramps across, 2026-11-18). A bracket that selects nothing refuses rather
than doing nothing, and `trim()` with no bracket at all refuses - it is the one instruction whose
empty form would delete the shape.
THE THREE EDGE WORDS ANSWER THREE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS AND ONE BRACKET TAKES ONE OF THEM: `rim` is
where the SHAPE stops, `sharp` (split by `concave`/`convex`) is where it FOLDS, and
`border=$Patch` is where a saved REGION stops - the edge word for a CLOSED solid, which has no rim
at all, so `round(2.0) [border=$Panel]` bevels a patch with no lip of its own.
AND AN EDGE BRACKET MAKES `save()` ANSWER WITH A PATH, its third kind after a region and a point:
`save($Hem) [rim]` or `save($Edge) [border=$Patch]` gives back a plane()-kind value - the same
currency `$Edge = plane` captures - so `sweep(along=)` and `add(along=, repeat=)` take it with no
change, which is piping, a welt, a band round a hat or drips hung off a scalloped lip. A set of
edges has no order, so two things REFUSE naming the number: several separate runs (a shelled box
snapped open has an ANNULAR rim; a plate with two holes has three borders) and a junction where
three chosen edges meet. A path is a SNAPSHOT, so a `subtract()` below it cannot move it.
AND `save($Cores) [inside, scatter=24, apart=8.0, seed=]` PUTS N PLACES IN THE MIDDLE OF A
SOLID, which is the first kind of place that is not on a surface - seeds, bubbles, voids,
inclusions, and the points a break is built around. Points are drawn in the bounding box and
kept when they are inside, so a shortfall DROPS and is reported with both numbers, none landing
REFUSES, and an OPEN shape refuses counting its open edges - a winding number through a hole is
not an inside test. `scatter=24` -> `scatter=25` adds a place and leaves the first 24 alone.
`[inside, repeat=(4,3,2), jitter=30%]` is the OTHER arrangement: a LATTICE of cells over the
shape's own box, keeping the centres that are inside it. Here `repeat=` is x, y and z of the
box, which is not how an array reads that word (there the DIRECTIONS come from `step=`), and
`jitter=` is a fraction of the CELL - never a length, because how big a cell is, is decided by
`repeat=` and the shape. `apart=` belongs to a draw and `jitter=` to a lattice; each is refused
by name on the other.
AND `fracture(scatter=24) { ... }` BREAKS ONE SOLID INTO N REAL SEPARATE PIECES, which no other
verb can do - `cut` keeps one side, `subtract` removes, `roughen(form=faceted)` draws the
pattern without splitting. The cells are Voronoi, and WHICH ARRANGEMENT THE POINTS ARE IN IS
THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ROCK AND BLOCKS: a cell around a RANDOM point is an irregular chunk, so
`scatter=24` is rock and rubble; a cell around a point on a CUBIC LATTICE is exactly a cube, so
`repeat=(4,3,2)` is uniform blocks and `repeat=(4,3,2), jitter=30%` is cut stone and masonry.
`gap=` on a lattice is GROUT, so a tile floor and a brick wall come out of this verb rather
than a masonry feature. Its other words are all borrowed: `apart=` keeps DRAWN points from
clumping (large is uniform rubble, 0 is a natural break with a few big pieces), `seed=`,
`gap=<cm>` holds the pieces slightly apart, `scale=(x,y,z)` STRETCHES the pattern so flat gives
slabs and one axis gives splinters - only its RATIO is read, since how big a cell is, is
decided by how many there are - and `from=$Cores` breaks around a saved point set instead.
Exactly ONE of `scatter=` / `repeat=` / `from=`; two is refused as an arrangement stated twice.
THE BRACES RUN ONCE FOR EACH PIECE, WITH THAT PIECE AS THE SUBJECT, which is NOT what braces
mean anywhere else: a `taper()` inside tapers THAT piece. Largest first. A `fracture()` inside
the body breaks each piece again, so recursion costs no argument, and `roughen(by=2.0,
scale=8.0, form=faceted) [cut]` inside it weathers the break faces and leaves the outside alone
- a Voronoi face is perfectly FLAT, which reads as diced rather than broken, so this is the
biggest visual difference available and it is free. The pieces come back as ONE mesh in N
components, which is what `parts` has always counted; there is no name for the set, because no
verb takes one. A body sees no names captured outside it, and `socket()` inside one is refused.
THE BODY CAN ASK WHERE ITS PIECE IS (agent-spelled 2026-11-18): `output.index` (largest first),
`output.count`, `output.place` (the piece's bounds centre) and `output.outward` (unit direction
from the break's centre, zero at it), with `.x` `.y` `.z` reading one number - so
`place(by=(output.outward.x * 3, output.outward.y * 3, 0))` explodes the pieces apart.
`[in=$Zone]` BREAKS ONLY WHAT IS INSIDE A SOLID ZONE (placed by `at=` etc. on the bracket): the
inside breaks exactly as a whole shape would, the outside comes back WHOLE as one more part, and
at the zone's boundary the outside wears a `cut` cap lying on the pieces' own caps.
`apart=` TAKES A PROFILE WHEN `to=` NAMES WHERE THE BREAK IS DENSEST, the impact (G7, 2026-11-19):
`fracture(scatter=80, apart=profile(0 = 12, 1 = 1.5), to=(100, 100, 0)) [in=$Crater]` is a crater,
fine at the hit and coarse at the rim. `t` is 1 at `to=` and 0 at the farthest point of what breaks,
NOT rescaled, so a target off the solid never reads the profile's `t = 1` end; a small value at
t = 1 means fine at the hit, and the reverse, `profile(0 = 1.5, 1 = 12)`, is a crumbling rim. The
profile is the LEAST spacing in cm and the shape of the density (points drawn as 1 / apart cubed);
the pieces' actual size follows `scatter=`. Two places keep the smaller of their two spacings.
Three differences from `displace(to=)`: the profile is on `apart=`, absolute lengths, not a 0..1
`slope=`; `t` starts at the farthest point, not a region's border; and `to=` is ONE point, `(x, y, z)`
in this entry's frame or a `$Name` holding one saved place (a mesh or a path is refused, for now).
`to=` also moves the centre `output.outward` is measured from to the impact, beside `from=` and a
constant `apart=` too. `save($S) [inside, scatter=, apart=profile(…), to=]` draws the same graded set.
AND `place(by=, rotate=, scale=, mirror=)` MOVES THE SHAPE THE ENTRY IS ALREADY STANDING ON,
which nothing else here does - every other `at=` places a thing being brought IN. So the move
is `by=(0,0,5)`, an AMOUNT and not a destination: `at=` is refused by name, because two lines
must stack and because inside a `fracture()` body - where this verb earns its keep, one run per
piece - a destination would move every piece's centre onto the SAME spot and collapse the
object into a heap. Three numbers, since one would be a diagonal rather than a lift.
`rotate=` and `scale=` act about the SUBJECT'S OWN CENTRE, which is not what they do on `add`
(there a part is built at the origin and has no position yet), or a piece 60 cm out would be
flung sideways by a 12-degree turn. `mirror=X|Y|Z` reflects it across its own centre plane.
ONE HAZARD, REPORTED RATHER THAN REFUSED: a build line's pivot defaults to `base`, so moving
the WHOLE shape is erased on the way to an asset unless that line says `[pivot=(0,0,0)]`, and the
build says so only for a build line's own entry. It survives where the entry is used as a
PART, and inside a `fracture()` body. `onto=`, `along=`
and `align=` are refused by name - they belong to something being brought in.
`resize(z=178)` fits the current mesh's measured Z span to 178 cm, scaling all three axes
uniformly. Name exactly one of x=, y= or z=, or write resize(125%) for a multiplier. Numeric
expressions work. pivot=center is the default; base, corner and (x,y,z) use the build-line
pivot vocabulary and keep that point fixed during scaling. The build-line pivot still runs
afterwards. A zero source span cannot acquire thickness. Resizing is whole-mesh only;
assembled sockets and follows anchors move with it, while plain saved coordinates stay snapshots.
AND A PART PUBLISHES THE NAMES IT DECLARED. `$output.Tip` is the most recent eligible part,
and `hand = add($Hand)` also publishes the durable instance-qualified `$hand.Tip`. The caller
of a part it
did not author cannot point at a place ON it - `[top]` after an add means the host's top AND
the part's, and a bounding box is not a surface - so the PART says: it writes
`save($Tip) [at=, project=]` inside itself and the caller reads `$output.Tip`. **The prefix
is a NAMESPACE**: a local `$Tip` and a part's `Tip` both stand and cannot collide, which a
flat capture could not manage. A dot continues a `$name` only when a LETTER follows it, so
`$Wide.5` is unchanged. ONE SPELLING, TWO FRAMES: inside a `{ }` body the part is not placed
yet so `$output.Tip` is its own space; after the line it is where the tip landed, having
ridden the placement exactly as the part's SOCKETS do. Only what the part DECLARED crosses,
never its working-out. A declared REGION crosses on an attribute layer rather than by stale
triangle ids, and is read normally as `[$hand.Crown]`; `[$hand]` still means all faces that
placement brought in. A cutter publishes nothing, and a repeat publishes no ambiguous single
variable name - write separately handled placement lines when each copy must be addressed.
AND A SAVED REGION MAY CARRY ITS OWN PROFILE RULER. `save($Band) [top, measure=$Axis,
start=20%, end=50%]` measures stations along the open directed plane() path `$Axis`; an inline
`measure=((x,y,z),(x,y,z))` is the same finite ruler without a separate entry. A socket
declared above the line is a natural ruler too: its origin is t=0, its own +Z points
toward the mesh's furthest positive projection, and that natural tip is t=1. All forms insert
both interval boundaries into crossed mesh edges and retain normalized t for a later
`raise(by=profile(0=0,1=8)) [$Band]`. Plain start/end numbers are centimetres of path arc
length; percentages are fractions of that PATH, not the mesh bounds, and the forms may mix.
The ruler is normalized first: start=20%, end=50% selects global t=0.2..0.5 and does not remap
that band to 0..1, so profiles keep one base-to-tip coordinate.
One field-bearing region is implicit; intersecting two different fields needs `field=$Band`
or refuses naming both. The ruler travels and transforms with `$hand.Band` / `$output.Band`.
Its normalized t rides later deformation as an ordinary per-vertex mesh weight; remesh and
blend rebuilds transfer it barycentrically from the nearest source triangle. A socket's
natural tip currently measures the whole mesh; active-subregion endpoints, reevaluation and
transverse coordinates are not implemented yet. `[above=]`/`[below=]` keep their Z cuts.
AND `add($Brick, repeat=240) { ... }` SHAPES THE PART ON ITS WAY IN - `subtract` and
`intersect` too, where it shapes the TOOL before it cuts. The body runs BEFORE the placement
and BEFORE the boolean with the incoming part as its subject, so a face word inside is THAT
PART'S and nothing of the host is in scope or reachable. That is not `[$n]`, which names the
faces only AFTER the union has welded and re-cut them. **`repeat=` is what it earns its keep
on: the body runs once per copy**, so 240 bricks can differ by any INSTRUCTION rather than
only by the parameters the brick's author declared - and the draws are keyed by the copy's
index, so 240 -> 241 rolls the new one and leaves the rest. Same rule as `fracture`: the
braces' subject is what the step brings into being. A body that leaves nothing of the part
is refused, and `socket()` inside one is refused.
A `material()` ENTRY IS A SLOT AND ITS PATH IS A FIRST-BUILD DEFAULT: the slot names and their
order are this file's, and what the asset WEARS stays kind:static_mesh's .gc. The header
carries `smooth:` (chord tolerance), `shade:` (the angle above which an edge shades hard) and

and `[bounds=(x,y,z)]` as a contract the finished mesh must fit, `*` freeing an axis.
AND ONE LINE MAKES MANY COPIES: `repeat=` up to three dimensions, spaced by `step=` (explicit,
growing from the placed copy) or `spread=` (fill an extent, centred on it); `turn=`+`around=` for

running bond. `onto=<direction>` casts the grid at the faces the `[ ]` bracket names and
`along=$Path` spaces by ARC LENGTH, both taking `orient=normal|tangent|keep`; `jitter=` and `seed=`
make it irregular - a jittered copy is keyed by its own index, so adding one re-rolls nothing
else, and a drawn ARGUMENT is keyed by this same seed (below). A projected line takes
no `at=` - the surface or the path decides - and a ray that hits nothing PLACES NOTHING, reported
rather than silent. Every copy measures the same pre-union shape, so an array cannot climb.
AND AN OUTLINE CAN CARRY A HOLE: group 5 combines OUTLINES while an entry is still flat -
in a `plane()` body always, and in a `mesh()` body until its depth instruction - so a wall
with a window is `rect() subtract($Window) extrude()` and the extrude cuts it in one pass.
`widen()` around a closed path is a ring. An outline is ONE boundary and its holes: a
boolean that leaves several disjoint pieces refuses naming the count, and `revolve` `sweep`
and `loft` each carry a cross-section of one loop and refuse a holed one.

`add($Brick, w=41.0)` at the call. Every parameter carries a DEFAULT, so `add($Brick)` always
builds, and a parameter may not shadow a top-level entry name. The arguments ride on `add`,
`subtract` and `intersect` only, and an argument no verb and no parameter claims is REFUSED by
name with the list of what that line does take - `add($Cap, ate=(0,0,100))` used to build and
put the cap at the origin.
A BARE `$Entry` IN A PARAMETER LIST TAKES THAT ENTRY'S PARAMETERS AS THIS ONE'S, WITH ITS DEFAULTS (K1,
2026-11-19), and every line that calls or brings in THAT entry receives each one it does not write, as

unwritten, including ones this body cannot honour, so PIN those by writing them on every calling line
(`origin=` above): a knob every calling line writes is not taken, and a caller passing it is refused.
`deep=$deep` passes a knob on and pins nothing. A name the list declares keeps the list's default; two

THE WRAPPER BUILDS, and every asset built from it, with no line of its file changing -
`gc_describe preset:` lists the whole list and marks what is inherited and what is overridden. Refused,

(`seed`, `scale`), and v1 a taken default that names something.
AND A NUMBER MAY BE DRAWN: `random(min = 10.0, max = 20.0)`, declared as an entry or written
inline anywhere a number goes. THE SEED IS THE SWITCH. With one - `random(seed = 30, min =,
max =)` - the draw is ABSOLUTE: the same number everywhere it is used, which is the only way
the format can say TWO PARTS MUST MATCH; neighbouring seeds (`seed = $s * 100 + output.index`)
draw unrelated numbers. ONE RE-ROLL, 2026-11-18: seeded draws re-rolled once because the seed is
now mixed (neighbouring seeds drew a near-linear ramp), and composing draws once because their
stream is keyed by the line's place in its entry (it was the file line, so any edit above an
entry re-rolled it); a file with no random() is unchanged, and a built asset changes only when
its recipe is built again.
Without one it COMPOSES with the `seed=` of the line
that brings its entry in, so two walls off one declared draw differ - and away from such a
line it is refused, because there is nothing to compose with. A composing draw on a
duplicating line makes EVERY COPY ITS OWN BUILD: `add($Brick, w=39.0, repeat=(20,12))` builds

Both ends are written, each a number or a `$name` reaching a NUMBER entry - nothing else, so a
draw inside a draw's bound cannot make a ring.
AND A NUMBER MAY BE ARITHMETIC: `w=$Base * 2`, `at=(2 * $Bay, 0, 0)`,

percentage written directly at a value site is untouched.

something asks for it and has no position in the file to read from.

and the `$` is which. A set reads what is above it, keeps the name's KIND, and takes effect from

SELECTING one there is still refused, because a bracket on `add` names the faces an `onto=`

changes no geometry. `at=` takes a point, a fraction `(92%, 0%, 50%)`, a relation, or `$Pin` naming

source-surface distance from that protected edge fades the
reconstruction weight smoothly from zero to full. This slice can resample protected topology/UVs; exact preservation

AND `snap=` SEATS AGAINST THE SURFACE RATHER THAN THE BOUNDING BOX. Every placement lines up two

`join=blend, falloff=` melts the two together - that last one REBUILDS THE WHOLE SHAPE from a

count climbs sharply. Use `fillet` when only the seam should soften.

the noise's shape and `faceted` is the only one that makes FLAT PLATES MEETING AT SHARP EDGES -

positional distance and nothing else.
AND THE ONE THAT SAYS WHERE TO END UP RATHER THAN HOW FAR IS
`conform(to=, by=, within=, mode=, gap=, project=)`:
each chosen vertex moves toward a target by a fraction of its OWN distance to it, so `by=` is a
PERCENTAGE and `by=100%` lands every one of them on the target whatever it started at, which no
single offset can do. `to=plane` derives the chosen faces' own median plane - that is `flatten`,
folded in rather than shipped as a second verb; `to=Z` with `at=` names a plane; `to=$Mesh` is
another shape's surface, which is a strap on a pipe or a nail on a fingertip. `within=<cm>` is an
all-or-nothing miss rule, `mode=push` is a scrape and `mode=pull` a fill, and a `plane()` entry is
refused because it is a PATH here. `gap=<cm>` is CONTACT AND HOW FAR OFF IT - `against(gap=)`'s
word and its sign, positive holding the landing clear of the target and negative sinking it in,
spent from where the vertex landed so `by=` stays a fraction of the way to the gapped surface.
`project=<direction>` sends EVERY vertex ONE way instead of to its own nearest point, which is a
second operation and not a convenience: nearest-point is a shrinkwrap and compresses a label or a
decal wherever the host curves away, while a projection keeps the footprint it had as seen along
the direction. A vertex whose line never meets the target stays put and is COUNTED in the note;
a line that lands none is refused. It refines only when `[smooth=]` asks, and REPORTS how far the
faces between the landed vertices still stand off - a coarse landing reads perfect otherwise -
NAMING the `[smooth=]` that would bring that under the header's own `smooth:`, and for a `mesh()`
target counting how many landings settled, stopped still moving, or kept the nearest point
because the cast along the shaded normal missed, which is the one that folds above a convex edge.
AND `pinch(to=, by=, within=)` IS THAT SAME SENTENCE ONE DIMENSION DOWN, and the TARGET chooses
between them: `conform` takes a SURFACE and moves vertices ONTO it, while `pinch` takes a CURVE (a
`plane()` entry) or a POINT and slides them ACROSS the surface toward it - a crease, a knuckle, a
fold, a tip. `by=` is a PERCENTAGE on both and a length is refused, and each refuses the other's
target by name, saying which verb wanted it.
AND A BRACKET AIMS AT MORE THAN FACE WORDS: `[material=$Stone]` takes the faces WEARING that paint
and `[!material=$Stone]` the rest, which is the way into a bought mesh whose only useful regions
are its material slots; `[facing=+Z]` takes faces pointing a way; `[in=$Tool]` takes a volume, and
with `along=` casts that volume's OUTLINE at the surface as a projected brush; `[!in=$Tool]` takes
everything outside it, so `trim() [!in=$Zone]` keeps the zone as an open panel for `shell()`;
`[smooth=<cm>]`
buys local detail, while `[topology=preserve|refine|adaptive]` grants connectivity permissions.
Preserve keeps connectivity, refine permits subdivision, adaptive also permits reduction and
reconnection. Generated meshes default adaptive; mesh('/Game/Part', topology=preserve) is the
import default. An operation override lasts that operation; a build-line override governs final
output. A budget cannot silently reduce preserve/refine geometry. Smooth on coat is supported.
`[smooth=<cm>]`
overrides how finely the line refines what it touches, which is the density knob `[triangles=]`
sets for a whole build line. A moving brush uses `[in=$Foot, along=$Path, project=-Z]` or
`[in=$Foot, from=(...), to=(...), project=-Z]`; the fixed `along=-Z` brush remains valid.
Stroke `scale=<profile>` varies footprint size, or `width=<profile>` sets its width in cm,
preserving proportions. Separately, raise/displace/roughen `by=<profile>`, relax's distance
profile and taper's `to=<profile>` read strength along projected path length. Overlap applies
once. `[$Patch=affected]` captures selected input faces before the operation so later
`[$Patch]` follows them after deformation. `save($Patch) [<selection>]` declares that region
without deforming or painting: the name is inside save(), the selection inside []. It names
faces in the current mesh; it does not save an asset to disk. See Docs/GC-SHAPE-STROKES.md.
AND `[$<handle>]` SELECTS THE FACES AN `add` BROUGHT IN: `nail = add($Nail, at=on())` then
`raise(by=0.2) [$nail, top]` lengthens the nail and nothing else - a handle already said WHERE a
copy went, and this extends it to WHICH. It is an ordinary region, so `[!$nail]` and `[$nail, top]`
compose for free, and a body's FIRST `add` names the whole shape. A `subtract`/`intersect` handle
keeps no faces (a carve makes `[cut]`) and neither does `join=blend`, which dissolves the boundary;
both are refused by name.
AND `save($Tip) [at=, project=, within=, up=]` NAMES A POINT RATHER THAN A REGION - one word, two
kinds of answer, and the bracket says which: selection words name FACES, while `project=` with no
`in=` casts a RAY and names a place on the surface and the way it faces. `at=` is where the ray
starts - coordinates, or three percentages of this shape's own bounds - `within=<cm>` is how far it
may look, and `up=` pins the second axis a normal cannot fix. FIRST HIT WINS AND A MISS IS AN
ERROR, never a quiet point at the origin that would seat a part inside the shape with every number
on the build line still reading perfect. A region goes in a BRACKET and a point in an ARGUMENT:
`add($Nail, at=$Tip)` translates by it, and `socket(..., at=$Tip)` takes the cast's own normal as
its facing unless `facing=` overrides it.
Reusable mesh edits: `Erode = instruction(depth=.25, grain=8) { roughen(by=$depth, scale=$grain, seed=7) }`,
then `$Erode(depth=.5) [top]` - declared like a mesh, called by its own name, and every
argument named. Calls share the current mesh, with private locals and
handles. The call region follows edited faces; inner selectors narrow it. Stroke coordinates
and size/strength profiles carry through nested calls. Export input faces with `[$Changed=affected]`.
Whole-mesh operations such as booleans/remesh need an unselected call; a region is never ignored.
Recipe imports support caller numbers, profiles, paths, captured regions/geometry and material
parameters. Materials use the caller's declared slots. Named draws need their own seed.
Presets includes `/GraphCodeShape/Presets/Surface` (Erode, FacetedWear) and `Damage` (CornerCrack).
Instruction entries are called in mesh bodies, not build targets; socket declarations stay in
the owning mesh body. See Docs/GC-SHAPE-INSTRUCTIONS.md.
AND A CALL EXPORTS ANY NAME THE RECIPE HOLDS: `[$v1 = <name>]` on the call reads that name back out
into the caller - a number, a position, a region, a point or a shape, every kind crosses - so a
recipe that MEASURES something can hand the measurement back rather than only changing the mesh. A
name the recipe never set reads as a zero. The `mesh()` half is refused by name: a part arrives
through a placement, and what an exported name would have to ride is not ruled yet.
AND AN EXISTING STATIC MESH IS AN ORDINARY OPERAND: `add(mesh('/Game/Scans/SM_Hand', lod=1))`.
`lod=` is an exact source-model LOD, default 0, with no render or Nanite fallback. Shape copies
the geometry, UVs and materials; the body may save regions, deform it and declare sockets, and a
build publishes a NEW asset without modifying or inventing construction parameters for the source.
AND A .gcshape MAY BRING ANOTHER IN: `Fixings = shape('/Game/Kits/Fixings')` - an ENTRY, so it goes
BELOW `build { }` with the other entries - and `$Fixings.HexNut` reaches inside. Nesting walks
(`$A.B.C`), an imported body resolves its own `$names` against ITS OWN file, and an argument
crossing the boundary is settled in the CALLER's scope first. v1 threads NUMBERS across a file,
not geometry.
AND THE BUILD REPORTS HOW THE PARTS ACTUALLY FIT, which no count could say: a part that does not
REACH what it is joined to is named with the gap in centimetres and the place, because placement
seats boxes and a curved or roughened surface is not its box; a `subtract` whose tool misses
entirely is named too, since it removes nothing and would otherwise report success; a part sunk
WHOLLY INSIDE the shape is named, contributing nothing; and each entry says how many of its own
PART PAIRS overlap, which is how most parts attach and is therefore a number to watch rather than
a fault. A loose `add` is held until the entry ENDS - assembling parts and then connecting them is
ordinary - and reported only if the finished shape really is in more than one piece.

AND THAT WRITE BUILDS WHAT THE LEVEL DERIVES. A .gcw's `terrains { }` programs run, its
`water { }` bodies go into the level, and its `populate { }` lines all raise what they
name: `pcg(...)` generators reconcile, `foliage(...)` lines plant, `audio(...)` lines put a
reverb zone in the room they name, `postprocess(...)` lines put a LOOK on one,
`triggervolume(...)` lines put a tagged trigger there, and `physicsvolume(...)` and
`killzvolume(...)` lines put a place where movement obeys different rules - or ends,
`spline(...)` lines put a RUN into the world as a real spline component on a plain actor -
`Patrol = spline(along=$Town.high, tags=(Route))` - which is how a course a region declares
becomes something a character, a spline mesh or PCG can read at runtime, and the actor is a
bare AActor so the level needs no GraphCode to load it, and a
line whose type is a CLASS PATH raises that class - any AVolume subclass, including one your
own project declares - with the properties that class declares, all as
part of the same write - the block appearing IS the build, so build and REBUILD are one act
and re-sending the document runs it again. There is no build: any more; it refuses by
naming this. Needs the level OPEN, and terrain and water need GraphCode World.
NAVIGATION IS THE EXCEPTION and it lives IN the file: put the line `build nav` in the
payload. Recast reads the level's COLLISION rather than the document, so nothing a block
says can tell when the mesh went stale - the .gc omits built_data by design. The line is an
operation: carried out, reported, then stripped from what lands on disk.

A GENERATED FOLIAGE LINE MAY FILTER THE GROUND ITS INSTANCE TRACE ACTUALLY HIT:
    Firs = foliage(types=(/Game/Foliage/FT_Fir), in=$Forest, seed=7) [all(not(inside=$Trail), height=(Max=1800), slope=(Max=28))]
Height is world Z in cm; slope is degrees from horizontal, with inclusive Min/Max bounds.
The sampler keeps each point's ordinal when a filter rejects it, so a new mask does not
renumber every hand-edited tree beyond it. Numeric ground tests and region exclusions
combine in all(...); a mixed numeric/region any(...) or not(...) is refused by name. PCG
and volume verbs still refuse these per-sample tests. A painted forest takes no filter.

A FOREST SOMEBODY PAINTED IS CAPTURED ON SAVE, NOT TYPED. Saving a level whose .gcw exists
puts every brush stroke no line owns into a file under /Game/_GraphCode/Foliage/<level>/ and
adds one line to `populate { }`:
    Painted_01 = foliage(source=file'/Game/_GraphCode/Foliage/Maps/M/Painted_01.gcfoliage')
The same verb, naming its file where a scatter names a palette, and nothing else: types=,
density=, seed=, a place, a band or a filter beside source= is refused, because the file
already holds every instance's type and transform. The next apply ADOPTS the painted trees
where they stand - it plants no second copy - and the line owns them from then on; deleting
the line removes the forest on the apply after. Only brush strokes are captured; a
procedural spawner's instances are its own to rebuild.

WHAT A HAND DID TO A FOREST A LINE OWNS IS `instances { }`, scattered or painted alike: one
entry per line and type, every number a DIFFERENCE from what the line computes, and each tree
named by its ORDINAL - its place in that type's own sequence:
    instances {
      Firs./Game/Foliage/FT_Pine = moved(13 -510 710 260) scaled(13 8.75 8.75 11.5) removed(4, 22)
    }
moved(i dx dy dz, ...), turned(i dpitch dyaw droll, ...) and scaled(i dx dy dz, ...) nudge a
tree; removed(i, ...) takes one away, by ordinal alone. A save writes what a hand did, and YOU
MAY WRITE ENTRIES TOO: removed(3) deletes exactly that tree on the next apply, and every other
ordinal keeps its tree. Deleting a term, or the whole block, puts those trees back where the
line says. A save writes a removal only for a type the level already holds some of, so a line
not applied yet is never recorded as erased. No read lists which ordinal stands where yet.

A REGION OWNS ITS POINTS AND EDGES AND NOTHING IS SHARED. Each room declares its own
corners and walls inside its braces, and THE ORDER OF THE WALLS IS THE RING - there is no
loop: line, and no way to write a region whose membership and whose ring disagree:
    regions {
      Hall = region(min=0, max=400, anchor=(600, 400), anchorZ=0) {
        p1 = (0, 0)      p2 = (1200, 0)
        p3 = (1200, 800) p4 = (0, 800)
        altar = (300, 200)  forward:180  # a landmark: a point NO wall runs through
        a = (200, 400)   b = (1000, 400)
        south = p1 -> p2
        east  = p2 -> p3   bulge:0.4     # a bowed wall is TWO points
        north = p3 -> p4 -> p5           # one wall with a step in it
        west  = p4 -> p1
        Humanoid = nav(type=walkable)    # authored: this room's relationship to one mesh
        spine = course a -> b  bulge:0.5 # a LINE the room holds; no wall runs along it
        road  = course b -> $Crypt.gate # a course MAY reach into another room
      }
    }
    world  anchorZ:0 {                  # EVERYTHING. Not one of the rooms, so not in the
      shrine = (9000, 9000)             #   block above; it has no walls and no bounds.
      road = course far -> shrine       #   Landmarks and courses that are in NO room.
    }

THE ROOMS LIVE IN ONE `regions { }` BLOCK AND A ROOM IS AN ENTRY OF IT, spelled
`Name = region(args)` - the same shape every other keyed entry in this format has, with the
brace on that line or the next. NOTHING INSIDE A ROOM CHANGED: corners, walls, bulge: and
connects: are written exactly as they were. The older file-scope `region Hall  min:0 {`
still reads, so a document written before 2026-08-20 applies untouched; what a read gives
you back is the nested form. Copy what you read rather than converting by hand.

A ROOM MAY DECLARE ITS OWN `populate { }` OR `terrain { }`, AND THE MAIN BLOCK SAYS WHEN IT
RUNS. Describe the macro pass in the file's own block and fine-tune per room: name the block
in the room's body and put `$Room.Block` on its own line in the main block, at the point in
the order where it should run. Its lines are spliced in THERE, so a terrain program's
coarse-to-fine order stays one visible sequence in one place.
    regions {
      Forest = region(max=900) {
        p1 = (0, 0)  p2 = (8000, 0)  p3 = (8000, 6000)  p4 = (0, 6000)
        south = p1 -> p2  east = p2 -> p3  north = p3 -> p4  west = p4 -> p1
        Greens = populate {
          Firs = foliage(types=(/Game/Foliage/FT_Pine), density=1.0, seed=11)
        }
      }
    }
    populate {
      Scrub = foliage(types=(/Game/Foliage/FT_Gorse), in=$Moor, density=0.2, seed=3)
      $Forest.Greens
    }
A LINE INSIDE A ROOM'S BLOCK NEEDS NO `in=` - stating no place means that room, and the
writer does not put a key back that you did not type. Stating one is honoured as written,
including a place in ANOTHER room or in `world`. A block NOTHING references is legal and
INERT: it keeps its text, fills nothing, and the parse warns you by name. What refuses is a
contradiction - a reference naming no such block, the same block referenced twice, a
`populate` block named from a terrain program, a block inside a block, and `paint { }`
inside a room's terrain block, which belongs to the whole landscape - all `gcw_bad_region_block`.

WHERE A ROOM CAN BE ENTERED IS DERIVED, NEVER AUTHORED. A build writes four keys onto the
wall each fact is about - connects:Store (both ways), to:/from: (one way, and only where a
directional link exists), and sealed:Store, which says these two rooms MEET along this wall
and nothing gets through it. sealed: is written even when they are joined somewhere else, so
bricking up one of two doors CHANGES that wall's line instead of going silent. A wall says
one thing about one room: naming it in two of the four is refused. Write them only by
copying a document you read; a `build nav` line is what measures them, and an apply that
does not rebuild carries the ones already in the file.
one declaration per line. The LEFT SIDE IS THE NAME - there is no as: alias - and names
are scoped to the region, so every room can have its own `north` and its own `p1`. Two
rooms that meet each draw their own wall there; gcw_ask's crack list measures the gap
between them, and 0 is a clean join. min, max, anchor, anchorZ, forward, corners and minted
are the
room's own ARGUMENTS, inside the parentheses of `Name = region(…)`, because the braces hold
declarations. forward: is the one of them that ALSO goes on a point, where it keeps the
trailing key:value spelling every declaration uses.

A POINT NO WALL RUNS THROUGH IS A LANDMARK - a place the room HOLDS rather than a corner
the ring carries - and $Hall.altar resolves to it exactly as $Hall.p1 resolves to a corner.
Moving a wall moves the corner and leaves the landmark alone; that is the difference, and
it is why they are not one kind. A landmark outside its own region is refused.
ANY POINT MAY ALSO STATE forward: - which way that place FACES, in degrees, the same word
and the same measure the region head uses. Unstated it takes the region's, so a file
written before the token means what it always meant; forward:0 is a STATED north and is
not the same claim. It is what @anchor[target=$Hall.altar] turns the thing it places to.

AND A RUN THAT IS NOT A WALL IS A COURSE - spine = course a -> b. The same distinction as
the landmark, one dimension up: a wall BOUNDS the room and a course is drawn INSIDE it. It
is not part of the ring, so nothing that walks the ring sees it, and the four ring keys
(connects:, to:, from:, sealed:) are refused on one - each says what you can do at a
BOUNDARY. Everything geometric is a wall's: bulge:, several points, $Hall.spine@t=40% by arc
length. It FACES ALONG ITS OWN RUN where a wall faces into the room, because a course has
no inward. A region of courses alone is refused - it still has no walls, so it has no shape,
unless it says corners=smooth, where the shape is its points and the courses are beside it.
The bulge apex sits at the middle of the line and is not movable: bulge: is a circular arc,
so put a point where you want the bend instead.

A PLACE ALONG A RUN IS @t= - $Hall.north@t=25% is a SHARE of it, $Hall.north@t=300 is an
ABSOLUTE distance along it, and $Hall.north@t=bend is a point it passes through. % marks
the share; without one the number is absolute, and NO UNIT IS EVER SPELLED. A bare @25%
with no t= is refused - one slot, one key, three value forms.
On a chain a fraction cannot reach a
bend: north = p3 -> bend -> p4 is ONE wall and @t runs by arc length over the whole of it, so
the bend sits at a ratio of two segment lengths that moves whenever any of the three points
does. Naming a point the run does not pass through is refused, and the refusal lists the ones
it does.

A RUN MAY CLIMB - [z=<cm>] on a POINT, beside [round=] in the same bracket. The region stays a
prism on a flat base: containment, the outline, the ring and every plan answer ignore it, and
only a run drawn THROUGH the point reads it. A point that states no height takes the region's
anchorZ:, so a rail climbs out of the floor and back to it without naming the floor twice, and
the height interpolates between the points that stated one. [z=0] is a claim about the world
origin while silence means wherever the region is - the two differ once the region moves.
    rail = course a -> b -> c
    c  = (1200, 400) [z=400.0]               # the far end is four metres up
    p3 = (19000, 20000) [round=0, z=250.0]   # a point may state both

A RUN MAY BEND SHARPLY - a bare linear, clamped or custom on a POINT, in the same bracket,
plus tangent=(in=(x, y, z), out=(x, y, z)). These are WATER'S OWN WORDS on a water control
point and mean the same thing here. A point that says nothing is the ordinary curved one, so
a course through it is smoothed by the engine - which is why a fence written as a course
round a right angle came out ROUNDED before this existed and no character in the file could
say otherwise. linear keeps the corner. A stated tangent already means custom, so state one
or the other and never both; a tangent states BOTH in= and out= or it is refused, because one
alone leaves the engine to derive the other and the point reads back with two.
Read by the COURSE path alone, exactly as [z=] is: [round=] is how the OUTLINE turns this
corner and this is how a RUN bends through it. Vertices the solver invents between two
declared points - an arc's middle - never take one.
    b = (600, 400) [linear]                              # the run keeps this corner
    c = (1200, 400) [z=400.0, tangent=(in=(600, 0, 0), out=(600, 0, 200))]
Both the spline-actor class line (Rail = /Game/BP/BP_Rail_C(along=$Track.spine)) and a water
body following a course read them.

A COURSE MAY REACH INTO ANOTHER ROOM - road = course b -> $Crypt.gate. The course belongs
to the room that DECLARED it, and merely reaches; $Hall.road keeps meaning one line with
one name and the crypt's corner keeps belonging to the crypt, so moving it moves the far
end of this run. A WALL MAY NOT: the ring IS the room's shape, and a wall on a borrowed
corner would move this room when somebody edited that one. Naming a point in your OWN
region this way is refused - write the bare name. A reach into a region the payload does
not declare is refused too, which is what stops a course outliving the room it points at.

A NATURAL SHAPE IS corners=smooth ON THE REGION - a lake, a clearing, a cave mouth. It is
the same grammar with the default flipped: sharp is every room you have ever written, and
smooth makes the region's OWN POINTS a curve running through them in the order they are
declared. [round=0] on one of them breaks the curve back into a hard corner; a radius there
is refused, because its corners are already curves.
    Lake = region(anchor=(16000, 16000), corners=smooth) {
      p1 = (12000, 12000)  p2 = (20000, 13500)
      p3 = (19000, 20000) [round=0]      # the one hard corner
      p4 = (13000, 19000)
    }
IT DECLARES NO WALLS AND ONE IS REFUSED. A wall is what a named spot anchors to, and a
smooth point's shape belongs to its NEIGHBOURS - so a natural shape names nothing to anchor
to, which is exactly why it may curve. Three points at least. A COURSE is still allowed and
its points are NOT on the curve: in one of these a point is either on the shore or on a
course, never both. connects:/to:/from:/sealed: live on a wall, so a natural region states
none. Everything else is unchanged - min/max/anchor/forward, containment, terrain, scatter
and gcw_ask all read it the way they read a room, because every span of the curve is
circular arcs underneath.

AND `world { }` IS EVERYTHING - the region that excepts nothing, at FILE SCOPE and never
inside `regions { }`. It exists because a landmark that is in no room had no owner: every
point in this format belongs to a region, so a place outside every room could only ever be
written as a bare coordinate. Now it is $world.shrine. It CONTAINS EVERY POINT, including
the ones inside rooms - it overlaps them rather than being cut by them, so a landmark just
outside the Hall does not leave the world the day the Hall grows. It has NO RING: a wall
in it is refused, because a wall would bound it, and min:, max:, anchor:, forward:, from:
and radius: are refused for the same reason. anchorZ: is the one key it takes - the height
its landmarks sit at. An empty `world { }` is legal where an empty region is not. Bare
$world is unchanged: still the level anchor, an identity frame and no volume.

A REGION HAS ONE MIN, ONE MAX AND ONE ANCHOR, and either bound may be left out to be
UNBOUNDED on that side - a room with neither is a column and Z is not tested at all.
min:/max: are absolute world Z and they bound CONTAINMENT only. The ANCHOR is where the
region IS: a render aims at it, `in=$Hall` places things at its height, and gcw_ask
reports it. Its plan and its height are two keys, so a room whose centre is already right
states anchorZ: alone. Unstated, the anchor is the centre of the SHAPE - which for an
L-shaped room is not the centre of its bounding box - and its height is 0. An authored
anchor outside its own region is refused (gcw_anchor_outside). base: and height: were
retired for these and refuse by name: base: was doing two jobs, and max: is an absolute
Z where height: was a span.

Its declarations are COMPLETE - an omitted point, edge, region or .gcs
subscription is REMOVED - so call dry_run:true first and read `removals`, which names every
one and says what still references it. create:true is required for a level's first region
file. A name that was minted and then dropped can never come back, because every
@anchor[target=$Crypt.e9] in the project would silently follow it onto the new wall; that
is refused by name. A block this build does not own at all is carried over untouched.
Read it back with gc_read kind:"regions"; ask questions about it with
gcw_ask, which answers a wall's curvature in centimetres and the file's crack list.

A `<name>.gcs { }` block declares a tracked document (spatial design 18.3i). IT IS A BLOCK
OF LINES AND EACH LINE IS ONE GROUP, stating its filters whole plus its own two references,
because where a thing STANDS and which way it LOOKS are measured off different things:
    enemies.gcs  listen:true {
      in:$BossRoom  class:BP_Minion  anchor:BP_Boss_01  as:polar  facing:(relative=Throne_01)
      in:$BossRoom  class:BP_Boss    anchor:Throne_01   as:offset  fields:Health
      exclude  in:$Cellar
      exclude  class:BP_Debug
      exclude  name:Minion_Test  tag:temporary
    }
EVERY FIELD IS key:value, filters and clauses alike - class, name, tag, in, near,
within, plus anchor:, its as: and align:, facing: and fields:. An unstated filter filters
nothing, so a
line with only `in:` is everything in that place; a line with NO filter is refused, because
it means every actor in the level - say that with in:$world if you mean it. in: names a
REGION or $world; a wall is a line and nothing stands inside a line. facing: takes a
keyed member - (relative=X) is measured off that frame, (target=X) is aimed AT it, and
(toward=X) is aimed at the NEAREST POINT of X's run. A ROW ALONG A STREET WANTS toward=:
a course with no station in it answers at its MIDDLE, so target= aims every member of the
row at one spot and only the one nearest the middle looks right.
`fields:` names top-level properties only. `listen:` is configuration and rides the
declaration's own line, where a region's min:/max: ride theirs.
A GROUP HAS NO NAME - its filter line IS its header - so the same line stated twice is
refused, while two lines sharing their filters and differing in anchor or facing are two
groups and stay legal: one actor measured from two anchors is two true measurements.
A declaration-wide `exclude` is also one complete selector PER LINE. Fields on one line
are AND; several exclude lines are OR. A match is removed from every group and from
untracked. A region is not special: `exclude  in:$Region` uses the same in: field as a
tracking line. The retired `exclude:$Region` spelling refuses with that replacement.
The `track:` mouth, named group blocks, `anchor: from X` and `facing: relative X` are the
shape 18.3i replaced; each refuses by name and carries the new spelling in its sentence.
Saving the level compares its OLD .gc before replacing it and refreshes only listening
declarations affected by changed actors, membership, anchor/facing/near dependencies, or
actor add/remove. Each affected .gcs is regenerated whole under Saved/GraphCode/Slices;
a hand-edited output is reported and preserved, and an orphan is never deleted. Edit the
generated values, defaults, anchor or facing and apply the WHOLE `gcs 1` document with
asset_path naming the open level, ir holding the document, and omission:"patch". Receipt
filters and fields remain the .gcw's authority; snapshot is structurally refused. Repeated
actor entries apply in document order, last one winning.
AN ENTRY MAY ALSO NAME ITS OWN class=, which is the class a NEW actor is created as - the
way one street mixes house types inside ONE group. It takes a FULL class path
(/Game/Path/BP_House.BP_House_C), because a creation has to resolve an asset where the
group's class: only has to match a name. A class= that disagrees with the actor already in
the level refuses, naming both, and the generator never writes one - so a factored default
can never hoist it onto the head line and rewrite which actors the group claims.
A HOUSE ALONG A STREET NAMES ITS STATION with t= - the three forms @t= takes: t=25% a share
of the run, t=1500 centimetres from its start, t=p4 a point it passes. The group must be
anchored on a COURSE with as:offset, and right= is then how far the entry stands off the
street at that station, negative for the other side. A save writes every member back the
same way - t= in centimetres, then right= - so a row along a bending street stays a row. A
group anchored on a wall, a landmark or an actor is still measured from its middle.
A ROW OF DIFFERENT-SIZED HOUSES SHARES ONE FRONTAGE with align: on the group line -
`align:(right: self=0%)` puts each member's near FACE on the point its entry states instead
of its middle, so right=-600 is six metres from the street to the wall and a wider house
grows backwards rather than into the road. self= is a share of the SUBJECT'S OWN span along
that axis - 0% its low end, 100% its high end - and an axis nobody names stays centred,
which is what every placement already does. Several axes in one list:
`align:(right: self=0%, up: self=0%)` also sits it on the ground. It rides the anchor like
as: does and refuses standing alone, and it lives on the GROUP line and never in an entry,
because a save measures distances and a measurement never answers a fraction.

AND A REGION CAN BE TRACED OFF A PLACED ACTOR instead of typed as corners. Write
`Crypt = region(from=FloorSlab_01) { }` declaring nothing, and the actor's SIMPLE COLLISION
footprint in plan becomes the loop - its convex hull, so a rotated slab traces its own
rectangle and not the larger box around it. An actor with no simple collision falls back
to its oriented bounds, and `promotions[].traced_from` says which of the two happened.
SEVERAL ACTORS ARE ONE BOUNDARY: `from: Wall_N, Wall_E, Wall_S, Wall_W` gathers every
footprint and hulls them ONCE, so four walls trace the room they stand around rather than
four rooms. That hull is convex and follows the OUTSIDE of what it traced - a room traced
from its walls includes their thickness - which `promotions[].note` says outright; move the
corners afterwards to tighten it. `traced_from` is `mixed` when the list disagreed, and
`receipt` then says which actor answered which way. An actor with no footprint at all is
refused BY NAME rather than dropped, because a boundary that quietly went missing leaves a
hull around somewhere else. anchorZ: is taken from the top of what was traced - the highest
of a list - unless you state one; min:/max: are never guessed. AND `radius:` STANDS THE
REGION OFF WHAT IT TRACED: `Camp = region(from=$Village.altar, radius=30000) { }` is 300 m
around the altar. A BARE source is an actor and a $-marked one is a place THIS file already
declares - a landmark, a wall, a course, or a whole region, which contributes its ring and
not the box round it. The sources are hulled and THEN pushed out, so two far-apart houses
give ONE ring with the ground between them inside; separate keep-outs are separate regions.
Every corner is a real arc, so one place is a disc of two bowed walls and two are a stadium
- nothing is tessellated into a polygon you cannot edit. radius: is greater than zero and
only ever sits beside from:. `traced_from` reads `declared` for a $-marked source. THE
SOURCE IS A STENCIL, NOT THE REGION: `from:` and `radius:` are resolved once, here, and
neither lands in the file - the points and edges they mint are ordinary authored geometry
afterwards, editable corner by corner, and moving the slab later does not move the room. An
ACTOR needs an editor with THAT level open; a promotion does not - a payload whose sources
are all $-marked is arithmetic over the file and resolves with nothing open, like every
other .gcw question. Read `promotions` for the corners, the area and the minted names, and
dry_run:true traces without writing.

THERE IS NO split AND NO round. Both were apply-time rewrites that left nothing in
the file saying they had happened, and both were retired 2026-08-21. A wall cut in two
is TWO WALLS - declare them, since a payload states the file whole. A rounded corner
belongs to the CORNER and is written on the point that declares it, so it survives the
wall beside it being moved instead of having to be run again. A file that still carries
either line refuses by name.

The block name routes the call. The writers below are INTERNAL - this tool is the whole
public write surface, and nothing here asks you to call anything else:
  graph, functions, macros -> the BlueprintIR graph writer, one graph at a time, each
      against its own sig:
  widgets                  -> the WidgetIR Designer writer, one complete Designer document.
      The input is a proposal; data.canonical_block is the compact tree the engine projects.
      A valid widget or @slot property that equals its class default is accepted as a hint,
      omitted from canonical output, and reported in mode_notices. Whitespace, indentation,
      equivalent value spellings, and property order are not reasons to refuse. Unknown or
      invalid properties, structural differences, compile errors, and genuine readback
      changes still refuse and return the engine-built canonical block for diagnosis.
  struct properties/settings -> identity-preserving struct writer
  enum entries/settings       -> identity-preserving enum writer
  Blueprint properties -> the identity-preserving declaration writer backed by
      blueprint.update_variables. THE WHOLE BLOCK APPLIES IN ONE CALL AND ONE COMPILE:
      adds, removals, renames and field edits together, validated end to end before
      anything is touched and rolled back if any step fails. A name in the text that the
      asset lacks is created; a name the text drops is removed; a RENAME IS STATED as
      `rename <Old> -> <New>` at the block's own depth, which preserves the variable's
      GUID and so keeps referencing assets repairable. Leftover names used to pair by
      their ORDER in the block, which could carry a GUID onto the wrong declaration in
      silence; since 2026-08-09 only one-against-one pairs without a token, and anything
      wider is removed and added with the unpaired names reported. Two renames may
      exchange names. Removals and type changes with live references
      need allow_breaking_changes:true. A removal reports EVERY node it orphans in
      data.orphaned_references - blueprint, graph, node GUID, plus the declaration's name,
      type and default - on refusals and dry runs as well as on success, so the next call
      can restore or repoint them without re-reading anything.
  components, class_defaults -> the actorir/1 tree writer, on an ACTOR Blueprint only.
      An Actor-parented Blueprint projects both and this writes them back with explicit
      component delete/reset and scratch validation.
      On a non-Actor Blueprint they are PROJECTED AND REFUSED, which is not the same as
      omitted: since 2026-08-02 EVERY Blueprint carries both blocks, and on a data-model
      Blueprint class_defaults{} is its entire authored content. Editing those values in
      the editor changes the .gc; you cannot write them back through here yet. This is
      the only pair in GraphCode whose read scope and write scope differ.
  timelines -> WRITABLE. Create, remove, rename and re-key, for timelines and for their
      tracks. A track's KIND cannot change at a surviving name, property=/function= is
      derived from the names and refuses a direct edit, and a graph write naming a
      timeline nobody created is refused at resolution.
  Blueprint inherited, defaults -> REFUSED. Inherited state belongs to the parent, and
      defaults describes the grammar every declaration below it is written against.
  Blueprint interfaces -> THE LIST IS WRITABLE as of 2026-08-07. Declaring a path
      implements the interface and the engine creates the graphs it brings. A REMOVAL
      STATES ITS POLICY: `remove <path> preserve_functions` keeps the implemented
      functions as ordinary members and turns its events into custom events with their
      wires; `remove <path> discard` deletes them with the interface. A bare `remove` is
      refused rather than defaulted, because RemoveInterface's bPreserveFunctions
      defaults to false and would silently delete authored graph bodies. Omission
      PRESERVES here - an omitted interface cannot say which of those two it meant - so
      there is no snapshot mode and dropping a line never removes one. A function BODY
      IS WRITABLE as of 2026-08-09: edit the graph inside the interface's braces and it
      goes through the same graph writer functions{} runs, addressed by interface path
      plus function name so it can never land on a member function of that name. An
      unchanged body writes nothing. THE FUNCTION SET IS CLOSED BY THE INTERFACE: a name
      the payload invents is refused and one it drops is a truncated payload, so there is
      no create and no delete - add the function to the interface asset instead. An
      interface implemented as EVENTS has no graphs at all; those are event nodes and
      graph{} already writes them.
  Blueprint dispatchers -> WRITABLE as of 2026-08-07: add, remove and re-signature. A
      dispatcher is TWO objects - a PC_MCDelegate variable entry and a graph in
      DelegateSignatureGraphs whose entry node carries the parameters - and both halves
      are written together. A re-signature edits those pins IN PLACE and never remints
      the variable, so every bind, unbind and call node keeps resolving. OMISSION
      DELETES, the same rule properties{} follows, since this block is where a delegate
      variable is declared instead of that one; a dispatcher a node still resolves is
      refused with the node named. Binding/unbinding/calling stays an ordinary graph
      statement in the graph blocks.
  material_instance parameters -> WRITABLE. Runtime override families only; a static
      permutation parameter still refuses, because changing one recompiles the
      permutation rather than overriding a value.
  material, material_function settings and graph -> WRITABLE. settings{} is the shared
      reflected-property codec against class defaults; graph{} carries exact links, and a
      base Material also writes its MaterialResult bindings. ALIASES ARE THE IDENTITY:
      an alias present in both the signed current document and your payload reuses that
      UObject, one only you supply CREATES an expression, and one only the current
      document has DELETES it. Class replacement and changes to a surviving parameter or
      function-interface GUID refuse; deleting an externally identified expression needs
      allow_breaking_changes:true.
  Any other Material block -> refused by name rather than as 'not a writable block', so
      the message never tells you a block does not exist while you are looking at it.
      See Docs/GRAPHCODE-MATERIAL-PLAN.md section 11 for the identity questions still open.
  data_table settings and rows -> WRITABLE. A row is a DELTA against a default-constructed
      row struct, always on one line, and the type token is the literal word `row` because
      the struct is named once in settings{}. CREATE BY PRESENCE; DELETE ONLY BY AN
      EXPLICIT `delete <Name>` LINE. A payload that simply drops a row is refused and names
      it: a row's referencers live in other assets and nothing in the document can
      enumerate them. There is NO rename - a row has no GUID, so remove+add is what a
      rename already is. Changing RowStruct empties the table and needs
      allow_breaking_changes:true, reporting every dropped row.
  data_table import -> REFUSED BY NAME, and it is projected, so the block in your file is
      real. It records where the asset was imported from so the source file enters git;
      re-running the import would rewrite the very rows the same document's rows{} block
      states, so one file would carry two answers.
  level actors -> WRITABLE, including create and delete. Same asymmetry as a row: an entry
      naming no live actor spawns one, and a removal needs `delete <Name>`.
  curve settings and curves -> WRITABLE. The CHANNEL SET IS CLOSED by the class, so a channel
      the payload adds is refused and one it drops is a truncated payload - there is no delete,
      unlike rows. Keys are spelled exactly as a Timeline track's are, because a track can
      point at one of these assets and the same curve would otherwise read two ways. A
      single-channel curve's channel is `Value`, not the engine's label, which is the asset's
      own name. `keys=` is written always and last; `keys=()` is an empty channel.
  curve import -> REFUSED BY NAME, same ruling as a data table's: re-running the import would
      rewrite the very keys the same document's curves{} block states.
  input_action settings, triggers, modifiers and input_mapping_context settings, mappings
      -> ALL WRITABLE, under the OPPOSITE identity rule to every kind above. A trigger, a
      modifier and a mapping have no name and no GUID, and modifiers apply in array order,
      so THE LIST IS THE VALUE: the payload carries all of it and a write rebuilds it
