      wholesale. No `delete` line, no create-by-presence, no rename, and nothing for
      allow_breaking_changes to gate, because nothing outside the asset can reference one.
      The cost is real and is not refused: A SHORT PAYLOAD TRUNCATES THE LIST silently -
      send four modifiers when the asset has five and the fifth is gone. Statements are
      rule 7 with the left-hand side elided - `Negate()`, `mapping(Action=…, Key=…)` - and
      a class token that does not resolve, is mis-based or is abstract is refused BY NAME
      rather than skipped. A mapping with no Action= is refused as malformed; Action=null
      is accepted, because a mapping with no action chosen yet is real saved state.
  data_asset values -> WRITABLE as one complete deviation set. Omission resets a field to
      its archetype. The writer imports and projects a scratch duplicate before touching the
      asset, then verifies live read-back and restores the original values on failure. Missing
      soft-reference packages refuse. Reference changes are reported; removing an existing
      edge needs allow_breaking_changes:true when package referencers cannot be inspected
      semantically. A C array spells as Name[i] and round-trips. An Instanced owned object
      carries presence, concrete class, owner-relative identity and recursive contents inline;
      omission deep-resets it to an owner-local copy of the archetype.

THE PAYLOAD IS THE COMPLETE BLOCK, and the same omission-is-deletion rule bp_apply has
for statements applies here to graphs: a graph in the asset that this payload leaves out
is refused as a truncated patch, not read as a deletion, and it comes back before
anything is written.

graph, functions AND macros CARRY A LIFECYCLE on top of that, and only when the block is
sent whole - no graph_name. A name the asset does not have CREATES that graph,
`delete <Name>` removes one, and `rename <Old> -> <New>` moves one keeping the GraphGuid
every call site resolves through. A created entry needs no sig: and any it carries is
ignored - the engine has just made it, so there is nothing for it to be stale against.
Narrow the call with graph_name and the lifecycle is off: that addresses one graph which
already exists. Every other block still refuses a graph it did not project.

A multi-graph payload is preflighted in full - every graph dry-run against the live asset
- and refused as a whole if any of them fails, because bp_apply is atomic per graph and
there is no putting the first one back once the second is refused. A CREATE CANNOT BE
PREFLIGHTED: the graph does not exist yet, so its entry says not_attempted and names the
statements nobody validated rather than reporting a pass it never performed.

base_sig is the DOCUMENT sig: from the `.gc` you read - the one on its `gc 1` line. It is
REQUIRED on graph, functions and macros, and it is the only guard those blocks have: graph
headers stopped carrying a sig: of their own on 2026-08-21, because the document digest
moves whenever any graph in the asset moves and a per-graph one could only agree with it.
A header that still states one is accepted and ignored, so older .gc files still apply.

IT IS ALSO WHAT MAKES A STALE PATCH RECOVERABLE rather than refused. When the asset has
moved since you read it, base_sig is the key that finds your base document in local
history, so the two edits are three-way merged and the write proceeds against the result;
the refusal is what happens when that merge cannot be made, and it names the lines the two
of you changed differently. Send it on every write.

A MERGE PROPOSAL IS GATED ON ITS PARENT, NOT ON ITS OWN sig:. A `.gc` that states
`merged-from:` came out of a three-way merge, and its sig: is `conflicted` or a digest of a
body woven from two parents - it equals neither by construction, so it is not read here.
What is checked is that the asset still projects to the FIRST parent named, which is ours.
Send such a file whole - no block: - and it applies; the response says merge_proposal:true
and ours_parent_sig. It is refused only when the asset has left that parent, and the remedy
there is to redo the merge against the asset's current text, NEVER gc_sync, which
regenerates the sidecar and would delete the merge. One block: of a proposal is refused for
the same reason: it would land that block and drop the rest of the merge.

This call syncs the sidecar first, so the payload is always checked against a file that
is this build's projection of this asset - and on success it re-projects the sidecar over
the now-dirty asset, so the next gc_read sees what you just wrote. That rewrite states no
bin:, deliberately: the package has unsaved edits, so its bytes on disk are not what the
text was read from.

source:"live" skips the file and projects the running editor's asset instead. Both sources
check the payload against a fresh projection of the same in-memory object - a sync projects
too, it just writes the result down - so 'live' is the same guard minus the file. That is
what makes it the write route to an asset outside /Game and this plugin's own mount, where
no `.gc` can be generated at all. AN EXCLUDED FOLDER IS NOT THAT CASE: user-ruled
2026-08-24, both sources reach it and neither leaves a file, because that setting governs
where FILES go and never which assets may be read or edited. Prefer the default everywhere
else, because the file a sync leaves current is what the next read, diff and merge all work
from. The reply always states write_source.

A WRITE FINISHES ITSELF. The apply saves the package and the save hook restamps both digests,
so the .gc beside the asset always describes the bytes on disk. There is no second call.
Pass save:false to leave it dirty on purpose; the reply always states saved, and says why
when that is false.

READ asset_compile_status BEFORE ANY PER-GRAPH RESULT. graphs[] answers one graph at a
time and its attribution is positive-only, so an error the compiler could not pin on the
graph you wrote lands on a SIBLING - twenty-five graphs can each say compile_status
'succeeded' beside a class that does not compile and whose every function returns null.
asset_compile_status is the class's own answer, asset_compile_errors names them, and when
it is 'failed' the message LEADS with it. Absent where no compile was owed - a dry run,
and every kind that has no compiler.
A GRAPH SAYING compile_status:'deferred' HAS NOT BEEN LOOKED AT. A whole-document apply
compiles the asset ONCE, after its last block, so each graph is written before anything
judges it; that one compile is what asset_compile_status reports. Deferred is not a pass
and not a failure - it says the answer is at the top of this reply.

diagnostics[] IS NOT AN ERROR LIST AND DOES NOT BLOCK THE WRITE. It is what a graph the
engine accepts can still get wrong, on graph blocks, in dry_run and on the real apply:
  - an IMPURE node nothing reaches by exec whose output another statement reads. It never
    runs, so the reader gets that pin's type default forever, and it compiles clean. The
    finding names the alias, the consumer and the pin.
  - an input pin with neither a connection nor a literal, which will use its type default.
These are reported rather than refused because a half-wired branch is what ordinary
mid-construction looks like and the Blueprint editor builds them all day. Read them; they
are usually a missing exec edge.

PROJECTED AND REFUSED BY NAME, generated from the registry so the list cannot go
stale as kinds are added - 34 pairs: animation_blueprint.defaults, blueprint.defaults, blueprint_function_library.defaults, blueprint_interface.defaults, blueprint_macro_library.defaults, control_rig.hierarchy, control_rig.rig, curve_float.import, curve_linear_color.import, curve_table.import, curve_vector.import, data_table.import, external_actor.data_layers, groom.groups, groom.provenance, groom_binding.binding, groom_binding.groups, groom_binding.provenance, import.factory, import.import, import.members, import.pipelines, import.settings, level.data_layers, metahuman.pipeline, metahuman.settings, metahuman.textures, metahuman.wardrobe, niagara_sim_cache.emitters, niagara_sim_cache.frames, niagara_sim_cache.system, pcg_graph.comments, procedural_vegetation.comments, widget_blueprint.defaults.
Refused BY NAME rather than ignored: the block in your file is real, it is read,
and sending it back gets a refusal that names it instead of a success that wrote
nothing.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Asset or package path, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login. AN ACTOR is addressed by its object path - /Game/Maps/M.M:PersistentLevel.FixtureSun - which on a One File Per Actor or World Partition map resolves to the actor's OWN package, whose name is a content hash and contains the actor's name nowhere. That is the path gc_search kind:"asset" returns and the one a .gc writes for a cross-actor reference. Required unless asset_paths is given.

parameters.name: asset_paths
parameters.description: ONE SETTINGS CHANGE TO MANY ASSETS, in place of asset_path: block:"settings" with an ir: holding only the lines to change, e.g. `settings { NaniteSettings.bEnabled = true }` to 164 meshes in one call. It is a PATCH - a line the ir leaves out is kept on every asset - and runs each asset exactly as a single apply would (same checks, its own save), so one refusal does not stop the others; a cancel lands between two assets. The reply's assets[] carries each asset's own reply. base_sig, omission, create, compile, resave, graph_name and mode are refused beside it.

parameters.name: block
parameters.description: Which block this payload is. Generated from the capability registry, so it cannot drift from what the writer accepts: actors, animations, animgraph, axes, behaviortree, blend_profiles, bodies, capture, cards, class_defaults, collision_pairs, comments, components, constraints, curves, dispatchers, emitters, entries, envquery, eyes, face, font_fallbacks, functions, goals, graph, group_materials, head, import, inputs, interfaces, interpolation, level_blueprint, lods, macros, makeup, mapping_profiles, mappings, materials, meshes, metasound, modifiers, notifies, notify_tracks, objects, ops, outfit, outputs, parameters, partition, physics, pipelines, player_mappable, profiles, properties, rendering, retarget_definition, retargeting, rows, samples, sections, sequence, settings, skin, slot_groups, slots, sockets, solvers, soundcue, source_poses, splines, statetree, strings, sublevels, sync_markers, system, target_poses, timelines, track, triggers, typeface, user_parameters, values, variables, virtual_bones, volumes, widgets. Not every kind writes every one of these - ask gc_describe(kind:"<token>") for one asset's blocks. Passed explicitly rather than sniffed out of the text, because a payload whose wrapper disagrees with the block being patched is a mis-aimed patch. OMIT block and ir together to apply the `.gc` FILE ON DISK instead - whatever edited it.

parameters.name: ir
parameters.description: The complete block, with or without its `name { … }` wrapper. THE ORDINARY ROUTE OMITS IT, along with block:: edit the `.gc` beside the asset the way you would edit any other file, then call this with asset_path alone. Every block is compared against a fresh projection and ONLY the ones whose text changed are written, so that route costs your edit rather than the whole document, and it rebuilds no graph you did not touch. THE FILE TO EDIT IS `sidecar_path`, which every gc_read reply carries. REACH FOR ir: WHEN THERE IS NO FILE TO EDIT, or nothing in it to edit yet: a block the asset's projection does not carry (the file route refuses to ADD one, so this is the only way to introduce it), source:"live" where no sidecar is generated, or a `gcw 1` / `gcshape 1` / `gcmove 1` document that does not exist beside the asset yet - once one does, this verb reads it from disk. Creating an asset goes through the file too: write the .gc at the sidecar path and call create:true with neither block nor ir. Editing ONE graph of many is graph_name: on the file route, not a hand-written block. Sending a block the file already carries is accepted and not refused; the reply says how many of the lines you sent were that file's own text.

parameters.name: base_sig
parameters.description: The document sig: from line one of the `.gc` this edit was computed against - or from the source:"live" read you took, which carries the same digest. A stale value is refused, never merged.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Where the state this payload is checked against comes from. THE SAME WORD gc_read uses, meaning the same thing on the write side. 'saved' (the default) syncs the `.gc` first, so the payload is checked against a file that is this build's projection of this asset, and a successful write re-projects that file. 'live' projects the running editor's asset instead and writes NO file. Both check the payload against a fresh projection of the same in-memory object - the difference is only whether a `.gc` is written on the way past, which is why 'live' is the route to an asset outside /Game and this plugin's own mount, where a sidecar can never be generated. A folder on GraphCode's excluded list is NOT that case: 'saved' reaches it too and simply leaves no file. It is what retires bp_apply and ui_apply. Use it for exactly that case; 'saved' is right everywhere else, because the file it leaves current is what the next gc_read and every diff and merge read.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Graph blocks only. 'differential' (the default) keeps unchanged nodes in place - same GUID, same position. 'replace' rebuilds every node with a fresh GUID and re-runs layout, so hand-tuned positions are lost.

parameters.name: graph_name
parameters.description:
Graph blocks only. Patch exactly this one graph and leave the block's others alone, so changing one event graph does not mean echoing back all of them. Without it the payload must carry EVERY graph in the block, because a dropped graph would otherwise be indistinguishable from a deletion.
WHAT THE PAYLOAD MAY CARRY DEPENDS ON WHERE IT CAME FROM. An inline ir: must contain this graph and no other - a second graph you typed is a patch whose scope disagrees with its own declaration. The whole .gc FILE (the no-block form) may carry every graph the asset has, because a projection of the asset IS every graph; it is narrowed to the one you name and the rest are read and left untouched. Reach for that form when editing one function of many - applying the whole block rebuilds every graph in it, and a rebuild can settle state the .gc does not show.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description:
Validate everything against the live asset and touch nothing - including the .gc on disk, which comes back byte for byte even though validating re-projects it partway through. Both routes have a real preflight and this uses it.
A dry run that would REMOVE anything prices it: one 'deletion_impact' line per removed entity, saying how many citations gc_search kind:"reference" found project-wide and where, plus whatever it could not read. Longer than 'deleted', which reports omission alone - an explicit 'delete' line and a declaration you dropped cost the same. This is the last place to notice a removal you did not intend.
What it WOULD change comes back as 'changes', one line per entity - the placed actors an actors block would move, the fields a settings, interface or dispatchers block would write. Read it instead of re-reading the asset: a dry run touched nothing, so there is no diff to look at and this is the only account of what the payload actually does.

parameters.name: allow_breaking_changes
parameters.description: Proceed with a schema or widget edit whose impact scan found references. It suppresses the refusal, never the report. For widgets it does NOT cover a graph node reading a widget you removed - clear those with gc_apply block:"graph" first.

parameters.name: allow_broken
parameters.description: Save a Blueprint this write breaks. By default a Blueprint that compiled before the write and does not compile after it is NOT saved: success:false, saved:false, compile errors first, the file on disk unchanged. One already broken before the write is saved either way, so it stays fixable.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: Human identity stage only: character build output name or package path. Use with through:'identity' or preview:'update'.

parameters.name: through
parameters.description: Human only. 'identity' stops before rig, texture-source and assembly requests; a normal apply saves identity. Omit to build every declared stage.

parameters.name: preview
parameters.description: Human only. 'update' evaluates one selected identity in memory and returns preview_id and a renderable preview_asset; no destination writes or service requests. Reuse preview_id to replace its preview, or 'discard' to release it. Updates start from a fresh identity and keep the last good preview on failure. Skin, eyes and makeup are included; outfits and animation are not. Handles expire at editor shutdown; at most eight may be open.

parameters.name: preview_id
parameters.description: Human preview handle returned by preview:'update'. Pair with preview:'update' or 'discard' and the same document asset_path. Render the latest returned preview_asset; its path changes on update.

parameters.name: on_failure
parameters.description: Graph blocks with more than one graph. What happens to the OTHER graphs when one will not validate. 'refuse' (the default) is all-or-nothing: nothing is written and the asset is untouched, which is right when re-sending is cheap. 'skip' writes every graph that validated and leaves the failures alone, each coming back marked skipped in its mutation_status with the full error list a refusal would have carried - so the second payload is only the graphs that failed, not the block again. A skipped graph is UNTOUCHED, never half-written: gc_apply is still atomic per graph. It changes nothing when every graph fails - with no survivor to write, the block is refused as usual - and nothing on a dry run, which writes nothing either way and owes you the whole failure list. The default does not move: atomic is still the right answer when you have not already been told which graph is bad.

parameters.name: create
parameters.description: Build the asset if there is nothing at asset_path. THE SAME COMMAND MAKES AND EDITS: you do not have to know which one you need before you call. Whole-document only - pass neither block nor ir - because a new asset is built from a complete .gc. Without it, an empty path is not an error: the create is PLANNED, proven on a throwaway scratch asset, and reported as would_create with the kind, the parent it resolved and the blocks it would write, and nothing is built. That is deliberate - asset:/Game/Blueprints/BP_Romo would otherwise mint a second Blueprint beside BP_Room and report success, so the announcement is also the typo check. Blocks you leave out are NOT deleted: they keep whatever the factory gave the new asset, so the smallest legal recipe is a header plus parent: and everything else is filled in for you. create_caveats lists what the created asset will not have - read it, because a create is the one write with no earlier version to diff against. Against a path that already holds an asset this changes nothing and the call is an ordinary apply. The new package is left DIRTY AND UNSAVED like every other GraphCode write. DO NOT ADD compile:true - it is a whole call of its own, it runs before this one and finds no asset, and the pair is refused. A create compiles what it built and reports compile_status on the same result. With dry_run:true you also get projected_text - the WHOLE .gc the created asset would project back to, canonicalised values, omits: line and every field the factory filled in that you never mentioned. It is the only way to see a create before it happens, because there is no earlier version to diff against.

parameters.name: omission
parameters.description: What LEAVING AN ENTRY OUT means. 'patch' (the default) is a partial payload: four blocks - actors, rows, components, widgets - refuse it by name rather than guess, so you carry every entry and spell a removal with that block's `delete` token. 'snapshot' says the payload IS the block's complete authored state, so an entry you leave out is DELETED and a `delete` line is refused as a contradiction. Never guess with this: under snapshot a hand-written partial payload deletes everything it forgot. It exists for a payload you did not truncate - a merged .gc or one you round-tripped through gc_read - where the deletion cannot be spelled any other way, because `delete` is imperative and the next regeneration would strip it. Authority is per BLOCK and never per asset: `omits:` means the file is not the whole asset. Every omission-deletion comes back in `deleted`, on dry runs and refusals too. Blocks whose identity model already fixes the rule (a graph deletes by omission, an input list is the value, a curve's channels are closed) proceed under their own rule and say so in `mode_notices`. NOT the same parameter as `mode`, which is the graph rebuild strategy.

parameters.name: save
parameters.description:
Leave the asset DIRTY instead of saving it. Default true, and true is almost always what you want: a write finishes itself, so there is no second call to remember.
The result says 'saved', and when that is false it says why - you passed save:false, nothing was written, or the save was REFUSED (a read-only file, a checkout nobody holds). A refusal matters: the edit already happened in memory, so the asset is changed and the change is not on disk.
A dry run ignores this entirely and touches nothing. A document apply saves ONCE, after its last block, not once per block.
Pass false when you mean to inspect the result in the editor before committing it, or when you are staging several edits by hand. Be aware a save commits every OTHER unsaved change in that package too, including a human's open-editor work.

parameters.name: organise
parameters.description:
OPT-IN: after the write, re-lay-out the target's supported graphs and fold the moved positions into this call's ONE save. Off by default - placed nodes do not move unless you ask, and this is you asking; it does not change the default.
'true' tidies EVERY graph in the Blueprint, so gc_apply becomes a cleanup pass - the event graph and every function and macro, whether or not this edit touched them. An array of graph names (["EventGraph","OpenDoor"]) tidies just those. The motivating case is a node that changed type and grew, overlapping neighbours the don't-move rule had frozen; whole-graph layout lets those neighbours flow out of the way.
Positions are absent from .gc, so this NEVER moves sig: - new_base_sig is unchanged and that is not organise doing nothing. The report comes back under 'organise': one entry per graph with its node moves, plus warnings for an unknown graph or an unsupported kind. Materials support true for their single graph. Niagara supports true, system, or emitters.<handle> in the name array; stage and event nodes share their emitter graph. Niagara structural writes also arrange their native graphs automatically. A dry run reports what WOULD move and writes nothing. For surgical Blueprint/material layout, gc_render mode:"layout" is the tool; this is the whole-asset cleanup that rides the write.

parameters.name: compile
parameters.description:
Compile the asset and report what the compiler said. WRITES NOTHING, and takes neither block nor ir - it is the whole call, so it does not combine with create: either. A create compiles what it builds and reports it on the same result - asset_compile_status for the CLASS, compile_status per graph in graphs[]. Asking for both is refused, because this gate runs first and there is nothing at the path yet.
Every other route here compiles as the last step of a write, which answers 'did what I just sent survive?'. This answers 'is this asset broken RIGHT NOW?' - the question you have after Live Coding, after a parent class or a struct changed, or after somebody edited the graph in the editor. Nothing else in the gc_ family asks it.
You get compile_status ('succeeded' or 'failed'), compile_errors and compile_warnings as separate lists. A failed compile is still a successful CALL: the errors are the answer, not a tool failure.
Blueprint-derived assets, and product kinds with their own compiler (a Niagara system: Niagara's compile, each script's events named by emitter and script usage) - anything else is refused by name rather than reported as compiling clean. The compile regenerates the class; asset_dirty usually comes back false anyway, because the engine restores the dirty flag around a compile on purpose.

parameters.name: build
parameters.description:
RETIRED, and kept on the card only so the old spelling gets an answer. Every value refuses by naming where its capability went.
A LEVEL'S DERIVED DATA IS REALISED BY THE WRITE THAT DECLARES IT. Send the level's .gcw and its `terrains { }` programs run, its `water { }` bodies go into the level and its `populate { }` lines all raise what they name: `pcg(...)` generators reconcile, `foliage(...)` lines plant, `audio(...)` lines put a reverb zone in the room they name, `postprocess(...)` lines put a LOOK on one, `triggervolume(...)` lines put a tagged trigger there, `physicsvolume(...)` and `killzvolume(...)` lines put a place where movement obeys different rules - or ends, `spline(...)` lines put a RUN into the world as a real spline on a plain actor, and a line whose type is a CLASS PATH raises that class - any AVolume subclass, including one your own project declares - with the properties that class declares, all as part of that one write. The block appearing IS the build, so build and REBUILD are one act: re-send the document to run it again. create: still gates the two creations it always gated - a landscape the level does not have, and the AWaterZone.
NAVIGATION IS THE EXCEPTION, and it moved into the FILE rather than off it: write `build nav` as a line in the .gcw payload. Recast reads the level's COLLISION - a mesh somebody dragged in, a terrain pass that just ran, volumes that just spawned - and none of that is in the document, so no block's text can say when the mesh went stale. The line is an operation: carried out, reported, and stripped from what lands on disk, so it is a request made at the moment you mean it and never a standing policy. It is also much the most expensive of the four, which is the second reason it is asked for rather than implied. A level with no .gcw yet needs create:true, and a payload of `gcw 1` plus `build nav` is enough to build one.
What a .gcw write reports for all of it: navigation_compiled and its actor counts, generation_compiled and its volume counts, terrain_realised with a `terrain` object (terrains[], landscapes_created), and water_realised with a `water` object (bodies, zones, islands, exclusions, spawned, created_zone, applied[], plus carved[] and skipped[] when there is something to say). dry_run:true resolves and evaluates all of it, refuses everything that can refuse, and touches nothing.
Terrain and water REQUIRE GRAPHCODE WORLD, and water requires the Water plugin on top of it; a .gcw that declares neither never asks for either. The two water refusals differ on purpose: one names the product to install, the other names the build switch.

parameters.name: resave
parameters.description:
Re-serialize the package: load it, compile it if it has a compiler, and write the SAME authored state back to disk. Takes neither block nor ir - it is the whole call.
THIS IS THE ONE REPAIR THE TEXT SURFACE CANNOT SPELL. A .gc describes AUTHORED state, and a package can be broken in its DERIVED bytes while every authored line is correct - a compiled class holding a struct reference that no longer resolves, so the asset logs errors on every LOAD and compiles clean afterwards. Sending the block back is answered 'already matches the Blueprint; nothing changed', which is true and does not help: the fix is not an edit, it is the same bytes written again by a build that can resolve what the old ones could not.
Reach for it when errors { } carries a LoadError, or when an asset logs load errors that compile:true says nothing about. Not for authored changes - those are an ordinary block write, and this one deliberately cannot carry any.
sig: is unchanged BY CONSTRUCTION and bin: is what moves; that pair is how you check it did what it says. You get compile_status ('succeeded', 'failed', or 'not_compiled' for a kind with no compiler - all three are re-saved) plus compile_errors and compile_warnings.
IT ALSO SWEEPS ORPHANED GRAPH NODES, and that is a SECOND cause with the same symptom - so reaching for this on load errors is right either way. A node left outered to a graph by an older write is still an export, because SavePackage harvests by walking outers rather than references; it is in the .uasset, invisible to every projection, and the engine reconstructs it on every load and can log an Error about it. Re-serializing alone carries them along - the sweep is what removes them, and this is the only route to it that does not cost you your node positions (a no-op gc_apply short-circuits before the graph write; mode:'replace' re-GUIDs and re-lays-out every node). Reported as orphans_removed, which is zero for a healthy asset and for every kind that is not a Blueprint - and it is the only evidence available, since an orphan cannot move sig:.

tools.name: gc_asset
tools.description:
The asset as a package or an external artifact - rename it, move it, copy it, export it.
gc_apply changes its contents; this verb changes or emits the asset as a whole.
A noun with its verbs on mode:, the shape gc_versions has.

  mode:"rename",    asset_path, new_name:"BP_Player"      -> same folder, new name
  mode:"move",      asset_path, destination_directory:"/Game/Chars" -> same name, new folder
  mode:"duplicate", asset_path, destination_path:"/Game/Chars/BP_Copy" -> a second asset
  mode:"export",    asset_path, destination_file:"D:/Share/Body.fbx" -> native exporter
  mode:"delete",    asset_path                          -> recoverable; force:true is not
  ... plus dry_run:true on any -> say what would happen and touch nothing

THE SIDECAR FOLLOWS, and it is never byte-copied. A rename or a move takes the `.gc` with
the asset through GraphCode's own lifecycle; a duplicate PROJECTS a fresh one for the copy,
with its own asset: line and its own digests, because copying the source's text would give
two files the same identity and, for every kind whose entities carry GUIDs, the same GUIDs.

IT SAVES WHAT IT WRITES and leaves nothing at the old path. save:false is the opt-out, the
same parameter gc_apply carries. A rename whose source file survived would leave the project
holding one asset under two names, which is the failure this verb exists to not have.

EXPORT USES UNREAL'S INSTALLED NATIVE EXPORTERS. The destination is an absolute external
file and its extension selects the exporter. It refuses existing files by default; pass
overwrite:"replace" explicitly. A dry run without destination_file discovers every
format loaded for that exact asset. Export never changes or dirties the source package.

DELETE REFUSES WHILE ANYTHING STILL REFERENCES THE ASSET, and `force` does NOT override
that - the two are different decisions. force decides whether the deletion is RECOVERABLE;
accept_breaking_references decides whether references may break. Without force the asset
moves to GraphCode's recovery trash and its `.gc` moves with it, so it can come back. With
force the recovery copy goes too and there is NO way back: local history holds the asset's
TEXT, never its bytes, so every facet the format omits is lost with it.

CREATE IS NOT HERE: it is gc_apply create:true, because a create carries a payload. Neither
is save, because no gc_ verb leaves a package dirty any more.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Required, no default: "rename" | "move" | "duplicate" | "export" | "delete"

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: The asset to act on, e.g. /Game/Blueprints/BP_Old. Required.

parameters.name: new_name
parameters.description: Required by the rename mode: the new name, a NAME and not a path. Pass a path and it is refused rather than guessed at - changing folder is what the move mode does.

parameters.name: destination_directory
parameters.description: Required by the move mode: the long package path to move into, e.g. /Game/Characters. The asset keeps its name, so renaming and moving is two calls.

parameters.name: destination_path
parameters.description: Required by the duplicate mode: the copy's WHOLE path, folder and name together, e.g. /Game/Characters/BP_PlayerCopy. A duplicate is the one mode that can change both at once, so it takes the whole destination rather than half of it.

parameters.name: destination_file
parameters.description: Export mode: an absolute external filesystem path whose extension selects Unreal's native exporter, e.g. D:/Share/Character/Body.fbx. Paths under the project's Content directory are refused to prevent an export/import feedback loop. Omit only with dry_run:true to discover the formats available for this exact asset.

parameters.name: overwrite
parameters.description: Export mode only: "refuse" (default) or "replace". The check covers every file the selected exporter says it will write.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: Resolve the destination and report what would happen, touching nothing. Default false.

parameters.name: save
parameters.description: Save the moved package when it is written. Default true; false leaves it dirty and the reply says so.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Delete mode only: make the deletion PERMANENT instead of recoverable. The recovery copy is removed too and there is no way back - local history holds the asset's text, never its bytes. Default false. It does NOT let a referenced asset be deleted; that is a different flag, and this one never widens what may break.

parameters.name: accept_breaking_references
parameters.description: Delete mode only: proceed even though other assets still reference this one, leaving them pointing at nothing. Default false, which refuses and names every referencer. The same word gc_versions uses for the same decision.

tools.name: gc_describe
tools.description:
Describe one GraphCode block through a unified read-only surface. The block selects the
existing reflection engine: widgets uses WidgetIR's throwaway tree, graph/functions/macros
use BlueprintIR's throwaway graph, and components/class_defaults inspect the Blueprint's real
SCS templates or CDO against the correct baseline. No asset is dirtied, compiled or saved.

The response always separates two meanings that compact text must not blur:
  authored:false  the property is valid but equals its baseline, so compact .gc omits it
  coverage:omitted the entire facet is outside the current sidecar projection
Widget properties and slot properties return every managed leaf, including default-valued
ones. Component properties and attachment properties do the same for owned SCS templates.
On an ACTOR Blueprint, components and class_defaults are projected as actorir/1 and are
gc_apply input: G4 shipped. On a non-Actor Blueprint they remain inspection-only, and the
response says so in write_status - read that field rather than assuming either way.

block:"defaults" is the exception to all of the above: it takes no asset and describes the
document's own vocabulary - what a `defaults { }` set name expands to, every specifier a
properties declaration can carry, and which of them the block always states outright. Ask it
when a .gc names a set you cannot expand from the file in front of you.

type_path:"/Script/Engine.ECollisionChannel" is the other exception, and it takes no asset
and no block either: it reflects a NATIVE C++ UENUM or USTRUCT, which has no package and no
sidecar for unreal_gc_read to address. That is the question to ask when you are about to
write a native enum literal into a graph statement and need its exact spellings. A BLUEPRINT
enum or struct is refused here by name and sent to unreal_gc_read, which is the verb that
owns an asset. Passing type_path is what selects this route, the way kind: selects grammar.

Pass kind:"<kind>" for GRAMMAR instead - the format's own rules, answered without an
editor. Omit it, as everything above assumes, and this verb reflects a real asset.

parameters.name: block
parameters.description: GraphCode block: defaults, widgets, graph, functions, macros, components, or class_defaults. 'defaults' needs no asset_path and expands the specifier-default set names a .gc uses. Not needed at all with type_path, which reflects a native C++ type rather than a block of a document. A macro graph is described against ITS OWN graph, not an event graph's: graph_name resolves through the Blueprint's MacroGraphs and that graph is the schema context, so macro-only rules apply.

parameters.name: token
parameters.description: ANY TOKEN A .gc SPELLS, answered with what it is — the reverse of the grammar routes. Paste it as you see it: `@placement[Location=…]`, `[ExtraFlags=201457664]`, `FunctionEntry`, `!types`, `$succeeded`, `covers`, `Actor:GetAllChildActors()`. GraphCode's own vocabulary — every directive, annotation, sigil, reserved name, block verb and value constructor — is answered by the bridge with no editor. Anything else is resolved by REFLECTION, in this order: `Owner:Member` — the shape a graph statement names what it calls, gets or sets — returns that one function, property or macro graph with its parameters, their PIN directions and the class that really declares it; a type token returns the class or struct it names (under the family prefix the writer strips) together with its editable properties, which is where a key such as ExtraFlags comes from; an object path such as /Script/Engine.StaticMeshComponent returns the type at it; and a bare property name returns every reflected type that declares one. An authored name — a node alias, a variable, a state — belongs to gc_search kind:"entity", and a refusal here says which of these readings it tried rather than assuming the last one.

parameters.name: preset
parameters.description: A .gcshape PRESET entry to describe, from the shipped library — "$Surface.Erode", "Surface.Erode", a bare "Erode", a whole family "Surface", or the file's own content path. Passing it selects the preset route and needs no block and no asset: a preset is a program on disk, so this answers from a parse, with no editor and nothing built. Returns the entry's kind, the '#' block written above it, every declared parameter with its default, the import line and the call line you would actually type. A bare name matching in two families names both rather than picking one. Use gc_search kind:"preset" to find a name; use this once you have one.

parameters.name: root
parameters.description: With preset: a content folder of .gcshape files to look in instead of the shipped /GraphCodeShape/Presets — for example /Game/Steampunk/Recipes. Omit it for the library.

parameters.name: type_path
parameters.description: A NATIVE C++ UENUM, USTRUCT or UCLASS to reflect, by object path — /Script/Engine.ECollisionChannel, /Script/CoreUObject.Vector, /Script/Engine.MaterialExpression, or one of this project's own such as /Script/MyGame.EItemType. Passing it selects the native-type route and no block or asset_path is needed. Returns the enum's entries or the struct's members, and — since CP2 R5 — a `derived` list of every LOADED type deriving from it, which is how a grammar's <Type> token is turned into the set it came from. answered_by names which reader resolved it. ONE TYPE ANSWERS WITH MORE THAN ITS MEMBERS: /Script/InputCore.Key also returns `keys`, every key this editor has registered, grouped by the engine's own menu category and read live off EKeys. That is the only route to a key name there is - EKeys is a static registry, not a UENUM - and a key name is what `Key=` takes in a kind:input_mapping_context mapping. A Blueprint enum or struct is REFUSED and sent to unreal_gc_read: this route exists for types that have no package and no sidecar, which is exactly what stops gc_read addressing them.

parameters.name: include_native
parameters.description: type_path only, and structs only: report inherited/native members as well as the struct's own.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Target Blueprint/Widget Blueprint. Required except for a context-free widgets fragment.

parameters.name: ir
parameters.description: Headerless hypothetical fragment. Required for widgets, graph, and functions.

parameters.name: graph_name
parameters.description: Exact graph/function name providing K2 context for graph or functions.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Optional exact component handle. Omit to describe them all. Covers this Blueprint's own SCS components AND the NATIVE ones its C++ parent built - and for a native component the handle is its FName, not the name the Details panel shows: a Character's are CharacterMesh0, CollisionCylinder and CharMoveComp, where the panel says Mesh, CapsuleComponent and CharacterMovement. Each native entry reports both names, so ask here before writing a components{} payload against a Character or Pawn.

parameters.name: parent_class
parameters.description: Prospective widget parent class; reveals the actual slot class.

parameters.name: parent_named_slot
parameters.description: Prospective named slot on parent_class for a widgets fragment.

parameters.name: max_inline_options
parameters.description: Maximum inline enum choices per reflected property (default 64, maximum 512).

parameters.name: describe_aliases
parameters.description: For graph/functions, aliases to return in detail after constructing the whole fragment.

parameters.name: include_option_hints
parameters.description: For graph/functions, include bounded pin/property option hints.

parameters.name: selection_requests
parameters.description: Contextual value searches in the underlying widget or graph describe format.

tools.name: gc_diff
tools.description:
The same `.gc` at two versions, as a diff - or, with no asset_path, every `.gc` those two
versions disagree about.

  gc_diff()                                    -> WHICH files differ: HEAD vs working tree
  gc_diff(asset_path)                          -> that file's diff, HEAD vs working tree
  gc_diff(asset_path, from:"live", to:"HEAD")   -> unsaved editor state against the commit
  gc_diff(asset_path, from:"2026-08-04T09:00:00Z") -> against local history at that moment
  gc_diff(asset_path, from:"1am")              -> against what it was at 1am this morning
  gc_diff(asset_path, from:"HEAD", format:"split", blocks:["graph"]) -> both graphs, stacked
  gc_diff(from:"main", to:"saved")             -> every file this branch changed

Presence of asset_path is the only difference between the list and the diff, the same way
conflict_id splits gc_versions mode:"resolve".

A VERSION IS ONE OF FOUR THINGS:
  saved     the `.gc` file on disk (the default for `to`). `working` is an accepted alias
  live      this editor's own state, UNSAVED EDITS INCLUDED - no git client can ask this
  <ref>     any git revision: HEAD (the default for `from`), main, origin/x, a sha
  <when>    a moment in local history
`saved` IS THE SAME WORD gc_read AND gc_apply USE for the same state, which is the point:
one vocabulary across every verb. UNSAVED WORK IS `live`, on all of them - `saved` and
`working` both mean the file that is already on disk.
`saved`, `working` and `live` are RESERVED WORDS. A git branch really can be called `live`
and it is not reachable here - rename it or pass its sha.

A MOMENT IS WRITTEN THE WAY A PERSON SAYS ONE, and every form is LOCAL time except the
ISO one, which carries its own zone. `at_local` in mode:"history" is the clock these read
against:
  1am, 1:30pm, 13:00, 13:00:05    the most recent time that reads that way - today if it
                                  has passed, yesterday if it has not
  today, yesterday                that day's midnight
  today 3pm, yesterday 13:00      that day at that clock
  2026-08-28, 2026-08-28 09:00    an explicit date, with or without a clock
  2h ago, 30m ago, 3 days ago     counted back from now (s/m/h/d/w, spelled out or not)
  2026-08-04T09:00:00Z            ISO-8601
  <id>                            an entry id from gc_versions mode:"history"
THE REPLY SAYS WHICH INSTANT THE WORD BECAME - `asked_at` and `asked_at_local` on each
side - because `1am` at half past midnight means LAST night's, and nothing else in the
answer would show that. These forms are reserved the same way `live` is: `today` and
`yesterday` are not reachable as branch names here, and no other bare word was taken.
A NUMBER ALONE IS NEVER A CLOCK - `13` stays a ref, because it is also a short sha; a time
has to carry a `:` or an am/pm.

THE LIST IS ENUMERATED DIFFERENTLY PER PAIR, and the response says which way, because the
honest scope differs. Two git-ish versions are one `git diff --name-only`. Anything against
`live` can only differ where this editor holds an unsaved package, so that is the scope -
projecting every asset in the project to answer would cost minutes and find the same set.
Anything against a moment is scoped to the assets local history actually holds.

DIGEST-ONLY CHANGES ARE REPORTED AS SUCH. `sig:` and `bin:` move on every regeneration, so
a file whose only difference is its own digests has not changed in any sense a person
means: `differs` is false for it while `raw_differs` is true.

TWO WAYS TO LAY THE ANSWER OUT, and `changed_only` composes with both.
  format:"unified" (default)  one stream: `-` and `+` lines in file order
  format:"split"             TOP AND BOTTOM. The `from` version as one document, then the
                             `to` version as another, every line marked - `-` for what
                             went, `+` for what came, a space where they agree. With
                             changed_only:false that is gc_read of both versions at once,
                             marked; with it true the top holds only what went and the
                             bottom only what came, which is the changed-only answer laid
                             out the same way rather than a different one.
Both formats render the SAME comparison. Nothing is compared twice, so the counts in the
reply and the marks on the page cannot disagree.

`blocks` IS gc_read's OWN, over the same scanner: blocks:["graph"] compares just that
block of both versions, envelope kept so each pane still says which asset it is. A version
that will not parse, or that lacks every name asked for, is compared WHOLE and says so in
`sliced` - answering it with nothing would read as `this version had no graph`.

It reads. Nothing here writes a file, an asset, or the git index - not even the working
tree. To make a version real, use gc_apply.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Asset or package path. Omit to list every file the two versions disagree about.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: The left side, and the EARLIER end: "saved", "live", a git ref, or a moment. A moment is written the way a person says one and read in LOCAL time - "1am", "13:00", "yesterday", "yesterday 3pm", "2026-08-28", "2h ago" - or as ISO-8601, or as an entry id from mode:"history". The reply says which instant it became, in asked_at and asked_at_local. Default HEAD.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: The right side, and the LATER end. Same vocabulary, clock words included. Default "saved" (the file on disk); "working" is an accepted alias for it.

parameters.name: changed_only
parameters.description: Single-file mode: return only the changed lines rather than the whole file. Composes with either format - in "split" it leaves the top pane holding only what went and the bottom only what came. Default true.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: How the single-file answer is laid out. "unified" (default) is one stream of `-` and `+` lines in file order. "split" is TOP AND BOTTOM: the `from` version as one document, then the `to` version, every line marked - which with changed_only:false is gc_read of both versions at once. Same comparison either way; only the layout differs.

parameters.name: blocks
parameters.description: Single-file mode: compare only these blocks, e.g. ["graph"] or ["widgets","properties"]. gc_read's own parameter over the same scanner; a comma-separated string is accepted too. The envelope is kept on both sides so each pane still names its asset. A version that will not parse, or that carries none of the names, is compared whole and says so in `sliced`.

tools.name: gc_history
tools.description:
Which versions of a `.gc` this project can still speak for. Local history archives the
previous canonical body on every save that changed one, and this is the list.

  gc_history()                 -> the project: what is tracked, and how far back
  gc_history(asset_path)       -> that asset's versions, newest first

TWO DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, which is why the parameter changes the answer rather than
filtering it. `How far back can I go` is a PROJECT fact - and asking it per asset is how
somebody concludes the store is empty when it is merely young.

NOTHING TRIMS ITSELF. `budget_bytes` is the figure a launch WARNS above, not one anything
enforces: no save, sweep or tool deletes a version you did not ask it to. A store past
that figure is a message, not a countdown.

EVERY VERSION IS A FILE, AND THE ANSWER SAYS WHERE. A version is one `.gcc` - ordinary
canonical GraphCode text - named for its own `id`, so the entry `BP_X_2026_08_28_...` is
the file `BP_X_2026_08_28_....gcc`. `store_root` is the folder the whole store lives
under; with an asset_path, `store_directory` is that asset's own folder inside it. They
are ordinary files you may read, copy or delete by hand - nothing here holds a lock on
them, and the gap between `tracking_since` and `earliest_restorable` is exactly what has
already been deleted that way.

An `id` from here is a version spec for gc_versions mode:"diff", as is any moment: an
ISO-8601 instant, a clock (1am, 13:00), a named day (today, yesterday, "yesterday 3pm"),
a date, or a count back ("2h ago"). `at` is UTC;
`at_local` is the same moment as a person would write it, and the clock words above are
read against that same local clock.

TWO TIMES, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME. `tracking_since` (T) is stamped once by a clean
whole-project sync and never moves; `earliest_restorable` is as far back as the store can
actually reach today. The gap between them is what has already been removed by hand. A
project with no stamp reports tracking_since empty, and a revert to a MOMENT refuses until
it has one - a revert to a branch or to the last commit does not.

It reads. Nothing here writes a file, an asset, or git.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Asset or package path, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login. Omit for the project-wide answer.

tools.name: gc_import
tools.description:
Import a source file in two steps, so the settings are something you READ rather than
guess. Call it once with no `document` to PLAN, and once with the document to IMPORT.

  1. gc_import(source, destination)      -> a kind:import document. Creates NOTHING.
  2. edit the settings in that text
  3. gc_import(document: <the edited text>) -> runs the import

The plan is the pipeline stack Interchange itself would use for this file, read from the
project's Interchange settings and each pipeline's class defaults. There is no table of
import settings anywhere in GraphCode, so the plan cannot drift from what the editor does.
Only deviations from those defaults are written, so an unedited plan is nearly empty and a
diff of two plans is the settings that differ.

The pipeline settings you want are usually in the NESTED blocks. An Interchange pipeline is
a few scalars plus instanced sub-pipelines - MeshPipeline, MaterialPipeline,
CommonMeshesProperties - and those children carry most of what a person edits.

A TEXTURE PLAN ALSO CARRIES settings { }, WHICH IS THE ASSET'S OWN GRAMMAR AND NOT THE
PIPELINES'. A pipeline decides how the file is READ; settings state what the asset
becomes - CompressionSettings, SRGB, MipGenSettings, LODGroup, AddressX/AddressY. It is the
same block kind:texture_2d projects, written by the same writer against the same policy, so
every name you spell here is a name you will read back in the sidecar - which will also show
what the pipeline chose, since both are deviations from the class default. gc_describe
kind:"texture_2d" is where the spellings are. The block ships empty: name only what you want
changed, and anything you leave out keeps whatever the pipeline chose. It is applied AFTER
the import, to the single texture_2d the file produces, which costs one extra encode; an
import that produces no texture or several refuses the block by name and leaves the
imported assets alone. Only a texture-only source gets the block at all - one settings
block cannot mean a mesh and its three textures.

WHAT GUARDS STEP 2 IS THE SOURCE FILE, NOT sig:. You are meant to edit the body between
the calls, so its digest cannot be the staleness check; the import block carries
source_hash and the import refuses when the file on disk no longer matches it.

AN ARCHIVE IS A SOURCE. Point `source` at a .zip or .7z (also .tar, .tgz, .tar.gz,
.tar.bz2, .tar.xz) and it is unpacked under Intermediate/, and the plan gains a
members { } block listing every file inside it this build can import. THE WHOLE BATCH IS
ONE DOCUMENT WITH ONE SET OF SETTINGS - that is the point rather than a shortcut: a pack's
192 meshes share one pipeline stack, so you decide the settings once and every member is
imported with them. Edit the batch by DELETING member lines. `destination` is a FOLDER for
an archive and the archive's own directory tree is mirrored under it, with folder names
Unreal rejects repaired, so FBX/Colobus and GLTF/Colobus do not collide. `members:` on the
plan call narrows it before the document is written, which is worth doing on a big pack -
it takes wildcards over the path inside the archive.

Members that do not all import through ONE route are refused by name: a pack's meshes want
the Assets stack, its loose PNGs want Textures and its .mp3 wants SoundFactory, and one
document carries one set of settings. Plan each group with its own members pattern. A
member that fails on its own does NOT fail the batch - the result names it in
failed_members and the rest still import.

TWO IMPORT ENGINES, AND A DOCUMENT RUNS ONE. Where Interchange claims the format the plan
carries pipelines { } (FBX, glTF, OBJ, images, and whatever else this build's translators
claim). Where it does not, the plan carries factory { } instead and the editor's own
UFactory runs it - that is how audio imports, because a stock build ships every
Interchange audio flag off. A factory entry is the same rule 7 shape and its EditAnywhere
settings are what you can edit: SoundFactory(bAutoCreateCue=true, CueVolume=0.5). There is
no stack line on a factory plan, because there is no pipeline list for one to guard, and a
document carrying BOTH blocks is refused. A factory that also creates assets it does not
hand back - a SoundCue beside the wave - is still reported and still saved.

A pipeline stack with per-translator overrides is HANDLED, not refused: UE's stock Assets
stack defines them, so the plan resolves the same override list the editor would.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Absolute path to the file to import. Required when planning.

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: Where it lands: a folder (/Game/Props), existing or new. To choose the asset name, use an explicit object path (/Game/Props/SM_Chair.SM_Chair). A plain path always means a folder; its existence never changes meaning. A plain path ending in the file's own name (/Game/FX/T_Fire for T_Fire.png) is refused rather than nested: write /Game/FX/T_Fire.T_Fire for the asset, or /Game/FX/T_Fire/ for that folder. Required when planning.

parameters.name: members
parameters.description: Wildcards over the paths inside an ARCHIVE source, narrowing what the plan lists: ["*.fbx"] or ["3D Files/FBX/*"]. Omit to list every member this build can import. It is a convenience for a large pack — the document still states exactly what will import, and deleting lines from its members { } block narrows it further. Refused on a source that is one file, which has no members.

parameters.name: document
parameters.description: A kind:import document from a previous plan, edited or not. Its presence is what makes this call an import rather than a plan.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: Resolve the document - every pipeline, every property path - and import nothing. Proves structure, not values: whether a value imports into the property it names is only answerable by importing it.

parameters.name: save
parameters.description: Save every asset the import creates. Default true - a write finishes itself. Pass false only if you mean to leave them in memory, and know that an imported asset exists nowhere else: an editor that closes loses the whole import.

tools.name: gc_invoke
tools.description:
Activate one thing a `.gc` document names, in the live editor, by its authored name. TWO HANDLES, chosen by which one you pass - there are no coordinates, no Slate paths and no ids to invent for either.
`function` CALLS A FUNCTION on a live object: an actor in the open level, an open Editor Utility Widget, any instance of the class at `asset_path`. `[call_in_editor]` IS NOT REQUIRED - that flag only decides whether a PERSON gets a button in the details panel, and a button is also why the panel's own list stops at parameterless functions. Anything a Blueprint graph could call, this calls, with named arguments in the `.gc` value grammar (`args:"Damage=50,Knockback=true"`, in any order; positional is refused). It takes the same transaction and the same editor script guard the CallInEditor button takes, so undo behaves identically - and so an ordinary function runs in the editor world AT ALL, which without that guard it silently would not. Return and out parameters come back in `observed`; what the call wrote to the console comes back in `log`, so a function whose only evidence is a Print String still answers something - and `log` is also the dial for HOW MUCH of it, because a caller stepping one function twenty times pays for those lines twenty times. A repeated line is folded into one entry with a `count`, whichever setting you use. WHICH OBJECT is `instance`, AND OMITTING IT IS A REQUEST TO CHOOSE RATHER THAN A REFUSAL - most calls are a singleton or a function under test, where which instance was never the question. The strongest claim wins: on screen, then selected in the editor, then in the open level, ties broken by object path so the same one is chosen every run. It always says which and why in `warnings`, with the path to pass back; when nothing separated them, `instances` rides along on the success so a different one costs no second call. An instance in a Blueprint editor's preview scene or in PIE is listed but never chosen for you - name it to mean it. A level path plus `instance` addresses any actor in the open level, whether or not it has a Blueprint.
`widget` PRESSES A WIDGET in an already-open Widget Blueprint instance: it broadcasts the delegate a click fires - OnClicked by default, any parameterless event via `event`.
IT NEVER SYNTHESISES INPUT. The Automation Driver would take the user's real mouse and keyboard away for the duration; this fires the bound delegate instead and leaves the machine alone. That also means it can fire a handler no person could reach, which is why it CHECKS WHAT A REAL CLICK WOULD NEED first: realised, in a window, visible, hit-testable, non-zero size, and reachable by a hit test at its centre - the same call the engine's own mouse input makes, so a disabled ancestor or a dialog on top fails it and is named. Every condition comes back separately. Not clickable is REFUSED unless require_clickable:false, which fires anyway and says the click could not have happened - that tests the handler, not the control. Parameterised events (OnCheckStateChanged, OnTextCommitted) are refused rather than fired with invented values: a UMG event of that shape reports a change the widget has already made, so broadcasting one without making that change tells the handler something the widget itself contradicts.
WHAT RUNS IS THE ASSET'S OWN CODE and it can do anything a Blueprint can do; an Editor Utility Widget's button may delete assets or run a commandlet. Both handles report what they are about to reach before reaching it, and `dry_run:true` reports exactly that and fires nothing.
Needs the instance actually live - gc_invoke addresses live objects, not the asset - WITH ONE EXCEPTION, AND IT IS THE ASSET SCRIPTS. An AssetActionUtility or ActorActionUtility is never placed, never opened and never spawned: the right-click menu builds one, runs the function and drops it. So `function` builds one the same way when you name no `instance`, and says it did. That object carries no state between calls, and it reads the CONTENT BROWSER or the LEVEL selection the same way the menu's would - `warnings` names what is selected, including when nothing is, which is the difference between a call that worked and one that looped zero times. A utility whose function takes its subject as a parameter needs no selection at all: pass it with `args`, the way the menu forwards a matching first parameter one asset at a time. gc_render source:"live" is the read-only half: observe first, then press.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: The asset whose live instance to act on, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login

parameters.name: function
parameters.description: The function to call on a live object of that class. Does not need `[call_in_editor]`.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: Named arguments for `function`: `Damage=50,Knockback=true`, any order, `.gc` value grammar. Positional is refused — a signature's order is not something you can read off the document. A STRUCT is a parenthesised field list, `Where=(X=1,Y=2)`, and A CONTAINER IS A PARENTHESISED LIST TOO, not a bracketed one: an array is `Points=((X=1,Y=2),(X=3,Y=4))`, `Names=("a","b")` and `()` when empty; a map is `Slots=((Key,Value),(Key,Value))`. The `callables` list names each parameter's full type, element type included, and marks only the ones that come BACK as `(out)`.

parameters.name: log
parameters.description: How much of the console log the call brings back. `loud` (default) is the errors and warnings in full, with the quieter lines counted in `log_quiet` and left behind; `all` is every line it wrote; `none` watches nothing at all, and then `log_errors` is absent rather than zero. UNDER EVERY MODE, A LINE THE CALL WROTE MORE THAN ONCE COMES BACK ONCE, carrying `count` - so a complaint printed on every iteration of a loop costs a number rather than a line, and the 200-line cap counts DISTINCT lines.

parameters.name: widget
parameters.description: The authored widget name inside it, as the document spells it. Presses that widget instead.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: Which declared event to fire. Default OnClicked - the one a mouse click fires. Must take no parameters.

parameters.name: instance
parameters.description: Which live object. THREE SPELLINGS, all accepted: its name, an actor's outliner label, or the full object path every list here prints - and the path is the one to use when the name is not unique, which for widgets and component Blueprints it routinely is not. OMIT IT AND `function` CHOOSES: on screen beats selected in the editor beats in the open level, and equals are broken by object path. Which one and why comes back in `warnings`; a tie also brings `instances` so retargeting costs no second call. A preview scene or a running game is still never chosen for you. AN ASSET OR ACTOR ACTION HAS NO LIVE OBJECT EVER, so omitting this is what lets one be built for the call; naming an instance there refuses rather than inventing a target you did not choose. `widget` is stricter - it refuses several on screen with the list, because pressing an arbitrary one of 57 live buttons is not what any caller meant; the rest are counted rather than printed, since one in no Slate window has nothing to click.

parameters.name: require_clickable
parameters.description: Refuse when a real click could not have reached the widget. false fires anyway and warns.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: Report the preconditions and every handler that would run, and fire nothing.

tools.name: gc_layout
tools.description:
Tidy one live Blueprint graph headlessly, preserving the aliases and node GUIDs gc_read
returned. Omit aliases (or pass []) for the whole graph; otherwise every value must be an
exact statement alias such as n4. Unknown aliases refuse the entire call. Pass the document
sig: as base_sig - the one on the gc 1 line, the same value gc_apply takes - so a stale read
cannot move the wrong nodes. A renumbered alias still RESOLVES; the sig is what catches it.

Reaches BLUEPRINTS (by graph_name) and MATERIALS / MATERIAL FUNCTIONS (which have one
unnamed graph, so they take no graph_name). A material keeps positions on its expressions
rather than on graph nodes, and only those move: no wire is touched.
This is a LAYOUT-ONLY binary asset edit. Positions are deliberately absent from .gc, so the
response reports every node move and comment-box move/resize and says sidecar_changed:false.
It never compiles, reconstructs nodes, mints GUIDs, or rewrites the sidecar. It DOES save
what it moved - save:false leaves the asset dirty instead. dry_run returns the identical
movement report without writing or saving.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Blueprint, material or material function asset/package path, e.g. /Game/Blueprints/BP_Door or /Game/Materials/M_Glass.

parameters.name: graph_name
parameters.description: Exact EventGraph, function, or macro graph name. REQUIRED FOR A BLUEPRINT AND ILLEGAL FOR A MATERIAL, whose one graph has no name - the `graph { }` block a material projects to carries none - so a material takes no graph_name and reports an empty one back.

parameters.name: base_sig
parameters.description: The document sig: from the `gc 1` line of the gc_read you took the aliases from - the same value gc_apply takes. Required; a stale one refuses without moving anything.

parameters.name: aliases
parameters.description: Statement aliases to move. Omit or pass [] to lay out the whole graph.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: Report exact node and comment movements without changing the asset.

parameters.name: save
parameters.description: Save the asset once nodes have moved. Default true - a write finishes itself. Pass false to leave it dirty for a caller staging work by hand.

parameters.name: horizontal_spacing
parameters.description: Horizontal gap in graph units, 16..2048.

parameters.name: vertical_spacing
parameters.description: Vertical gap in graph units, 16..2048.

tools.name: gc_market
tools.description:
The GraphCode Market: signed packs of GraphCode text (shape presets, Move pose libraries, guides,
agent skills) to
find, install into this project and use. Free; no purchase, no entitlement check.

  mode:"search", target:"chip"                      -> packs whose title, entries, tags or summary match
  mode:"search", kind:"shape", state:"installed"     -> filters, no words needed
  mode:"describe", pack:"GraphCode/Damage"          -> form, library, entries with every setting, choices,
                                                     needs, used by, requires, description
  mode:"install", pack:"GraphCode/Damage", dry_run:true -> what would be written, nothing written
  mode:"install", pack:"GraphCode/Damage"           -> installs it and every pack it needs, first
  mode:"list" | mode:"update" [pack] | mode:"remove", pack

EVERY PACK ANSWER CARRIES EACH ENTRY'S IMPORT LINE AND CALL EXAMPLE, ready to paste into a file.
A pack installs to /Game/GraphCodeMarket/<Publisher>/<Name>/ and is recorded in
Content/GraphCodeMarket/market.lock.json; gc_search kind:"preset" then finds its entries with
source:"market". A skill pack is also copied to .claude/skills/<Name>/, and the answer says so.

NOTHING IS WRITTEN UNLESS EVERYTHING CHECKS: the catalog's signature, then every file's SHA-256,
then the dependencies (each a minimum version within its major) and the products each pack
requires. A pack is written as one swap: a failure leaves the old version whole. Each refusal
names its code, the pack, the file and the reason: bad_signature, bad_catalog, hash_mismatch,
bad_id, path_escape, dependency_cycle, version_conflict, missing_product, missing_pack,
edited_files, needed_by, no_content_folder, not_installed, bad_lock, skill_exists, bad_query,
unreachable, write_failed, cancelled, outside_pack (a file writes or reads outside its pack).

update never writes over a file you edited (edited_files names them); remove moves the pack's
text to the trash (Content/__MCPTrash, never emptied for you), refuses while another installed pack
needs it, and leaves assets you built. Building a pack's assets is NOT this verb: gc_apply its main
file, an authoring write that needs a GraphCode authoring licence. `main` in the install and describe
answers is the main file's asset path WITHOUT its extension (/Game/GraphCodeMarket/GraphCode/Damage/Damage):
pass it to gc_apply as asset_path. A pack's `form` says what it is (Operation, Mesh, Mesh + Operation,
Poses, Guide, Skill). A LIBRARY (library:true: every file builds nothing, e.g. the Move pose libraries)
has no build: use it from your own file (a Move library's `use` line goes in your clip file's header).

MATERIALS AND TEXTURES (R20): a pack may bring its own materials (describe says materials:true) and an
OPTIONAL texture set (describe's textures: files and bytes). install downloads the textures only with
textures:true; installing again with it adds them to a pack installed without. Building the pack (gc_apply
its main file, or the tab's Build) first makes its materials: with the textures, imported and bound; without,
flat colours under the same names, upgraded in place once the textures are installed and it is built again.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: "search", "describe" or "list" read; "install", "update" or "remove" write.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: search: what to look for, in plain words, matched over title, entry names, tags and summary; every word must match. Filters are their own parameters, not words in here.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: search: only packs of this kind: "shape", "move", "rig", "groom", "garment", "gc", "guide" or "skill".

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: search: only packs carrying this tag (the tab calls tags Category).

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: search: "installed", "updates" (installed with a newer version in the catalog) or "available" (not installed). Omit for all.

parameters.name: needs
parameters.description: search: needs:"GraphCode/Profiles" lists the packs that depend on Profiles (its dependents). What a pack itself depends on is in describe.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description: search: "relevance" (the default with words), "updated" (the default without) or "name".

parameters.name: max_results
parameters.description: search: at most this many packs (default 50). The answer's total_matches, returned and truncated say how many matched and how many came back.

parameters.name: pack
parameters.description: A pack id, <Publisher>/<Name>, e.g. GraphCode/Damage. Required for describe, install and remove; update without it updates every installed pack that has a newer version.

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: install: an exact version. Omit for the newest. One version of a pack per project.

parameters.name: textures
parameters.description: install: also download the pack's optional textures (describe says how many and how large). Without them its materials build as flat colours. Installing again with textures:true adds them to a pack installed without (refused, edited_files, when you changed its files). An update keeps textures you have. Default false.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: install, update, remove: plan and write nothing. It checks the dependencies, versions, products, edited files and what a remove would move; on a local catalog it also fetches and checks every file's SHA-256. On the hosted catalog nothing is downloaded, so the hashes are checked at the real install. Default false.

tools.name: gc_read_live
tools.description:
Project the asset AS IT IS IN THE RUNNING EDITOR, unsaved edits included, into the same
one-document `.gc` blocks gc_read returns from disk. This is the backend half of
gc_read's source:'live'; call gc_read, not this, unless you are the bridge.

It replaces bp_read and ui_read at once: a Widget Blueprint comes back with widgets{} AND
graph{} in ONE document, so the asset no longer needs two tools to be seen. Ask for what
you want with blocks:['graph'] rather than by picking a different tool.

Nothing is written. No sidecar is created, nothing is dirtied, and an asset outside /Game
or excluded from GraphCode still reads fine - it simply reports sidecar:'none' and carries
no sig:, because there is no file for a signature to be a signature OF.

THE SIGNATURE IS CONDITIONAL AND THAT IS THE POINT. A `.gc` has exactly one legal
rendering per asset; that is what makes sig: a digest. Set include_inherited,
include_defaults, verify_values or graph_name and the text is no longer that rendering, so
the response comes back sig:'none' with non_canonical listing what did it. Text like that
is for reading. Do not send it to gc_apply and do not pass its sig as base_sig.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Asset or package path, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login. AN ACTOR is addressed by its object path - /Game/Maps/M.M:PersistentLevel.FixtureSun - which on a One File Per Actor or World Partition map resolves to the actor's OWN package, whose name is a content hash and contains the actor's name nowhere. That is the path gc_search kind:"asset" returns and the one a .gc writes for a cross-actor reference.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Pass 'regions' to read the open level's .gcw with live navigation staleness recomputed. Pass 'rig' to read a skeletal mesh or skeleton back out as .gcrig text: a STARTING declaration you edit, not this asset's canonical text. It carries every bone's name, parent, place and, where the source frame differs from the derived one, orientation= - and no range=, closes=, regions or skin, because a skeleton holds none of those. It writes no file, so nothing you author onto a readout can be overwritten by another.

parameters.name: blocks
parameters.description: Block names to return, e.g. ['graph'] or ['widgets','properties']. Omit for all. Names not in the document come back under missing_blocks rather than as an error.

parameters.name: include_body
parameters.description: Return each block's text. False returns the envelope and block inventory only.

parameters.name: graph_name
parameters.description: Restrict graph/functions to one graph by exact name. NON-CANONICAL: suppresses sig:.

parameters.name: include_inherited
parameters.description: Include inherited variables - hundreds of entries on a Character subclass. NON-CANONICAL: suppresses sig:.

parameters.name: include_defaults
parameters.description: Widgets: include reflected properties equal to class/slot defaults. NON-CANONICAL: suppresses sig:.

parameters.name: verify_values
parameters.description: Widgets: prove every value survives export-import-export, reporting the rest as UNSUPPORTED. Slower. NON-CANONICAL: suppresses sig:.

tools.name: gc_render
tools.description:
Render one material, material instance, material function, static mesh, skeletal mesh, Actor Blueprint or the OPEN LEVEL off-screen and look at it. Text answers what was authored; this answers what it looks like, which no .gc can carry.
THE CAMERA IS THE POINT. Omit it and the subject's whole bounding box is fitted through both fields of view - not by sphere radius, which frames a tall or wide subject by its diagonal - and the angle is chosen by scoring how much of the subject each direction actually shows. To adjust, send back the compact pose with one number changed: azimuth rotates around the subject's up axis, elevation moves above or below it and clamps short of +-90, zoom is logarithmic so zoom:1 is twice the size on a doorknob and on a building, and offset is in box half-extents so [0,0,1] aims at the top face of anything, or {"value":[0,0,20],"unit":"cm"} when 20 cm is what you mean. azimuth 0 is the subject's own front, not a compass direction. On a skeletal figure - a skeletal mesh, an animation on its preview mesh, the body a Blueprint plays animation: on - that is the FIGURE's front, the axis its mesh faces (a MetaHuman faces +Y), so front, right, left and rear are the figure's own; camera.basis world orbits the preview's own axes instead.
One to eight named views per call. With exactly one the PNG comes back inline as well as on disk; with several only the paths come back, because eight images is not a reply.
Output defaults to a transient folder under Saved and costs nothing to omit. To keep the pictures, set output.lifetime persistent and a path - a directory, or a template using {asset} {kind} {view} {capture} {date}. output.overwrite is refuse, replace or unique and never chooses for you. An absolute path needs output.external; a path under Content/ needs output.content, because Unreal will auto-import the PNG as a UTexture2D asset that then enters the corpus - it is allowed, it just has to be meant.
A material function renders through the preview material its author already chose, and refuses by name when none is set.
Named views are aliases and nothing more: camera can be the string front, rear, left, right, top or isometric, and what comes back is the azimuth and elevation it lowered to, ready to adjust.
An Actor Blueprint is spawned into an isolated preview world and its construction script runs, so what is framed includes what the script built. Bounds come from the engine's own rule first - a visible, non-hidden static mesh, skeletal mesh or geometry collection component with geometry assigned, which is what every Content Browser thumbnail is framed by. When that finds nothing, every visible non-editor primitive is measured instead and the result warns bounds_widened; that is what frames a Paper2D sprite, flipbook or tile map, which the engine's list does not know. No BeginPlay, no tick, no package dirtied.
A LEVEL is the map currently open in this editor, named as the asset. Any other map refuses by name and is never loaded, because opening one would install a second world beside yours.
