A level has no automatic camera - whole-map bounds are a sky sphere and a landscape - so it needs one of four: camera.anchor {actor:"Name"} or {actors:[...]} to orbit what is placed there, camera.anchor {region:"$Crypt"} to frame a ROOM YOU AUTHORED in the level's .gcw, camera {actor:"CineCameraActor_2", adjust:{truck,pedestal,dolly,yaw,pitch,roll}} to look through a camera somebody put in the map, or camera {location:[x,y,z], rotation or look_at} for a shot whose position matters. One actor orbits ITS OWN forward; a set orbits world axes; camera.basis world says so explicitly. A REGION FRAMES ITS OWN ORIENTED PRISM - the room somebody drew, not the union of whatever is standing in it - and orbits its own forward:, AIMING AT ITS ANCHOR. A region missing either its min: or its max: is a column, so the picture frames its PLAN at the anchor's height and the result warns region_is_column rather than inventing a ceiling. Adjustments are applied to a copy - the camera actor, your viewport, your selection and the map are all left exactly as they were, and the render FAILS rather than warns if any of them moved. What you see is the map's own lighting and post-process with game show flags, so no grid, icons, selection outlines or editor overlays.
Nothing is compiled, dirtied or saved. Requires an editor with a GPU: under -nullrhi it refuses and says so rather than returning a blank image. It waits for the subject's own shaders itself, at high priority and for up to 60 s (shader_wait_seconds in the result), so a fresh editor's first render needs no throwaway; only if they are still compiling then is the result marked incomplete rather than passed off as final.
THE OTHER DIRECTION: mode:"ask" takes up to 64 named image pixels from one retained capture and answers in text. A mesh preview returns MESH-LOCAL coordinates; depth 0 is the entry surface, 0.5 the midpoint through the entered part, and 1 its corresponding exit. A level returns WORLD coordinates and names the actor and component hit. It never edits a .gcrig or level. mode:"screen_to_world" remains the single normalized-pixel form for level placement. Both modes deproject through the exact retained camera.
mode:"screen_to_world" points at a pixel of a LEVEL capture this tool already took and returns the world surface it is on - location, normal, actor, component, distance. A model writing a level has never seen the room, so it writes coordinates, and guessed coordinates are a grid: round numbers, even spacing, everything hovering slightly off the floor. This lets it look instead of infer. Pass the capture id from an earlier render plus x and y normalized to [0,1] with (0,0) at the image's TOP-LEFT; a coordinate outside that is refused rather than clamped, because a clamped pixel is a different pixel. It deprojects through the EXACT camera that took the picture - not your viewport, not a recomputed orbit, not a named camera actor re-read now, all three of which can differ. trace_channel and object_types are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE and are not the same question: Visibility and Camera are trace CHANNELS, while WorldStatic is an object TYPE and belongs in object_types. The hit always names its actor and component, so glass, a translucent mesh or an unexpected prop cannot quietly pass for the wall you meant, and a MISS IS A NORMAL ANSWER - hit:false with the ray it traced, never (0,0,0) and never a guessed fallback. Only captures of the open level qualify: a preview render of an asset has no world coordinate to return, and a capture taken before the level's collision geometry changed refuses too, because tracing a new world through old pixels returns a confident wrong answer. It writes nothing at all; placing something is a separate, explicit gc_apply.

parameters.name: asset
parameters.description: Material, material instance, material function, static mesh, skeletal mesh, animation sequence, Actor Blueprint or open-level path, e.g. /Game/Materials/M_Wood, /Game/Meshes/SM_Tower, /Game/Fauna/SK_Deer, /Game/Anim/A_Walk, /Game/Blueprints/BP_Door or /Game/Maps/Lobby. An animation plays on its skeleton's preview mesh: at: poses it, to/fps/count play it.

parameters.name: overlay
parameters.description: Optional static mesh drawn in vertex colour on top of a static mesh, skeletal mesh or animation preview, ignoring depth. Use a rig diagnostic's DIAG_*_Bones asset here to see the coloured rig over the real mesh without replacing its authored materials. A garment's DIAG_*_Rings needs no overlay: named as the asset, it is drawn on its own body and the answer carries a legend naming each ring by colour.

parameters.name: reference
parameters.description: A reference picture (a PNG/JPG path, relative to the project or absolute) put BESIDE each view, scaled to its height: each view's answer gains beside_reference, the side-by-side file. A picture to look at, not a measure - a .gcshape measures itself against its pictures with [reference=$Ref] on the build line.

parameters.name: animation
parameters.description: Optional animation sequence played on a Groom's skeletal target, so hair is seen on a head that moves. at: poses the clip; simulate:true plays it from zero under the hair's own physics, which collides with the target's physics asset. The clip must be for the target's skeleton. On a MetaHuman character it plays on the body, with its correctives, and the head and what it wears follow; at: poses it. On an Actor Blueprint it plays on the skeletal mesh that leads its own pose and whose skeleton the clip is for, and the parts that follow it and what hangs on its sockets come along, so a built clip is seen on the whole character; at:/to: pose it and highlights bones and trails read that body. Preview only: nothing is written.

parameters.name: camera
parameters.description:
One of three forms, or just a preset name as a string. Orbit: {azimuth, elevation, zoom, offset, preset, basis: local|world, anchor}, where anchor is 'auto', 'origin', {actor:'Name'}, {actors:['A','B']}, {point:[x,y,z], radius:r}, or on a previewed asset {component:'Hand'} or {component:'Hand', bone:'index_03_r', radius:r} (a socket name works as a bone; the bone alone finds its component), framed where it stands at the view's first moment. Over a span a bone is followed (the camera moves with it, turning no more; camera_followed, each frame's camera in its row); a component alone stays framed where it stood. Named level camera: {actor:'CineCameraActor_2', adjust:{truck, pedestal, dolly, yaw, pitch, roll}} - distances in cm along the camera's own right/up/forward, angles in degrees, applied to a copy. Absolute: {location:[x,y,z], rotation:[pitch,yaw,roll] OR look_at:[x,y,z]}. Every orbit field is optional; an omitted angle is still chosen for you.
INSIDE IT: camera {inside:true} STANDS AT THE AIM POINT AND LOOKS OUT, which is how you photograph the inside of a tower, a room or a level rather than its outside. The same azimuth shows you the same face either way - azimuth 0 frames the subject's front from outside, and inside it looks at that same front from within - so turning round is the number you already know. offset moves the eye in box half-extents, so [0,0,0.5] stands halfway up, and {"value":[0,0,160],"unit":"cm"} stands at eye height instead - the same {value, unit} pair a point's depth takes. zoom has no distance left to divide, so it moves the LENS instead: zoom:0 is a 90 degree horizontal field, because a 35 degree one standing in a room photographs a patch of wall, and zoom:1 is still twice the size. Perspective only - an orthographic picture does not depend on where its eye stands, so inside refuses there by name. AND IT CANNOT SEE INSIDE A SOLID: a closed mesh's faces point outward, so from within one there is nothing facing you and the picture is correctly empty. inside is for what HAS an inside; to look into something solid, cut it.
THE LENS AND THE GRADE go beside any of the three: fov (horizontal degrees), projection perspective|orthographic, ortho_width (cm the picture covers - required for an absolute ortho camera, optional on an orbit where zoom:0 fits one), exposure (compensation in stops, + is brighter), temperature (kelvin) and tint. ONE CALL HAS ONE EXPOSURE: where the scene meters (a level, or hair and other warmed-up previews) the first kept picture meters and every later view and frame is exposed at that reading (pinned_exposure in the result), with its own exposure stops on top; a level already set to manual exposure keeps its own. Every view states camera_location, camera_rotation, space and camera_fov (or projection and ortho_width when orthographic); pinned_exposure is always present, 0 when nothing metered. A level view warns how many Niagara components and Anim Blueprint characters in frame were not advanced. settings_from:'CineCameraActor_2' borrows a placed camera's focal length, projection and post-process WITHOUT its position - what this angle would look like through that camera. Explicit fields beat a borrowed one; omitting them all changes nothing.
A KEY THAT IS NOT ONE OF THE ABOVE IS REFUSED BY NAME, and the refusal lists what a camera does take. The six under adjust are the ones to watch: yaw and pitch turn a NAMED camera actor and belong inside adjust, while what rotates an orbit around a subject is azimuth and elevation. Sending yaw and pitch at the top level used to be dropped in silence, which returned the DEFAULT angle and reported success.

parameters.name: views
parameters.description: 1-8 of {name, width, height, camera, cut, below, view_mode, ignore, highlights, at, to, fps, count, sheet, video, simulate, physics}. Omit for one 1024x1024 view named main. A key that is not one of these is refused by name rather than dropped, and so is one inside camera or output - a silently discarded key is a picture of a different thing that looks like it worked.

parameters.name: at
parameters.description:
WHEN the picture is of, in seconds. Without it a capture is a picture of whatever moment the renderer happened to be at, so two captures of a panning material, a world-position-offset wobble or anything else reading engine time were never comparable. at pins the clock; the result says which moment it took.
MATERIALS AND ANYTHING READING ENGINE TIME get the moment for free, whatever the subject. A skeletal mesh is additionally POSED at it, in a preview render only: posing one in the open level would move an actor's animation state in the world you are looking at, and a capture does not change the level - so a level render warns (time_not_seekable) and you render the asset itself to pose it. A mesh driven by an animation blueprint evaluates a graph rather than a position and warns by the same name. NIAGARA: a Niagara system asset is advanced to at in its own preview; in the open level, simulate:true with at warms up the level's active Niagara components (reset, then advanced to at), and without simulate they are left as they are and the render warns time_not_seekable.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description:
The last moment of a SPAN, in seconds - this is how you render an animation. Needs at. How far (to), how fast (fps) and how many (count) are three ways of saying one span: STATE ANY TWO and the third follows. to+fps pins playback speed, to+count pins the ends, fps+count pins the length and needs no to at all. One alone refuses and all three refuses, rather than quietly picking two.
Frames share one camera, so they are frames rather than separate pictures, and each one costs a render: the frame count MULTIPLIES into the same total-pixel ceiling eight views have always shared, which is why an animation renders at 512 rather than 1024. The ceiling is 120 frames per view.

parameters.name: fps
parameters.description: Frames per second across the span. THE RATE IS KEPT EXACTLY AND THE SPAN IS WHAT GIVES: a span that is not a whole number of frames stops at the last whole one and the result says where it actually ended, because stretching the rate to meet 'to' would make the finished animation play at a speed nobody asked for.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Total frames, both ends included - the other way round from fps, where the ENDS are exact and the rate is whatever falls out. Use it when the span is the point ('eight pictures across this door opening') and playback speed is not. A span stating neither fps nor count takes 8 and says so.

parameters.name: sheet
parameters.description: The frames tiled into ONE image - the contact sheet. ON by default for a span and off for a single picture, because a result returns inline image content only when it holds exactly one picture: a 24-frame request without a sheet hands you 24 paths and no pixels. The sheet is the one image that shows the motion, so it is what comes back inline. Set false to skip it.

parameters.name: video
parameters.description: Also write an ANIMATION of the frames - the thing a person can play. Off by default: it is for a person, and you cannot read either format - ask for the sheet instead. "apng" (or true) writes <view>.anim.png: lossless, no encoder involved, works everywhere, and a valid PNG, so anything that has never heard of APNG shows the first frame. "mp4" writes <view>.mp4 as H.264 through the operating system's own encoder - smaller, scrubbable, what you want to send to a person, and lossy. mp4 is WINDOWS ONLY and needs even pixel dimensions; asked for where it cannot be written, an apng is written instead and a video_format_unavailable warning says why.

parameters.name: simulate
parameters.description: Opt in to running an Actor Blueprint's BeginPlay, Tick, components, timers and latent actions in an isolated preview world. Requires at; moments must be between 0 and 60 seconds. Advances from zero in steps no larger than 1/60 second, with a fresh world for each view. Combine with to/fps/count and video:true for motion capture. For N frames use at, to and fps in ONE call; each call re-simulates from zero, so N calls pay the whole lead-in N times. Default false keeps construction-only previews. On the open level it warms up the level's active Niagara effects: each is reset and advanced to at (seconds of warm-up) in 1/60 s steps, and a span keeps advancing them frame by frame; nothing else in the level moves and no package changes. Not supported for other asset kinds. Executes project code: no PIE, player or game instance is created, and isolation of the preview world does not sandbox external effects of that code. Authored randomness is retained. A view's at replaces the entire shared time configuration, including this flag.

parameters.name: physics
parameters.description: Enable native world collision and rigid-body physics for an Actor Blueprint preview. Requires simulate:true and at. Default false preserves the animation/event-only preview. Uses the Blueprint's own collision, gravity, constraints and Simulate Physics settings; does not turn every component into a rigid body. Include the floor or other colliders in the Blueprint assembly. Hidden thumbnail furniture cannot collide. Each view starts in a fresh isolated world. Not supported for the open level or standalone meshes; wrap those meshes in an Actor Blueprint. A per-view at replaces this flag with the other time settings. With physics off, a component that asks to simulate physics (Simulate Physics, or a SetSimulatePhysics call such as a ragdoll) holds its last pose, and the view warns so.

parameters.name: cut
parameters.description:
A SECTION CUT, so a basement or an upper storey can be photographed and traced. A top-down picture of a building is a picture of its ROOF; cut it and you get what an architect's plan is - walls cut through, doorways open as gaps, the floor visible between them. Everything between the camera and the plane is discarded, per triangle rather than per actor, so nothing has to be classified as belonging to a storey and a stairwell needs no answer.
THREE FORMS, one key, chosen by what you give it: 'z=90' is the plane at 90 cm up the world z axis (also x= and y=); [[x,y,z],[x,y,z]] is two points and the plane through them PERPENDICULAR TO THE VIEW, which refuses if they are not at one depth; three points is the plane through all three, and three points ON A LINE mean the VERTICAL plane through it - that is how you ask for a vertical section whatever the camera is doing.
It is a PLACE, never a clip distance, and it is exact at any angle: the cut is the plane you stated even when the view is not square-on to it, so two buildings cut horizontally are cut at the same height. Orthographic only - a section drawing is an orthographic picture, and a perspective cut refuses by name. The pick agrees with the picture for free: screen_to_world on a cut capture starts its ray ON the cut, so it returns the floor of the storey you cut and never the roof above it.

parameters.name: below
parameters.description: How far past the cut this picture sees, in cm, measured perpendicular to it - so a stairwell opening does not show the storey underneath through it. Needs a cut. Omit to see all the way down. NOT called depth: the frame legend already spends that word on each actor's distance from the camera.

parameters.name: view_mode
parameters.description:
WHAT THE RENDERER DRAWS of the scene - four entries from the editor viewport's own View Mode menu, and the same pictures, because this is the engine's own ApplyViewMode rather than a set of show flags picked here. 'lit' is the default and is every picture this tool has ever taken.
'unlit' is base colour with no lighting, shadows or fog - what you ask for when a picture came back black, and the mode that can photograph the inside of an unlit room. 'detail_lighting' puts the lighting on a neutral material: the shape without the albedo, which is how you tell a normal map from a texture that painted the shading on. 'lighting_only' is the other half of that - the light, with every material colour taken out. 'checker' is lit with the subject's surface a grey checker on its first UV set, for that picture only: skin that stretches bends the squares and skin that tears breaks them.
It inherits across views exactly as cut and ignore do, so one call can hand back the same camera lit and unlit. An unknown name is refused and the refusal lists the four. The manifest records the mode of every picture, 'lit' included, because 'unlit' and a level whose lights were never built are the same image.
FOUR MORE ARE IN THE VIEWPORT MENU AND NOT HERE, each on a measurement rather than a preference: wireframe renders a solid white plate offscreen, lit_wireframe asserts in the renderer of any unattended process, reflections renders black in the preview world because there is nothing there to reflect, and the clay/zebra family writes a global console variable that would change how your own editor renders.

parameters.name: ignore
parameters.description:
ACTORS THIS PICTURE LEAVES OUT, by internal name - one name or a list. For what a PLANE cannot reach: a suspended ceiling belonging to the storey below, a fog volume, an overhanging roof. Level renders only, and it inherits across views exactly as cut does; a view stating its own list replaces the shared one rather than adding to it.
A HIDDEN ACTOR IS HIDDEN EVERYWHERE THIS CAPTURE ANSWERS: out of the pixels, out of the frame legend, out of the occlusion each legend row reports, and out of a later screen_to_world through the same capture - which reads the list back off the manifest, so a pick cannot return something the picture does not show. The result echoes views[].ignored, because a reader who did not make the call cannot otherwise tell 'there is no roof here' from 'the roof was hidden'. A name that matches no actor REFUSES: otherwise you get back the exact picture you were avoiding, with nothing about it reading as wrong. It hides per primitive at the view - nothing in the level moves.

parameters.name: highlights
parameters.description:
THINGS THAT DRAW NO PIXELS, MARKED so you can look at them - one type or a list. It takes TYPES, not actor names, which is the one way it differs from ignore: a caller marking navigation does not have to know which actors carry it. Known: navmesh, niagara, collision, volumes, camera, billboard, regions, splines, bones, trails, ghosts, landmarks ('navmesh' also spells 'nav mesh'/'nav_mesh'; 'volume', 'cameras', 'sprites' are accepted for the plural or singular of their own). An unknown type refuses by name and lists what it accepts, so this list can grow without reinterpreting an old call.
COLLISION IS THE SIMPLE COLLISION PER PRIMITIVE - a Character's capsule at its own half-height, a box or sphere component at its own extent, a static mesh's cooked hulls. It is NOT the bounding box, and the difference is tens of centimetres on exactly the subject you would ask about: 'is this capsule's bottom on the floor'. A skeletal mesh keeps its bodies on a UPhysicsAsset and cannot be read this way, so it is COUNTED in a warning rather than silently missing.
REGIONS draws GCW region outlines at their declared min/max, or at anchorZ when unbounded. SPLINES draws GCW courses at their region's anchorZ. Both use authored curved geometry, draw through scene geometry and report declaration names in the legend. They read the adjacent GCW file. VOLUMES IS EVERY AVolume BRUSH - trigger, physics, post-process, blocking, nav bounds - drawn from the faces somebody authored and NOT from its collision, which is why a PostProcessVolume appears at all. It draws THROUGH geometry, because a volume encloses the camera rather than sitting in front of it.
CAMERA IS THE BODY PLUS THE FRUSTUM. A camera has no billboard - it carries a real static mesh and a frustum component - so this is triangles, drawn at 1000 cm which is the length the editor's own frustum uses. It answers WHAT THE CAMERA CAN SEE, which its transform alone does not.
BILLBOARD IS EVERY UBillboardComponent, drawn as UNREAL'S OWN ICON: a light looks like a light and a player start looks like a player start. That population is doubly invisible - a visualisation component is dropped from actors{} and components{} as decoration, and it draws zero pixels in a capture - so before this the only thing naming a PlayerStart was the frame legend, with a rectangle and nothing in it. Each icon sits on a small ANCHOR SPHERE in the overlay's colour, because a sprite always faces you and holds its size: it says WHAT is there and nothing about where. The sphere is geometry, so it shrinks with distance and is occluded properly.
EVERY SHAPE IS DEPTH-SHADED so one angle is enough: a line on a surface facing you is full strength, a line on the hidden back of the same solid is dim, and depth across the shape's own span dims it further. The legend still reports the AUTHORED colour.
NAVMESH IS THE SURFACE NAVIGATION BUILT, not the volume somebody drew, painted OPAQUE over the ordinary picture. It COVERS the floor it marks - that is what a highlight is for, and 'what is underneath' is a second render without highlights. GraphCode gathers and draws it itself: the engine's own navigation rendering gathers nothing for a capture (measured, 0 of 262,144 px) because its gate reads a VIEWPORT's show flags, and a capture is not a viewport. So the picture depends on your request and never on which boxes are ticked in somebody's editor.
NIAGARA IS WRITTEN BUT UNPROVEN - no fixture has had an emitter in it yet. It marks each emitter with a sphere at its TRANSFORM, which is the placement question ('is the fire above the torch'), and the transform is authored and exact where the bounds of a system that never simulated are a 1 cm cube. Do not read a picture from it as confirmation yet.
BONES IS THE POSE VIEW, and the one type for an ANIMATION or SKELETAL MESH preview rather than a level: where each bone points at the moment drawn. Bare 'bones' draws the rig reader's default selection as rays; the object form {type:"bones", of:[bone or rig chain, ...], draw:[`ray`,`axes`,`range`], rig:"/Game/...IK rig"} chooses: `ray` the line each bone points along, `axes` its three axes (X red, Y green, Z blue, named in the legend by the rig's own words), `range` the edge of where it may point and its twist span, `bubble` a wire sphere round each chain's first joint as wide as the chain laid out; on a hinged limb's first joint (a shoulder, a hip) the picture shows ONLY one sphere round it in the part's colour (no globe, net or direction sphere beside it), size:N centimetres out, size:"current" as far as the hand is now or size:"full" the arm laid out (default: the bone's own length), bright where the chain's end (the hand) can be there, riding the forearm with the wrist as shown (as a build's reach with no facing holds it), with its shoulder and elbow in range, dark where it cannot; given aim:, bright only where the hand there also holds the held bone (a blade riding the hand) that way, rolled as a build rolls a blade with no up= (its edge along the forearm), every joint in range; the picture tries the JOINTS ONLY, and the body, the held part and the key's build are tried on the places an ask names (the user 2026-10-23: "query only when asked, not precompute"): where to put the hand at that size; ask a point on a bright part (bubble:, depth 0) for its place and line. Draw it on the key's SOURCE pose (its clip's source= at that frame), the pose its build starts from, never on an earlier build of the same key. share:0.6 (the key's reach [share=], beside aim:) tries each place with the trunk turned toward it as a build turns a reach's trunk, over the arm's whole laid-out reach (the hips left to the planted legs; balance's settle and the free arm are not tried); key:"<.gcmove>:<clip>" names the key the bubble places, and of its reaches the one on this arm (a two-handed key's other hand stays where the key puts it): its reach's [share=] where share: is not given, its balance and planted legs raise or sink the hips first as its build does (a place past the arm's span), and an ask of a place (or its max extension) also builds the key with its reach pointed there, a dry run, and answers the build's own verdict (`build`: accepted, refused, the arm stopped short or past its ranges), since the build's balance then leans the trunk (7-17 cm at the shoulder on BlueEdge's sword keys) where the sphere does not; every ray and axis is a pyramid pointing the way the bone goes, all of it thin lines a few pixels wide. On a bone ending a limb (a hand, or a blade riding it) `bubble` also draws its DIRECTION SPHERE round it, BRIGHT (the bone's colour) every way it could point with its grip kept where it is (the hand turning about it, rolled as a build with no up= rolls it), every joint in range (the joints only, as the reach sphere), and DARK every way it could not, as the reach sphere is drawn; white where it points now; aim:"(forward, down=55)" (the body's words a .gcmove writes) marks the wanted aim in cyan, joined to now by an arc, and the legend gives the degrees past a stop it needs; with it, a cyan ROLL RING square to the wanted aim on that sphere, bright where its +Z (a blade's edge) can face that way with every joint in range, dark where past a stop, a yellow cube on it at its up (the edge facing the body's up, its forward for an aim near straight up or down); one point asked on the ring answers frame(toward=<the aim>, up=<that point>). On a bone that ends another rig chain (the head on its neck) the sphere is its AIM sphere, the gaze sphere: where that chain can turn it to face (its rest forward), every joint in its arcs; the legend gives how far short the wanted aim stays. With a held part beside the bone (a Blueprint given animation:) the sphere is where the part's tip goes. Read off the very mesh the picture poses, redrawn every frame of a span; the legend gives each bone's colour and the same words and numbers as a build's [readings] (fold, side, twist against their ranges). With no reader that knows the rig, only named bones are drawn, along their long axes.
TRAILS IS THE CLIP TRAJECTORY on an animation: each selected bone over the WHOLE clip in one picture, a short pyramid at every sample standing on the bone, its tip where the bone points then, its pale side the bone's top (its +Z, or +Y where it points along Z), its dark side the opposite and a tick out of its right side, so a swing reads as a fan of the blade's whole orientation; their spacing is the speed, the first and last are bold, whatever moment the picture stands at. On a clip Move built, the body's centre of mass rides along as white dots, with its shadow on the floor in grey, by the mass model its builds balance with: a jump in the weight is a gap in the dots. Bare 'trails' draws the ends of the rig reader's default selection (hands, feet, head, a held thing's bone); {type:"trails", of:[bones or chains]} chooses. The legend gives each path's colour, samples, length and peak speed (cm/s) with the frame it peaks at. graph: adds a picture, views[].graph: each selected bone's VELOCITY BESIDE ITS ACCELERATION over the clip, a row per bone and quantity, to see a jitter: graph:true is its place and its joint, or name any of `place` (where the bone goes, cm/s), `turn` (how fast it turns, deg/s), `joint` (its three angles in the rig's words, as [readings] gives them) and `centre` (the centre of mass); a chain in of: is each of its bones. A red dot is a velocity step, an acceleration standing alone at one sample; the legend gives each trace's fastest and sharpest with their frames, its steps' frames, and how far apart most steps fall. points:{Name:{bone:"<bone>", at:[x, y, z]}} adds the path of a POINT RIDING A BONE, the offset in centimetres in that bone's own axes (a held blade's bone sits at the grip, so its pyramids are the hand's path; the cutting point is points:{Cutting:{bone:"blade_r", at:[85, 0, 0]}}): a dot at each sample joined by a line in its own colour, no pyramids, a thin pale line from its bone to it at every sample (the swept blade, so the blade's plane shows), and one legend line with its name, bone, offset, length and peak speed with its frame. With points: and no of:, only the points are drawn.
LANDMARKS ('landmarks') IS A METAHUMAN FACE'S NAMED POINTS, read off this character's own face: every name a .gchuman points { } block takes - Epic's fit points (rings, pt_*) and the Move handles (dots, nose_tip, upper_lid_r, mouth_corner_l...) - a numbered dot each, coloured by region (brows, eyes, nose, cheeks, mouth, chin and jaw, ears, head and neck), and a legend panel at the picture's right listing number and name; the picture's own pixels keep their coordinates. Points the head hides from the camera are left out and counted. Render it before measuring the matching spots on a reference; frame close (camera anchor on a point) to spread a crowded area. Only a MetaHuman character draws it.
Level renders only except bones, trails and landmarks, off unless asked for, and it inherits across views exactly as cut and ignore do. The result answers back views[].highlighted as 'navmesh: 1' - the count of SUBJECTS found, because a picture with no overlay in it cannot tell you whether there is no navmesh or the overlay failed. A type that resolves to nothing WARNS rather than refusing (highlight_nothing_found): unlike an unresolvable ignore, the picture you get back is correct. Nothing is added to the level - the marker is transient and gone before the call returns.

parameters.name: width
parameters.description: Shorthand for a single view's width, in pixels.

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: Shorthand for a single view's height, in pixels.

parameters.name: output
parameters.description: {lifetime: transient|persistent, path, overwrite: refuse|replace|unique, external, content}. Omit for one transient image.

parameters.name: details
parameters.description: 'compact' returns the pose you would paste back. 'full' adds the resolved absolute camera and the angle scoring.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: 'render' takes a picture. 'ask' resolves named pixels from one retained capture to mesh-local or world coordinates and returns text. 'legend' paints the identification image for a picture already taken - every actor a flat unique colour, every wall its own shade, and the exact #RRGGBB of each name returned beside it. 'screen_to_world' asks where a pixel of one already taken actually is. All three query modes name a `capture` and take no camera: they answer about the picture you are looking at. 'thumbnail' draws the asset through the editor's OWN registered renderer for its class - which is how you look at a texture, a font, a sprite, a Niagara system or anything else the scene route has no adapter for. It takes asset, width, height and output and NO camera, because a thumbnail renderer chooses its own view; a camera sent to it is refused by name rather than ignored. Every other parameter above belongs to 'render'.

parameters.name: capture
parameters.description: ask/legend/screen_to_world: the capture id a previous render returned. A pixel with no picture behind it is a guess, so this is required in those modes.

parameters.name: by
parameters.description: legend: 'uv_island' produces a retained static-mesh source LOD 0 color render, UV atlas, swatch legend and island entries with UV seeds/selectors. Ask the NEW capture with view main or uv. Missing UVs are white; atlas overlap is magenta. Omit for level actor identification.

parameters.name: uv_channel
parameters.description: legend by:uv_island: nonnegative UV channel index, default 0. UV coordinates normally use 0..1; tiled coordinates remain unwrapped. Ask returns the island label, color, UV and a Shape selector when unambiguous. Island labels are capture-local; use UV seeds in recipes with uv:keep.

parameters.name: view
parameters.description: ask/legend/screen_to_world: which view of that capture.

parameters.name: points
parameters.description:
ask: up to 64 {name, pixel:[x,y], depth} entries. Pixel coordinates are integer image coordinates from the top-left. On a mesh, depth 0 is entry, 0.5 is the midpoint through the same entered part, and 1 is its exit. Levels accept depth 0 and return the first blocking world surface.
DEPTH IN EITHER UNIT, because a tenth of the way through says nothing about how far under the skin that is: the bare number is the fraction, and depth {"value":1,"unit":"cm"} is 1 cm IN FROM THE ENTRY SURFACE, resolved against the thickness this ray actually measures. Deeper than the part is thick is refused with that thickness named rather than clamped to the exit, and every answer carries both readings - depth and depth_cm. It is camera.offset's {value, unit} spelling, and unit:"fraction" is the other reading, which is what a bare number already means.
ON A BONES BUBBLE: bubble:"<bone>" picks which bubble a point is asked of. up_of:"<other point's name>" makes this point the second of a TWO-POINT ask: the other point is where a frame points (toward=), this one where its up faces, taken square to the first (any point at least 10 degrees off that line), answering frame(toward=..., up=...) - all three axes, e.g. a blade's line and its edge. A point on a ROLL RING answers that frame by itself (toward the ring's aim, up that point); with key: on the bubble it is tried exactly where the key's reach puts the grip (its own at=), the arm and the held part against the body, and the key built so (a dry run, its verdict the answer); without key:, the picture's ring, the joints only.
IN A REACH BUBBLE (a limb's first joint, drawn with aim: or size:) the point is a hand PLACE, tried exactly where it is, and the answer adds its MAX EXTENSION: along the line from the bubble's centre through it (toward=, the character's words), the farthest place that still holds what the sphere tests (the aim held, every joint in range, the arm and held part clear, the trunk as share: turns it), searched in 1 cm steps from the chain laid out, with that place's ready line and the chain's joints. ASK AGAIN WITH NO NEW RENDER: {name, bubble:"<bone>", toward:"(down, forward=37)", distance:<cm>} in place of pixel tries the place that far out along that direction from the centre; with no distance it answers the max extension. With key:, that max is built as the key builds it, and where the build refuses it the line is walked inward, at most three more builds (1, 3 and 7 cm in); max_build says which.
ON A JOINT: every bone a bones highlight draws is a small target round its joint (3 cm); a pixel on it where no sphere is met (or bubble:"<bone>" with no sphere on it) answers that joint's place, point(at=(...)) from the character's origin as a .gcmove place is measured - on any capture, animations included (the knee's height, the hip's).
The answer is text/JSON; no marked image is made.

parameters.name: mesh
parameters.description: ask on a level: {actor, component?, instance?} selects one static mesh for triangle inspection, including collision-disabled meshes. Component and instance may be omitted only when unique. Other objects do not occlude this explicit selection. Returns exact numeric world/mesh-local points, normals, triangle corners and Shape tuples. Nanite uses full-detail editor source. Material displacement and spline-deformed components are not represented. Re-render old or changed captures.

parameters.name: relative_to
parameters.description: ask with mesh: {actor, component?, instance?} chooses the destination mesh's local coordinate frame for shape.position/normal and the directly usable Shape at/plane tuples. Default is the inspected mesh. Use the connector here when measuring another road. Shape must operate in that mesh-local frame (before its scene placement); an earlier recipe stage or a moved build pivot is a different frame.

parameters.name: snap
parameters.description: ask with mesh: none (surface hit), vertex (nearest corner of hit triangle), or edge (nearest point on its three edges), measured in world distance. Edge can be a triangulation diagonal; this does not claim a mesh boundary. surface_position and barycentric retain the original unsnapped hit.

parameters.name: inline_image
parameters.description: legend: return the PNG bytes as well as writing it. The file is written either way, beside the capture's own manifest.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: screen_to_world: normalized horizontal position in [0,1], 0 at the image's left edge.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: screen_to_world: normalized vertical position in [0,1], 0 at the image's TOP edge.

parameters.name: trace_channel
parameters.description: ask/screen_to_world on a level: a trace channel such as Visibility or Camera. Not for WorldStatic. Mesh preview queries use rendered triangles instead.

parameters.name: object_types
parameters.description: ask/screen_to_world on a level: object types to hit, e.g. ["WorldStatic"] for solid architecture only. Mutually exclusive with trace_channel.

parameters.name: max_distance
parameters.description: ask/screen_to_world on a level: how far to trace, in cm.

parameters.name: ignore_actors
parameters.description: ask/screen_to_world on a level: actor names or labels the trace steps over - the prop between the camera and the wall.

tools.name: gc_resolve
tools.description:
Read the unresolved merge conflicts in one `.gc`, and take a decision on one. This is the
tool for finishing a Git merge of GraphCode text; it replaces running the GcResolve
commandlet by hand.

Call it with no conflict_id to LIST. Each conflict comes back as fields — id, entity,
property, base, ours, theirs — rather than as text to re-parse, which is the one thing no
other tool does. Call it with conflict_id to PICK, which edits the file and removes that
construct. Presence of conflict_id is the only difference between the two.

Reached as gc_versions mode:"resolve" — the fourth version question, beside history, diff
and take. Call this name directly only if you are the bridge.

  mode:"resolve"                                        -> WHICH files a merge left something in
  mode:"resolve", asset_path                            -> every conflict, as fields
  mode:"resolve", asset_path, conflict_id:1, side:"theirs" -> resolves it, writes the file
  mode:"resolve", asset_path, conflict_id:2, value:"  Health: float = 150.0"

IT PROPOSES; IT DOES NOT COMMIT, and it does not touch the asset. A resolved file is still
only text, and its `sig:` deliberately still says `conflicted` — restamping it here would
let the file claim to describe an asset nobody has applied it to. `gc_apply` is what makes
it real, and it does NOT read that `sig:`: a proposal states `merged-from:`, and the apply
checks the asset against the first of those parents — ours — instead. So send a resolved
file straight to gc_apply; it is refused only if the asset is no longer that parent, and
the remedy there is to redo the merge, never gc_sync, which would delete it. Nor does this
tool commit to Git: resolving a conflict is a semantic decision about code not written here.

TAKING THEIRS IS EXACT OR IT IS REFUSED. The site is found by walking the entity path, and
the recorded `ours` text must occur exactly once there. Zero or several means the file moved
under the construct, and the answer is a refusal naming which — writing a value into a line
nobody chose is the one failure a merge tool may not have. Edit the text by hand and list
again. A refused pick has written nothing.

OMIT BOTH PATHS TO ASK ABOUT THE WHOLE PROJECT — the same rule every other gc_ verb follows.
It scans every `.gc` and returns the ones a merge left something in: the file, the LINE of
each `conflict { }`, and whether it is an unabsorbed merge proposal. Lines rather than sides,
so the list stays a list; pass one asset_path back for the fields. It is not a grep — a
conflict is grammar, not a `//` marker, and a clean proposal has no marker at all. To see
what the merge changed, read `git diff`, on text this format exists to make diffable.

A CLEAN MERGE PROPOSAL HAS NO CONFLICTS AND STILL NEEDS APPLYING, and it is the more
dangerous of the two because it carries no marker. When this tool reports zero conflicts it
also reports merge_proposal — true means the file is a merge nobody has absorbed, and the
next ordinary save of that asset regenerates over it. Send it to gc_apply.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Asset or package path, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login. The preferred spelling, and the one every other gc_ tool takes. OMIT IT (and file) to scan the whole project for the files a merge left something in, which is how you find out what to pass here.

parameters.name: file
parameters.description: The `.gc` by path instead, absolute or project-relative — what GcCheck and the startup scan report. Must be under the project's Content directory. Pass this OR asset_path.

parameters.name: conflict_id
parameters.description: The conflict to resolve, from a previous list. Its presence is what makes this call a pick rather than a list. Ids are 1-based and POSITIONAL, so they are only valid while the file is unmodified — list again after every pick.

parameters.name: side
parameters.description: "ours" (default) or "theirs". Ours is already what the merge left in the text, so taking it only removes the construct and edits nothing. Accepts `take` as an alias, the name this had before resolve joined a verb that already has a `take` mode.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: A third value, for when the right answer is neither side — the whole statement line as it should read, indentation included. Its presence overrides take.

tools.name: gc_search
tools.description:
One search surface over this project. 'kind' is required and has no default, because the questions below are not interchangeable.
  reference   - where is this cited? Crosses assets. The one nothing else answers.
  entity      - where is this declared, and what is it exactly called?
  description - which authored text (comments, labels, names) talks about this?
  node        - which addable node does this? Unreal's palette, searched by intent.
  identity    - the exact callable identity, when you already know the name.
  widget      - which widget class does this?
  asset       - which asset is this?
  preset      - which .gcshape library entry does this? Reads FILES, so root and not scope.

LIVE ONLY, by design: it projects the editor's current state, unsaved edits included. There is no saved-file mode, because grep over the committed .gc files already is one.

kind:'reference' is neither grep nor a registry reference scan. Whole-token matching separates ComponentPropertyName=RestartButton from the sibling widget Text_RestartButton and from the generated name BndEvt__Menu_RestartButton_K2Node_...; prose that merely says the name is kind:'description', not a citation. Cross-asset spellings are covered, so a WidgetClass=obj'/Game/UI/WBP_Menu.WBP_Menu_C' is found for a target sharing no substring with it.

Each hit comes back as its ENCLOSING CHAIN - graph { eventgraph EventGraph { <statement> } } - not as a line, with siblings elided. The excerpt is readable, never applicable: it carries no sig: and gc_apply will not take it.

Every answer states what it could NOT search. An asset whose class has no GraphCode kind (a Niagara system, say) is a row reading omits:everything, so an empty result means 'nothing cites this' rather than 'nothing readable cites this'. A member name that is not declared at all is said so outright, with near misses, because '0 references' is the answer that immediately precedes a deletion.

Results are RANKED and max_results returns the top ones. Every asset in scope is searched whatever max_results is set to - there is no scan budget - and the whole result is then ordered and cut. What ordered it is per kind and named in ranked_by, each hit carries its score, and total_matches is the honest total. So a small max_results is a small answer to the question asked, not an answer about the alphabetically earliest corner of the project.

kind:'entity' and kind:'description' SCAN THE CORPUS instead of following references, because nothing narrows 'which asset declares a name I half-remember'. That costs one live projection per asset in scope, and the scan is complete rather than capped, so scope is a COST lever now and not a correctness one: pass scope:'/Game/UI' when you know roughly where to look and the same answer arrives sooner. entity finds declarations under all four shapes the format writes - Name = value, Name: Type with no value, Name: Type = value, and a group header like function Foo { - and reports the EXACT spelling, so a name differing only in case is a hit labelled as such rather than a miss. Graph aliases (n1, c2) are minted identities, not entities.

kind:'description' searches what THIS PROJECT authored - graph comments, text literals, error messages and the names of things - which nothing else has ever searched. Names are split on camelCase, so 'restart button' finds RestartButton. Property values, engine enum spellings, paths and localization keys are deliberately not in that corpus. Every term must appear for a line to match, and terms that matched nothing come back in unmatched_terms.

Match tolerance is NOT a parameter - it follows the kind, because the right value is decided by the question and not by the caller. reference and entity are exact; description is fuzzy. Matching is lexical throughout - token overlap and a bounded edit distance, never an embedding - and EVERY HIT REPORTS match:'exact' or match:'fuzzy', so an answer says which one it is instead of a flag deciding it in advance. Near misses are always reported and can no longer be switched off, which matters most where it used to be optional: '0 references' is the sentence immediately before a deletion.

Parameters by kind - a word sent to a kind that does not take it is refused by name:
  reference    target, max_results
  entity       target, scope, max_results
  description  target, scope, max_results
  node         target, max_results, offset
  identity     target, max_results
  widget       target, max_results, offset
  asset        target, scope, max_results, offset
  preset       target, root, max_results

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Required, no default: reference | entity | description | node | identity | widget | asset | preset

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: WHAT to look for, whichever kind is asking. reference/entity: '/Game/UI/WBP_Menu' for the asset, '/Game/UI/WBP_Menu.RestartButton' for one of its members, or a short name - an ambiguous one is returned as the ambiguity, never narrowed for you, and for entity a bare name searches the whole scope. description: the words. node/identity/widget: the search text. asset: the name to match. The engines spell it query and name_pattern; this is that one word.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: WHICH assets to even look at, as a folder, a class, a Skeleton, or a list of them. '/Game/UI' is a folder; 'WidgetBlueprint' or '/Script/Engine.Blueprint' is a class; '/Game/Characters/SK_Mannequin_Skeleton' narrows to what will play on that rig (kind:'asset' only). Defaults to /Game. All three can be written as a path, so the reply states how each token was read in scope_read - check it rather than assuming. A skeleton is asset-only; naming a non-Skeleton ASSET is refused, because scope says which assets to search and not which one to find.

parameters.name: root
parameters.description: kind:'preset' only - WHICH FOLDER OF `.gcshape` PROGRAMS to index. A content path under any mounted root, so '/GraphCodeShape/Presets' is the shipped library and '/Game/Kits' is this project's own. Defaults to the shipped library. This is not scope: scope resolves a folder, a class or a Skeleton against the asset registry, and a preset is a file rather than an asset, so none of those three readings applies.

parameters.name: max_results
parameters.description: How many hits come back (default 50) — the TOP ones, not the first ones found. Every asset in scope is searched whatever this is set to; the whole result is then ranked and cut here. Each hit carries its score and the reply names what ordered them in ranked_by, so a short answer can be checked rather than trusted. total_matches and truncated still report the honest total.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: node/widget/asset: zero-based offset into the results, for the next page.

tools.name: gc_sync
tools.description:
Make one asset's `.gc` text sidecar exist and be current, and report which. Call this
before reading or patching a sidecar; it is the door the other `.gc` tools go through, so
nothing after it has to handle a file that is missing or describes an older asset.

status is one of:
  'created'     - no sidecar existed. One was written. Common the first time an asset is
                  touched: a `.gc` only appears when the asset is saved, so an asset that
                  has not been saved since GraphCode was installed has none.
  'current'     - the file on disk is already this build's projection of this asset.
  'regenerated' - it existed and disagreed. It was rewritten from the asset.

answered_without_loading says WHICH of the two proofs produced a 'current'. True means
the header's bin: digest matched the `.uasset` on disk and the asset was never loaded -
the cheap answer. False means the asset was loaded and re-projected and the text compared.
Both are correct; the fast one is guarded on kind, omits:, ir: versions, the source build
and the header's projector: revision all still matching, because a matching binary proves
the ASSET is unchanged and not that this build's projection of it is. The projector:
revision is the guard that covers a change nothing else declares - a pin hint, a sort key,
a spelling - so after a projector change every sidecar declines here and re-projects
instead of certifying itself. fast_path_declined names the guard that failed.

discarded_proposal:true means the file it replaced had a stale sig: - it was an edit in
flight that nobody applied. The sidecar now mirrors the asset again, and the edit is KEPT,
not lost: it was copied to Saved/GraphCode/Proposals/<UTC stamp>_<sidecar path>.gc before
the overwrite, and proposal_kept_in names that folder. Every save regenerates the sidecar
with no exception, so a `.gc` is a mirror of the asset and never a source of truth: apply a
patch with gc_apply rather than leaving it sitting in the file.

A LEVEL is regenerated by an ordinary save like every other kind, and this card said the
opposite until 2026-08-05. The hook takes the map extension for a .umap; measured by
GraphCode.Policy.SavingALevelRegeneratesItsSidecarLikeEveryOtherKind. So gc_read
source:"saved" on a saved level is current, and this tool is for a level you have edited
and NOT saved - the same rule as everything else.

Projects 59 asset kinds: anim_composite, anim_montage, anim_sequence, animation_blueprint, behavior_tree, blend_space, blueprint, blueprint_function_library, blueprint_interface, blueprint_macro_library, control_rig, curve_float, curve_linear_color, curve_table, curve_vector, data_asset, data_registry, data_table, env_query, external_actor, foliage_type, font, font_face, groom, groom_binding, hlod_layer, ik_retargeter, ik_rig, input_action, input_mapping_context, level, level_sequence, material, material_function, material_instance, metahuman, metasound_patch, metasound_source, niagara_parameter_collection, niagara_sim_cache, niagara_system, pcg_graph, pcg_graph_instance, pcg_settings, physical_material, physics_asset, procedural_vegetation, render_target, skeletal_mesh, skeleton, sound_cue, sound_wave, state_tree, static_mesh, string_table, texture_2d, user_enum, user_struct, widget_blueprint. Anything else has no projection and is refused by
name. Use gc_describe(kind:"<token>") for a kind's blocks and which of them write.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: Asset or package path, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Skip the bin: fast path and re-project unconditionally. The slow answer is never wrong, only slower.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: Report what a sync would do and write nothing.

tools.name: gc_versions
tools.description:
Put one asset, or the whole project, back to a version. The TAKE half of the version
surface: mode:"history" says which versions exist, mode:"diff" says what changed, and
mode:"restore" acts.
Reached as mode:"restore" - the bridge answers the other modes from their own
engines, and there is no separate revert name to look for. `take` is accepted as an
alias, the spelling this mode shipped with.

  mode:"restore", from:"HEAD"                     -> PLAN: what reverting the project would do
  mode:"restore", from:"HEAD", plan_sig:"<sig>"   -> do it
  mode:"restore", asset_path, from:"2026-08-05T13:00:00Z" -> plan, one asset, to that moment
  mode:"restore", from:"...T13:00:00Z", to:"...T14:00:00Z" -> UNDO THAT WINDOW, project-wide

`from` IS ALWAYS THE EARLIER VERSION AND `to` THE LATER ONE, the same as a compare. A restore
goes back to `from`, because going back goes to the earlier end. Omit `to` and everything
since `from` is discarded; pass it and only that window is undone, so work done after it is
kept - a real three-way merge, not a copy of the older text.

IT PLANS FIRST, ALWAYS. Without plan_sig this reads and writes nothing: it resolves every
asset in scope and reports the action set - restore, create, REMOVE, and every asset that
cannot go back with the reason in its own words. Pass the returned plan_sig to perform it.
Nothing is cached between the two calls: execute re-plans, and a plan_sig that no longer
matches refuses and hands back the new plan rather than performing the old one.

THE THREE CONSENTS ARE SEPARATE FROM plan_sig, because reading a plan and accepting its
worst part are different acts: accept_removals when anything would be removed,
accept_partial when anything is skipped, accept_replacing_backup when the undo of the last
revert would be destroyed. Each refusal names the one it wants and why.

A PARTIAL RESTORE IS ALWAYS ON OFFER. An asset GraphCode cannot rebuild is a reason to say
so, not a reason to hold the other three hundred hostage - accept_partial records that the
list was read, and every skipped asset is named in the plan and in the report.

PROJECT SCOPE TAKES A COMMIT OR A MOMENT, never `saved` or `live` - those are where the
project is now, not somewhere to go back to. One asset accepts all four version kinds.
`saved` means the `.gc` already on disk and `live` means this editor's UNSAVED state; they
are the same two words gc_read uses, and `working` is still accepted for `saved`.
A revert to a MOMENT also needs the timeline stamped; mode:"history" says whether it is.
A MOMENT IS WRITTEN THE WAY A PERSON SAYS ONE, in local time and in every mode: "1am",
"13:00", "yesterday", "yesterday 3pm", "2026-08-28", "2h ago", an ISO-8601 instant,
or an id from mode:"history". THE PLAN NAMES THE INSTANT THE WORD BECAME, so check the
target sentence before echoing plan_sig - `1am` at half past midnight is LAST night's.

IT SAVES WHAT IT WRITES, one asset at a time, and the way back is another revert rather than
Ctrl+Z: the state each asset was in before this ran is archived first, so mode:"history" can
still name it. A restore that refused to save would be the same verb behaving two ways.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: THE VERSION IT GOES BACK TO - the earlier end. A git ref, or a moment: ISO-8601, an id from mode:"history", a clock ("1am", "13:00"), a named day ("yesterday", "yesterday 3pm"), a date, or a count back ("2h ago"). Clock words are LOCAL time and the plan names the instant each became. With asset_path, "saved" (the file on disk) and "live" (this editor, unsaved included) are accepted too.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: One asset, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login. Omit for the whole project - the same rule the compare and list modes use, and it changes the answer rather than filtering it.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: The LATER end of a window. Omit to revert to `from` and discard everything since; pass it to undo only what happened between the two and keep later work.

parameters.name: plan_sig
parameters.description: Echo the sig from the plan to perform it. Omit to plan and write nothing.

parameters.name: blocks
parameters.description: One asset only, and REFUSED without asset_path: restore just these blocks, e.g. ["graph"]. Omit for every represented facet. A comma-separated string is accepted too. Project scope reverts whole assets, so there is nothing for it to select.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: With plan_sig: run the whole write path, including the preflight and the re-derive, and touch nothing - not the assets, not the backup. Default false.

parameters.name: accept_removals
parameters.description: Required when the plan would remove any asset. A removal is a move to GraphCode's recovery trash, never a file delete.

parameters.name: accept_partial
parameters.description: Required when the plan skips any asset. Records that the skipped list was read; it never stops the assets that CAN go back from going back.

parameters.name: accept_replacing_backup
parameters.description: Required when the plan carries a backup warning: this revert would destroy the undo of the previous one.

parameters.name: accept_breaking_references
parameters.description: Let a removal proceed when an asset outside the removal set still references it. Default false, which refuses that asset and names the referencer.

parameters.name: include_removals
parameters.description: Project scope: include assets that exist now and did not at the target. THE DESTRUCTIVE HALF. Default true, because a revert that left new assets behind matches no moment in the project's own history.

parameters.name: include_creations
parameters.description: Project scope: include assets that existed at the target and do not now. Default true.

tools.name: gcp_apply
tools.description:
Put a captured world back into the RUNNING game: spawn what the file has and the world
lost, destroy what the world has and the file does not, write every property in between.
This is the write direction of gcp_capture, and the two are one loop - capture a moment,
play on, come back to it, change one thing.

PIE MUST BE RUNNING. It writes live runtime objects and never an asset, so with nothing
playing it refuses rather than falling back to the editor world - those actors ARE the
level package, and changing them is gc_apply kind:'level', which has a sig: check and a
save you can revert. This has neither, by design: a running world has no undo.

Pass ONE of:
  capture:  a name from gcp_capture (name:'before' -> capture:'before'), or a path
  document: the text of a .gcp inline - which is how you request a state nobody captured.
            A capture and a patch are the same grammar; edit the values and send it back.

AN ENTRY IN THE FILE IS AN EXISTENCE CLAIM, so a restore reconciles existence and not only
properties. What bounds that is the scope: the file's own select: line, or the select you
pass here to narrow or widen it. Two bosses live, one in the file, scope 'class:BP_Boss' ->
the extra is destroyed and the player, not being in scope, is never considered. Pass
reconcile_existence:false to write properties onto what is already there and nothing else.

BASELINE DECIDES WHAT AN ABSENT LINE MEANS, and the file states it. 'archetype' (the
ordinary capture) means absent = at its class default, so every managed field is reset
before the file is written - without that, anything that drifted since the capture stays
drifted and a re-capture diff still comes back clean. 'none' means absent = unknown, so
nothing is reset. 'previous' is a DELTA and is refused: it is evidence, not a state.

WHAT IT CANNOT PUT BACK IS REPORTED, NEVER SWALLOWED - `not_restored` names every line the
codec could not import, with its reason. A .gcp restore is exact for reflected state and a
save-point primitive for everything else: timers, latent actions and engine-owned state
(anim blend position, physics sleep, audio playhead) are outside it, and a side effect that
already happened does not come back. Read that list before believing a clean diff.

BEGINPLAY RUNS BY DEFAULT, and `begin_play_classes` tells you which classes have one before
anything is touched - an empty list is a proof that no Blueprint BeginPlay logic ran.
Values are written LAST so they survive it. suppress_lifecycle:true unhooks Blueprint
BeginPlay and EndPlay for the classes this restore touches, which is what stops a spawn
sound, a 'wave started' broadcast, or the loot a destroyed extra would drop. It is not
deferral: a skipped BeginPlay is skipped for that actor's whole life, so a class that CACHES
something in BeginPlay is left without it. Off unless you decide otherwise.

dry_run:true resolves everything and writes nothing - the plan it returns is the same shape
the real call answers with, so read it first when the destroy list is the part you are
unsure about.

parameters.name: capture
parameters.description: The .gcp to put back: a name as passed to gcp_capture name: (the extension is optional, and it is looked up under Saved/GraphCode/snapshots), or a path. Give this or `document`, never both.

parameters.name: document
parameters.description: A whole .gcp as text, for a state that was never captured - edit a capture's values and send it back. Parsed by the same reader with the same envelope checks, including found:, so a hand-written file that lost an entry is refused rather than half applied.

parameters.name: select
parameters.description: Override the file's own select: line - the same forms gcp_capture takes (class:, name:, tag:, near:, '*'). This is the WRITE SCOPE: it decides which live actors may be destroyed for not being in the file, so narrowing it is how you restore part of a capture. Defaults to what the file says, which is what it was captured with.

parameters.name: reconcile_existence
parameters.description: Destroy in-scope actors the file does not mention. Default true, because an entry in the file is an existence claim and writing only properties reads half the file. False leaves every live actor alone and writes onto the ones the file names.

parameters.name: suppress_lifecycle
parameters.description: Unhook Blueprint BeginPlay and EndPlay for the classes this restore spawns and destroys. Default false. Reported back as suppressed_on_spawn / suppressed_on_destroy, which are different sets - a restore often does one end and not the other. Held only across the destroy and spawn passes, never across a wait, because the unhook is per CLASS and would otherwise silence live instances no restore is touching.

parameters.name: dry_run
parameters.description: Resolve classes, match names, check the baseline - and write nothing. Property paths are NOT pre-validated: the codec is the only authority on what a path means, so a value that will not import surfaces on the real call, alongside what was written before it stopped.

tools.name: gcp_diff
tools.description:
Subtract two captures and return what changed, as .gcp text. This is what the rolling
channel computes on every wake, offered to a caller who has two files and a question:
is this the same fight after the reload, did the treatment move anything the control
did not, what is different now from the beat I marked.

IT RETURNS TEXT AND WRITES NOTHING. A delta is small by construction - the states are
large and the difference between them is not - so the answer comes back in the reply
rather than as a path to one more file nothing would sweep.

before: is the EARLIER capture and after: the later one. Each is a name as passed to
gcp_capture name:, or a path; a bare name is looked for in the snapshot directory and
then in the running session's own folder, which is where Mark(Capture=true) puts things.

AN EMPTY ANSWER MEANS `IDENTICAL IN WHAT A CAPTURE CAN SEE`, never `identical`. The
delta's own omits: line names what no .gcp carries - execution_state covers timers,
latent actions, montage position and ability cooldowns - and it comes back with the
text so the caveat cannot be separated from the answer.

TWO DIFFERENT FILTERS ARE COMPARED, NOT REFUSED, and this is the one place the two files
need not match. Each absence is judged against the OTHER capture's select:. An entry the
other capture covered and did not hold is new (or gone); an entry it never looked for is
neither, and is dropped. So a filtered capture against a whole one reports what actually
changed inside the filter instead of calling every unselected actor gone. The delta then
carries from_select: naming the earlier scope, and omits: out_of_scope when entries were
in fact dropped for it - the answer is only about where the two scopes overlap and says so.

TWO RUNS ARE REFUSED, not computed. Names generated during play restart with each run,
so the same enemy is BP_Enemy_C_3 in one and BP_Enemy_C_7 in the next, and a whole-file
diff of those reports a death and a spawn that never happened. Across runs, compare the
marks in each run's log - named, ordered, typed - or read the two files. A changed
precision:, baseline:, omits: or always: is refused on the same grounds: each turns a
formatting difference into what looks like a finding.

parameters.name: before
parameters.description: The EARLIER capture: a name as passed to gcp_capture name: (the extension is optional), or a path. It becomes the delta's from: line, which is what makes every absent line in the answer mean `unchanged since this`.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: The LATER capture, in the same spellings as `before`. The delta describes THIS state: its frame, its time and its world are the ones in the answer's envelope, and `before` is only what they are measured against.

tools.name: gcp_run
tools.description:
Start and stop the game, and drive the run over it: attach as its driver, see what it is doing, answer a graph that is waiting on you, ask it to stop.

STARTING AND STOPPING ARE QUEUED, NOT IMMEDIATE. The editor services them on a later tick, so start and stop report what they ASKED for and never that it has happened. Poll mode:"status" - play_starting is the in-between state, and last_start says why a start that never completed did not.

ATTACH FIRST. Nothing else here works without the lease, and that is the safety model rather than ceremony: instrumentation runs in any development build, but only an attached driver may pause or change a running world. A packaged game has no way to attach at all. Starting a game where none is running is the exception, because it disturbs nobody - stopping one is not, because it may be somebody's run or somebody's playtest.

THE LEASE EXPIRES. It is not a connection - this bridge is request/response, so a driver that dies closes nothing and simply stops calling. Renew it while you are working. If it lapses, a graph waiting on you stops waiting and runs on, and anything you had said that the game had not yet acted on is dropped rather than executed later.

mode:"status" is free and needs no lease - start there.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: status (what is running, who holds the lease - needs nothing) | attach (take the lease) | renew (keep it, pass driver:) | detach (let it go) | start (with name: begin recording a session; with no name: press Play. If nothing is playing, a named start does both) | stop (end the game - needs the lease while one is playing) | continue (answer a parked Await, target: its name) | end (ask the run to stop THROUGH the graph, which is not stop) | load (branch: enter another state - target: the capture, entry: the Actor.Event that plays it) | invoke (make the game do something it already knows how to do - target: Actor.Function, args: named arguments. The only verb here the graph did not have to be written to receive, and the one that takes steps: for a whole sequence) | shot (photograph the game right now - target: names the picture. The run's own camera: it lands in the run folder with a Shot record, which gc_render does not - and it shows the player's HUD, because it composites the game's own Slate window) | activate (press a control in that HUD - target: WBP_HUD.StartButton, event: the UMG event when it is not OnClicked. It refuses what a player could not press) | query (ask the running game - what: actor, overlaps or nav_path; reads only, no lease) | spawn (put class: into a game GraphCode started, at: and rotate:, with the lease; it goes when the game ends) | set (one instance-editable property: of actor target: to value:, in a game GraphCode started, with the lease; replies old_value and new_value). follow is not built - see its refusal.

parameters.name: driver
parameters.description: The lease id attach returned. Required by renew and detach, and by anything that ends somebody else's work: stop while a game is playing, and start while a session is already recording. A lease that has already lapsed cannot be renewed - attach again, knowingly, because things may have happened while you were gone.

parameters.name: description
parameters.description: Who you are, for the log and for the other agents sharing this editor. attach only.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: What the command is addressed to: for continue, the parked Await's name; for load, the capture to enter from; for invoke, the `Actor.Function` to call; for activate, the `WBP_HUD.StartButton` to press - the host is optional when only one live widget carries that name. Unused by end.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: invoke only: named arguments, `(Damage=50,Knockback=true)`, in the same value grammar a .gc and a .gcp use - so an object is `obj'/Game/...'`, an enum is backtick-quoted, and a struct nests as `(X=1,Y=2)`. NAMED, never positional, and in any order: a function's parameter order is not something you can read off the game. An omitted parameter is zero, a name the function does not have is refused rather than dropped, and whatever comes back - return value and out parameters together - is written to the log as `observed=`.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description: invoke only, and instead of target: a sequence run INSIDE the game, in order, one step per tick - which is the only place frame-scale order exists, since each round trip is tens of milliseconds against a 16 ms frame. Each step is {act, target, args|entry, after, timeout, comment}. act is continue | end | load | inject | invoke | shot, or omitted - and an omitted act with an `after` IS the wait, because time is an attribute of every step rather than a kind of step. after is {frames:N} | {seconds:S} | {mark:"name"}, exactly one, where mark waits until the GAME says so; a predicate over world state is not offered, because that is an assertion and an assertion belongs in the graph. timeout is seconds for that step, covering its wait and whatever it hands over; without one it inherits the run's limit. A step that refuses stops the batch, and every step writes a record as it begins.

parameters.name: entry
parameters.description: load only, and REQUIRED there: the Actor.Event that opens the new slice, spelled `BP_Harness.grenade`. An entry is an ordinary custom event whose chain starts with Begin Slice, so read the graph for those to find the ones worth calling - the actor holding it is part of its address. A load with no entry is a `gc_play` apply, which already exists; this verb is the one that also PLAYS the state.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: activate only: the UMG event to fire, when it is not OnClicked - OnHovered, OnPressed, or an event dispatcher the widget authored. Only events taking NO parameters can be fired: a parameterised one reports a change the widget has already made, so firing it without making that change lies to the handler.

parameters.name: payload
parameters.description: Anything else the command carries, passed through untouched.

parameters.name: lease_seconds
parameters.description: How long the lease survives without renewal. Default 120. Long enough that ordinary thinking time does not look like a crash.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The session's name, and the folder the run is written to. start only - and it is what says you meant `begin a session` rather than `just press Play`. With a name and no game running you get both, in that order.

parameters.name: slice
parameters.description: The stretch of the game this run starts in. start only, and REQUIRED there - a session cannot open without a slice, because every record in the log lives inside one. Later slices are opened by the graph with Begin Slice.

parameters.name: slice_limit
parameters.description: Seconds of wall clock between pings for that first slice. start only, optional. Each time it comes round the game writes what has changed since you last looked, and it ends nothing - a slow slice and a dead slice look identical from outside, so the clock hands you the question instead of answering it.

parameters.name: session_limit
parameters.description: Seconds of wall clock the whole RUN may take. start only, optional, and this is the one clock here that ends something: when it comes round the graph gets On End Requested(Expired) and a few seconds to capture its last state and close, after which the run is closed for it with result=expired_unhandled. Set it for anything unattended - a graph that loops has no other outer bound. Paused seconds do not count, so parking a run does not spend its budget.

parameters.name: comment
parameters.description: WHY you did this, in the log beside what you did. On start it is the run's reason; on continue, load, invoke, end and shot it is the decision's - what you concluded from the delta you just read, and why this was the next move. Nothing parses it: prose for a person, the way Mark's comment is, while anything you want compared run to run belongs in the game as a value. Optional everywhere, and the field a run has no other way to carry - a log records what an agent did and, without this, never why.

parameters.name: for
parameters.description: Who this run is FOR: ai (the default here - your own test) or player (you are setting a scenario up for a person to play). start only. It decides two things and both matter: an ai run ENDS when your lease lapses, because a run answering nobody's questions should not carry on recording; a player run is never ended that way and is never judged - the reel reports what happened and draws no conclusions. A session a game's own graph opens is a player's by default, so this is only ever the agent claiming one.

parameters.name: request_id
parameters.description: Your own id for this run, written to the log header as request: so you can find it again. start only, optional - and omitting it is what makes an unattended playtest look like one.

parameters.name: what
parameters.description: query only: actor (where target: is, its rotation, velocity, tags, and property: if named) | overlaps (what a sphere of radius: at at: touches) | nav_path (a navigation path path_from: path_to:). Read as the world stands when the call arrives; it changes nothing, so it needs no lease and may read a Play a person started.

parameters.name: property
parameters.description: query what:actor and set: one property of the actor by its variable name; its value comes back as text.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: set only: the new value of property: on actor target:, in the value grammar a .gc uses (5, true, (X=1,Y=2,Z=3), obj'/Game/...'). Only a property a designer could edit on an instance (EditAnywhere / EditInstanceOnly, or a Blueprint variable marked Instance Editable). The reply carries old_value and new_value as the same text query returns; the change lives in the running game only.

parameters.name: clean
parameters.description: shot only: true turns on-screen debug messages (Print String to screen, map warnings) and showdebug off for the one frame the shot captures, and back on after it (or after 5 s if it is never taken). The game's HUD and widgets are left exactly as they are. Echoed as clean:true in the reply and clean=true on the run's Shot record.

parameters.name: at
parameters.description: query what:overlaps only: the sphere's centre, "(x, y, z)" in cm.

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: query what:overlaps only: the sphere's radius in cm.

parameters.name: path_from
parameters.description: query what:nav_path only: where the path starts, "(x, y, z)" in cm.

parameters.name: path_to
parameters.description: query what:nav_path only: where it ends, "(x, y, z)" in cm.

parameters.name: class
parameters.description: spawn only: the actor class, "/Script/Engine.TriggerSphere" or "/Game/Props/BP_Crate.BP_Crate_C".

parameters.name: rotate
parameters.description: spawn only: "(roll, pitch, yaw)" in degrees; at: is where.

tools.name: gcw_ask
tools.description:
THREE FORMS, ONE READ-ONLY SPATIAL ENGINE — they differ only in how you POINT at the subject.
1. {anchor:'Door_01'} asks about a named thing in the open level. Every answer from the open level carries `navigation`: whether a character could stand there, and with reach:'Exit_01' whether one could WALK from the first to the second. Unreachable says how far the route gets, so a wall reads differently from a missing floor.
2. {anchor:'$Crypt'} asks about a region AUTHORED IN THE LEVEL'S .gcw AND NEEDS NO EDITOR: pass level:'/Game/Maps/Dungeon' to say which file, or leave it out to use the open level.
