Also $Crypt.north (a wall), $Crypt.e2@t=25% (a spot along one), $Crypt.p2 (a corner) and $world. NAMES ARE SCOPED TO THEIR REGION, so every room can have a 'north' and asking for one always says which room. A wall answers with its curvature IN UNITS YOU CAN READ — bow depth in cm, radius, swept angle, length along — and with the 'region' that declares it. EVERY ANSWER FROM A FILE CARRIES THAT FILE'S CRACK LIST: two walls lying on top of each other, each finding carrying the gap AS A DISTANCE. Nothing is shared between regions, so two rooms that meet ALWAYS draw two walls there — a gap of 0 is a clean join and 4 cm is a crack somebody will fall through.
3. {capture:'...', view:'main', pixel:[643,388]} reuses the exact saved render camera and raycasts through that integer image pixel without rendering again. Pixel answers include the hit, object, actor-facing distances, containing regions, nearest authored edge, and anchor_gc: a ready-to-paste @anchor with the absolute world xyz and outward surface normal. Pixels are [x,y] from the top-left; the capture records the dimensions.
The anchor and capture forms are mutually exclusive.
THE SOURCE IS CHOSEN FOR YOU AND NAMED IN THE ANSWER - there is no mode parameter. `source` reads 'live' (the open editor, unsaved edits included), 'play' (the running game), 'saved' (the level's .gcw, no world involved) or 'literal' (a typed point, answerable with nothing running at all). Whatever the current state cannot answer carries `not_measured` with the reason instead of a value: NOT MEASURED IS NOT A NO, and a caller must never read 'no level is open' as 'this point is not navigable'. A subject that cannot be RESOLVED is still an error - an actor name with no world names nothing - while a subject that resolves and a facet that cannot be measured is an answer with holes in it.

Where is this, how big is it, which way does it face, and what contains it? GraphCode World's question verb — one named thing in, its facts out.

An anchor is one of three things and they are tried in this order: a literal point '(1500, 500, 0)', a placed actor's internal name, then a Zone: tag path like 'Dungeon/BossRoom'. A name that is an actor AND a zone path carried by some OTHER actor is refused as ambiguous rather than picked for you.

AN ACTOR ANSWERS AS AN ACTOR even when it carries a box. Describing a door gives you a door — bounds and a forward vector — not the zone that door happens to define. The volume comes back either way, so nothing is lost.

CONTAINING ZONES ARE RANKED SMALLEST VOLUME FIRST, and volume is what decides nesting - never the depth of the tag path. A zone tagged 'Dungeon/BossRoom' and dragged outside the dungeon still claims nesting in its name; the boxes are the fact. Where the tag and the geometry disagree BOTH are reported and the geometry is the answer.

CONTAINMENT TESTS THE ACTOR'S ORIGIN, not its bounds, because that is where the write surface records an actor's position. Bounds are reported beside the volume and decide nothing - so what @place puts in a zone is what this finds in it.

'contents' is filled for anything with a volume, tagged or not: a tag decides what can be LISTED, never what can be asked about.

An unsupported shape is NAMED in notes, never dropped. A sphere is not an oriented box, and answering from its bounding box would be confidently wrong at every corner.

LIVE ONLY. Reads the editor's current world, unsaved edits included.

REQUIRES GRAPHCODE WORLD. This tool is advertised on every install so you can see the capability exists; without that product installed the call is REFUSED by name and changes nothing. Core still authors levels completely — it places, diffs and blames actors — using explicit coordinates. What World adds is naming places instead.

parameters.name: anchor
parameters.description: Named form: a literal point, a placed actor's name, a Zone: path, or a $-marked name declared in the level's .gcw ($Crypt, $Crypt.north, $Crypt.e2@t=25%, $Crypt.p2, $world).

parameters.name: reach
parameters.description:
Named form: a SECOND anchor, asking whether a character could walk from the first to this one. Same grammar as anchor - an actor, a Zone: path or a literal point.
TWO DISTANCES, AND YOU RULE ON THEM: straight_line_cm through the air between the two points you named, path_cm along the navmesh between where those two points project onto it. Their ratio is how far around the route goes, and what counts as too far around is the asking AI's call, not this tool's - no threshold is applied anywhere.
A COMPLETE route or nothing. A goal Recast cannot reach answers reachable:false with partial:true and how far the route gets before it stops, which is what tells a wall apart from a missing floor. Both ends are projected onto the mesh first; goal_navigable says whether the far end was standable at all and goal_moved_cm how far it snapped to get there, which is what makes the two distances comparable.
straight_line_cm IS ALWAYS PRESENT - it needs no navmesh. On a level with nothing built this answers the distance and a reach_note saying so, with reachable and path_cm ABSENT: not measured is not unreachable. path_cm is likewise absent, never 0, when no route was found, since 0 is a real length for two points over one polygon.
It is the LEVEL's question, not a character's: it asks one navmesh, the level's default unless mesh: names another. Which areas a particular character may use is a nav filter and belongs to the AI that asks. A $-declared region is refused here - a region's connectivity is not one point's.

parameters.name: mesh
parameters.description:
Named form: WHICH BODY is asking - 'Mouse', 'Humanoid'. Unreal generates a separate navmesh per agent size out of the level's own geometry, so a gap a mouse walks through and a human does not is two different answers about the same two points, and this is how you ask for the one you mean. Applies to navigable, nearest_navigable and the whole reach measurement; `navigation.mesh` always names the one that answered.
The ID is an editor Supported Agent, which is the same string a .gcw writes on the left of a nav() line - `Mouse = nav(type=walkable, radius=8, height=12)` declares the body and mesh:'Mouse' asks the navmesh it generates.
A BODY THIS WORLD DOES NOT DECLARE IS REFUSED and the refusal lists what it declares: you named something that is not there, which is a different thing from a level nobody has built yet. That one answers not_measured and keeps the direct distance.
Omit it for the level's default agent, which is what this always asked. It is NOT a nav filter: whether a character may swim or use a ladder is who is asking, not what the ground is, and that belongs to the AI.

parameters.name: against
parameters.description:
Named form: answer RELATIVE to this second anchor instead of in world coordinates. Same grammar as anchor - an actor, a Zone: path or a literal point.
The answer comes back as @anchor and @facing lines you paste into a .gc and adjust, in BOTH spellings: forward/right/up for rows and grids, bearing/offset for rings. Neither is the default, because they survive different edits - a ring measured in bearing follows the reference when it turns and a row measured in forward/right does not.
This is what stops an author subtracting two positions by hand, which is the coordinate arithmetic the placement grammar exists to remove.
Measured midpoint to midpoint, so an off-centre pivot cannot skew it. A percentage is not answered - it would remeasure a standing actor the day somebody resizes the reference - so the reference's own half-extent comes back instead.

parameters.name: world
parameters.description:
Named form: 'editor' (the default) or 'play'. 'play' asks about the RUNNING game, so a spatial question can be asked mid-session - where the boss is relative to the player, what a spawned actor is standing in. Same word gcp_capture takes.
'play' refuses when nothing is playing rather than falling back: the two worlds are copies of each other, so an editor answer to a play question looks entirely plausible and is about a level nobody is playing.

parameters.name: level
parameters.description: Declared form only: which level's .gcw to read, e.g. '/Game/Maps/Dungeon'. Defaults to the open level; with it, no editor is needed at all.

parameters.name: capture
parameters.description: Pixel form: capture id returned by gc_render. The existing image is reused.

parameters.name: view
parameters.description: Pixel form: view name inside the capture.

parameters.name: pixel
parameters.description: Pixel form: integer [x,y] from the image's top-left. Required with capture.

parameters.name: trace_channel
parameters.description: Pixel form: trace channel such as Visibility or Camera; mutually exclusive with object_types.

parameters.name: object_types
parameters.description: Pixel form: object types to hit, e.g. ['WorldStatic']; mutually exclusive with trace_channel.

parameters.name: max_distance
parameters.description: Pixel form: maximum ray distance in centimetres.

parameters.name: ignore_actors
parameters.description: Pixel form: actor names or labels for the trace to pass through.

tools.name: get_level_actors
tools.description:
RETIRED 2026-08-10 (queue row 11h). Use unreal_gc_read kind:"level", which returns every actor with its transform, its authored properties and its components as one text document - the same document unreal_gc_apply writes back.

THE PAGINATION AND THE TWO FILTERS ARE GONE ON PURPOSE: the answer is text, so grep it. Both filters were a case-insensitive SUBSTRING match, the same defect T7 removed from delete_actors, so name_filter:'a' matched most of a level.

IN A PARTITIONED LEVEL the actors are not in that document: each is its own package, so enumerate them with unreal_gc_search kind:"asset" scoped to the map's __ExternalActors__ folder, then unreal_gc_read the ones you want.

Call it to get the full sentence.

parameters.name: class_filter
parameters.description: Optional class name to filter actors (e.g., 'StaticMeshActor', 'PointLight')

parameters.name: name_filter
parameters.description: Optional substring to filter actors by name

parameters.name: include_hidden
parameters.description: Include hidden actors in results

parameters.name: brief
parameters.description: Return brief info (name/label/class only). Set false for full transform data (default: true)

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum number of actors to return (1-1000, default: 25)

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of actors to skip for pagination

tools.name: get_output_log
tools.description:
Retrieve recent entries from the Unreal Engine output log.

Essential for debugging and monitoring engine activity. Use filters to focus on specific issues.

Common filters:
- 'Error' - Show only errors
- 'Warning' - Show warnings
- 'LogTemp' - Show UE_LOG(LogTemp, ...) output
- 'LogBlueprint' - Blueprint-related messages
- 'LogScript' - Script compilation messages
- 'LogActor' - Actor lifecycle messages

Returns: Array of log entries with timestamp, category, verbosity, and message.

parameters.name: lines
parameters.description: Number of recent lines to return (default: 100, max: 1000)

parameters.name: filter
parameters.description: Optional category or text filter (e.g., 'Warning', 'Error', 'LogTemp')

tools.name: get_script_history
tools.description:
Retrieve history of previously executed scripts.

Use this to understand what scripts have been run in this session. Helpful for context restoration and debugging.

Returns for each script:
- Script type (cpp, python, console)
- Filename (for file-based scripts)
- Description (from @Description header)
- Execution timestamp
- Success/failure status
- Error message (if failed)

Note: Full script content is NOT returned for security - only metadata.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Number of recent scripts to return (default: 10, max: 50)

tools.name: material
tools.description:
RETIRED IN FULL 2026-08-09 (row 11j). This tool writes nothing, and every operation answers by name with the call that replaced it.

Where the work went:
  set_skeletal_mesh_material  unreal_gc_apply block:"materials", on kind:skeletal_mesh
      or kind:static_mesh. THE SLOT IS KEYED BY NAME now, not by index —
      Body = obj'/Game/Materials/MI_Oak.MI_Oak' — and static meshes are covered,
      which this tool never did.
  create_material_instance    unreal_gc_apply create:true, parent: naming the parent material
  set_material_parameters     unreal_gc_apply block:"parameters"
  get_material_info           unreal_gc_read

      OverrideMaterials on the actor's mesh component

The last one to go was set_skeletal_mesh_material, and its exception was honest while it lasted: a mesh had no GraphCode kind, so there was no document to state a slot in. Row 11j minted the kind rather than re-reading the claim.

parameters.name: operation
parameters.description: Any former material operation. All five are retired; each answers with the unreal_gc_apply block or unreal_gc_read call that replaced it.

tools.name: move_actor
tools.description:
RETIRED 2026-08-10 (queue row 11h). Use unreal_gc_apply kind:"level" block:"actors" and write @placement on that actor's entry: Location, Rotation and Scale are ONE specifier, so a move, a turn and a rescale are one write rather than three calls.

An actor that lives in its own package is unreal_gc_apply kind:"external_actor" against that package, through the same writer and the same specifier.

Call it to get the full sentence.

parameters.name: actor_name
parameters.description: The name of the actor to transform

parameters.name: location
parameters.description: New location {x, y, z}. Omit to keep current.

parameters.name: rotation
parameters.description: New rotation {pitch, yaw, roll}. Omit to keep current.

parameters.name: scale
parameters.description: New scale {x, y, z}. Omit to keep current.

parameters.name: relative
parameters.description: If true: location and rotation values are ADDED to current transform; scale values are MULTIPLIED with current scale. If false: all values replace current transform.

tools.name: open_level
tools.description:
Open, create, save, or list level maps in the Unreal Editor.

Actions:
- 'open': Load an existing map by asset path (e.g., '/Game/Maps/MyLevel')
- 'new': Create a new blank map, or from a template if 'template' is specified
- 'save_as': Save the current level to a specified path (e.g., '/Game/Maps/MyLevel')
- 'list_templates': List all available map templates
- 'load_region': Load a World Partition editor region in the current map
- 'list_regions': List the current map's registered editor regions
- 'unload_region': Release one editor region by region_id

Region actions do not open or save a map and are refused during Play/Simulate. Loaded regions remain available to gc_read and gc_render until unloaded or the map closes. They use Unreal's editor loaders, not runtime streaming or Data Layer activation.

'open' and 'new' REFUSE while any loaded map package has unsaved changes, naming it. The engine would unload it, which opens a modal dialog no tool can answer: the call would hang until it timed out, and dismissing the dialog leaves the package loaded, which the engine treats as a fatal world leak. Save or discard first — neither is done for you.

Returns: The loaded map name and world info, save result, or template list.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: Action: 'open', 'new', 'save_as', 'list_templates', 'load_region', 'list_regions', or 'unload_region'

parameters.name: bounds

tools.name: open_sound
tools.description:
Hand back a sound's actual audio, so it can be LISTENED to rather than read about.

This is the counterpart of kind:sound_wave, not a substitute for it. The sidecar makes every
decision about a sound reviewable as text — compression, looping, attenuation, sound class —
and none of those answers whether the sound is RIGHT. A compression type is a claim about
audio. This is the audio.

TWO OUTPUTS FROM ONE CALL. A .wav is written under Saved/GraphCode/sounds (playable by a
person, and it outlives the conversation) AND the same bytes come back as an inline audio
content block. Sounds over 4 MB return the path alone and say so — the file is always
written, so nothing is lost, only not inlined.

The audio is the IMPORTED samples, losslessly: 16-bit PCM straight from the editor payload
in a canonical RIFF/WAVE container. It is not a re-compression and not the cooked platform
format, so what you hear is what was imported.

Only a USoundWave has imported audio. A MetaSound is a graph evaluated at runtime and a Sound
Cue holds no imported audio of its own. Use gc_render kind:audio to evaluate these through the mixer.

The internal render route returns a bounded WAV preview or records the running world mix, with original levels and peak/RMS measurements.

Returns: the wav as audio content, plus sample rate, channel count, duration and the path.

parameters.name: render
parameters.description: Render through the mixer instead of exporting imported samples; gc_render kind:audio owns this route.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Audio render: asset for an isolated preview, live for the running Play/Simulate world mix.

parameters.name: seconds
parameters.description: Audio render duration, 0.1 to 30 seconds; default 5.

parameters.name: parameters
parameters.description: Asset render: named float, boolean and string audio parameters, such as {Activity:1, Rate:3}.

parameters.description: Poll a pending audio-render capture. Internal to gc_render's wait.

parameters.description: Absolute .wav path to write instead of the default under Saved/GraphCode/sounds. The inline audio is returned either way.

parameters.name: inline_audio
parameters.description: Return the audio inline as well as writing it (default: true). Set false to write the file and keep the reply small — useful when exporting several sounds, or when you only want a person to be able to play it.

tools.name: open_widget
tools.description:
Run an Editor Utility Widget, so its panel is in front of the user — and so gc_invoke has something to press.

THIS IS THE OPEN HALF OF A PAIR. gc_invoke activates a widget by its authored name, but only inside an instance somebody is already looking at; it addresses live objects, not the asset. Its refusal used to end in 'for an Editor Utility Widget, run it', which no tool could do. This does it: open the panel here, then press its buttons with gc_invoke.

ALREADY OPEN IS A SUCCESS AND SPAWNS NOTHING. The point of this verb is that the thing ends up in front of the user, so a call that finds it already there says which instance is open and stops. A second tab would only hand gc_invoke an ambiguity this call had created.

EXISTING IS NOT OPEN, THOUGH. Closing an Editor Utility Widget's tab leaves its widget object alive in /Engine/Transient until the next garbage collection, so a leftover from a panel somebody already closed is stepped past rather than counted as open — otherwise a request for a panel would be answered by naming one that is not on screen. Leftovers are reported as closed_instances_ignored.

THE HANDLE COMES BACK READY TO USE. `instance` is the same name gc_invoke resolves and the same one it prints, so it can be typed straight into gc_invoke's `instance` when more than one is open.

ONLY AN EDITOR UTILITY WIDGET CAN BE RUN. A plain Widget Blueprint has no editor panel — it is refused by name, saying so, rather than by a cast that fails without a reason. So is an asset that was never compiled, because an uncompiled Blueprint has no class to instance.

THE PANEL IS NOT INERT: Event Construct runs when the tab spawns, and on an Editor Utility Widget that is Blueprint that can do anything — the same warning gc_invoke carries about its buttons.

Returns: whether it was already open, the instance handle, the tab id, and the window.

parameters.name: asset_path
parameters.description: The Editor Utility Widget to run (e.g. '/Game/Blueprints/EUW_RoomBuilder').

tools.name: run_console_command

Console commands provide access to engine features, debugging tools, and configuration.

Useful commands:
- 'stat fps' - Show FPS counter
- 'stat unit' - Show frame timing
- 'show collision' - Toggle collision visualization
- 'show bounds' - Toggle bounding box display
- 'r.SetRes 1920x1080' - Set resolution
- 'slomo 0.5' - Slow motion (PIE only)
- 'ce MyEvent' - Call custom event

Note: Some commands only work in Play-In-Editor (PIE) mode.

Returns: Command execution confirmation.

tools.name: struct
tools.description:
RETIRED IN FULL 2026-08-09. Every operation answers by name with the call that replaced it.
A Blueprint struct is a user_struct .gc document now, and a native C++ USTRUCT is a
reflection question rather than an asset one.

Where the work went:
  add_member / modify_member / rename_member / change_member_type / set_member_default /
  set_member_tooltip / set_member_metadata / reorder_member / remove_member /
  update_members      unreal_gc_apply block:"properties". That block IS the member list, in
      order, and omission deletes. A rename keeps the member GUID, so it still repairs its
      references rather than orphaning them.
  set_description     unreal_gc_apply block:"settings"
  create              unreal_gc_apply create:true with a whole user_struct document
  list                unreal_gc_search kind:"asset"
      scope:"/Script/Engine.UserDefinedStruct"
  get_info            TWO successors, because it answered two questions. A Blueprint struct
      is unreal_gc_read. A NATIVE C++ USTRUCT such as /Script/CoreUObject.Vector is
      unreal_gc_describe type_path:"<path>", with include_native under the same name.

What outlives the operations, because it is about the ASSET: a member's stable identity is
its GUID rather than its display name, native C++ structs are readable but never editable,
and the referencer gate is unchanged — a type change or a removal with live references
still needs allow_breaking_changes:true, and dry_run:true still prices it first.

tools.name: task_cancel
tools.description:
Cancel an async task.

For pending tasks: Immediately marks the task as cancelled.
For running tasks: Requests cancellation - the task will be cancelled at the next opportunity.
For completed tasks: Returns an error (cannot cancel completed tasks).

Note: Some tools may not check for cancellation during execution, so running tasks may still complete before the cancellation takes effect.

parameters.name: task_id
parameters.description: Task ID to cancel

tools.name: task_list
tools.description:
List YOUR async tasks in the queue.

Returns task IDs, tool names, status, and timing information for the tasks this MCP client submitted. Parallel agents share one editor, and a task belongs to whoever submitted it, so another client's tasks are not listed here and cannot be polled, read or cancelled from here.

The queue-wide totals are still reported, so you can see when the editor is busy with work that is not yours.

THE CALL TO MAKE IS unreal_info include:"tasks", which is this list plus those totals; add task_id: for one task, and include_completed is spelled `finished` there because a call already carrying include: must not have two words called include in it.

Options:
- include_completed: Whether to include finished tasks (default: true)
- limit: Maximum number of tasks to return (default: 50)

parameters.name: include_completed
parameters.description: Include completed/failed/cancelled tasks (default: true)

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum number of tasks to return (default: 50)

tools.name: task_result
tools.description:
Get the result of a completed async task.

Returns the full result data including success/failure status, message, and output data.
Only works for tasks in a terminal state (completed, failed, cancelled, timed_out).

THE CALL TO MAKE IS unreal_info include:"tasks" task_id:"<id>": it reads the task in any state and follows through to this result once there is one, so the error below is unreachable from there. This name is the bridge's own collection endpoint.

parameters.name: task_id
parameters.description: Task ID returned from task_submit

tools.name: task_status
tools.description:
Get the status of an async task.

Returns the current status, progress, and timing information for a task.

Status values:
- 'pending': Task is queued but not yet started
- 'running': Task is currently executing
- 'completed': Task finished successfully
- 'failed': Task encountered an error
- 'cancelled': Task was cancelled
- 'timed_out': Task exceeded its timeout

THE CALL TO MAKE IS unreal_info include:"tasks" task_id:"<id>", which answers this while the task runs AND carries the full result once it has finished — one door, so there is no wrong one to pick. This name is the bridge's own polling endpoint.

parameters.name: task_id
parameters.description: Task ID returned from task_submit

tools.name: task_submit
tools.description:
TRANSPORT. The MCP bridge submits every non-read-only tool through here on your behalf, then polls and collects the result, and hands you the answer as one ordinary call. You are not meant to call this.

THERE IS NOTHING TO OPT INTO: a gc_apply, gc_sync, gc_import or version restore is already queued for you, and the queue's single exclusive lane is already how parallel agents take turns on one editor. Just call the tool that does the work. The bridge waits up to 300s for the answer rather than the 30s per-request timeout, and a call still running then hands back its task_id instead of being cancelled. The editor lets it run for the call's own budget: in seconds, or a day when there is none.

To see what the queue is doing — yours, and the totals that say whether your write is waiting behind another agent — that is unreal_info include:"tasks", with task_id: for one of them. To stop one, unreal_execute mode:"cancel".

Submitting BY NAME is refused nothing and gains nothing: the payload is a tool name plus opaque parameters, so no schema can check it, and it would give every capability a second door with no help, no validation and no refusals of its own.

parameters.name: tool_name
parameters.description: Name of the MCP tool to execute asynchronously

parameters.name: params
parameters.description: Parameters to pass to the tool (same as calling the tool directly)

parameters.name: timeout_ms
parameters.description: Custom timeout in milliseconds, 1000 to 86400000 (one day); default 120000 = 2 minutes

parameters.name: priority
parameters.description: Whole number 1 (background) to 5 (highest); default 2. Among queued tasks the highest starts first; it never interrupts a running task or reorders one client's own calls. A waiting task gains one level every 120 s, up to 4.

tools.name: ui_render
tools.description:
Paint one Widget Blueprint off-screen at up to eight viewport sizes and report both the picture and the layout that produced it. Structural equivalence cannot see overlap, clipping, an unreadable contrast or an anchor that is only correct at one size; this can.
Each viewport returns the PNG's path on disk, the root's desired and allotted size, and every widget in the tree with its painted position, size, desired size and visibility - read off the widgets after the paint, not measured from the image. Warnings call out a visible widget that painted at zero size, one that painted wholly outside the viewport, a NaN desired size, and an image where every pixel is transparent because nothing painted at all.
Sizes are PIXELS. dpi_scale 0 - the default - applies the project's own DPI curve for that size, which is what the shipped game will do; the layout size the widget actually sees is reported back as root_allotted_size.
Viewports take either spelling: "1920x1080", "phone:390x844", or {name, width, height, dpi_scale}.
With exactly one viewport the image comes back inline as well as on disk. With several, only the paths come back - eight images is megabytes of response - so read the PNG files you care about, or re-call with the single size you want to look at.
Nothing is compiled, dirtied or saved: the preview is an instance of the already-compiled class, and the asset's dirty flag is checked before and after. Requires an editor with a GPU - under -nullrhi it refuses and says so rather than returning a blank image.
source:"live" answers a DIFFERENT question: not what the asset would look like, but what the instance somebody already has open looks like right now. It photographs that window with Slate and reports each widget's current visibility, enabled and hit-testable state, focus, geometry and displayed text - so a panel that says 'not refreshed' as a fresh preview and '1 file(s) need attention' in the open tab stops being indistinguishable. Read-only and passive: no construction, no tick, no handler, no synthesised input, and the user's mouse is never taken. Needs the widget actually shown; when it is open but not in a window the state still comes back with captured:false. viewports and design_time do not apply and are refused rather than ignored.
LIVE POSITIONS ARE DESKTOP COORDINATES - where you would point at the thing - and are converted, because Slate's own 'absolute' position for a widget in a window is window space and equals the screen only when the window sits at the origin. window_x/window_y come back beside them if you need that offset. A preview has no screen, so its geometry stays in viewport space.

parameters.name: widget_blueprint_path
parameters.description: Widget Blueprint asset path, e.g. /Game/UI/WBP_Login

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: 'preview' (default) renders a fresh off-screen instance; 'live' observes an instance that is already open.

parameters.name: instance
parameters.description: source:'live' only. Which open instance, by its name. Omit when there is one; several without it are refused with the list.

parameters.name: viewports
parameters.description: 1-8 sizes in pixels: "1920x1080", "phone:390x844", or {name, width, height, dpi_scale}. Defaults to one 1280x720. Those four keys are the whole object and a fifth is refused by name: this route paints with Slate, so a scene view's camera or view_mode has nothing here to reach and is refused rather than discarded.

parameters.name: design_time
parameters.description: Construct the way the Designer does, with PreConstruct and preview values - which includes PAINTING Collapsed and Hidden widgets, exactly as the Designer does, so the image always shows the MAXIMAL row of a show-only-when-needed UI. Each one comes back with painted_despite_visibility:true and a note; visibility and visible are the AUTHORED answer in both modes, so read those rather than the picture. false constructs the runtime instance instead, which honours Collapsed - but a widget whose content is filled in after construction can come back as an empty frame there, so check root_desired_size before trusting it.

parameters.name: inline_image
parameters.description: 'auto' (inline only when there is one viewport), 'none', or a viewport name.

parameters.name: write_files
parameters.description: Write each viewport's PNG under Saved/UnrealAIBridge/renders. Off returns geometry only.

parameters.name: max_widgets
parameters.description: Per-viewport cap on returned widget geometry rows, most deeply nested last. 0 omits them. Default 200.

tools.name: ui_search
tools.description:
Search the widget classes this editor can actually construct, by name or by what they do. The index is Unreal's own reflection - class name, display name, palette category, keywords and tooltip - so a plugin's widget and a project Widget Blueprint are found the same way a built-in one is, with no per-class tool code anywhere.
Each result carries the exact class identity to write, a paste-ready skeleton showing the containment endpoints the class really has, and describe_ir, one statement ready for gc_describe block:"widgets" ir:. Panels show braces; a named-slot host shows its slot blocks.
Pass asset_path to filter by the target's own context: this project's UMG palette settings, whether editor-only widgets are admissible, and the asset's own class, which cannot contain itself. Pass parent_class to be told what that parent can hold, and refused outright if it can hold nothing.
This is lexical metadata search, not an embedding guess: matched_terms and unmatched_terms are both reported, classes filtered as unconstructible are counted with their reasons rather than silently dropped, and an ambiguous short class name is returned as a full path.
Workflow: ui_search -> gc_describe block:"widgets" -> gc_apply block:"widgets" dry_run:true -> gc_apply. Only the first step is this family; ui_describe and ui_apply are retired and gc_* is the route.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: What the widget is called or what it should do. Omit to browse every constructible class.

parameters.name: widget_blueprint_path
parameters.description: Target Widget Blueprint, for project-settings and self-containment filtering.

parameters.name: parent_class
parameters.description: Prospective parent class token or path. Reports what it can hold; refuses if it holds nothing.

parameters.name: panels_only
parameters.description: Only classes that can contain other widgets, through children or named slots.

parameters.name: include_unusable
parameters.description: Include abstract, deprecated, experimental and settings-hidden classes, each with its reason.

parameters.description: Include asset-backed User Widgets from the asset registry, loaded or not.

parameters.description: Zero-based result offset (default 0).
